Review: The iPhone 18 Pro is Apple’s coolest smartphone (but only literally)

Ars Technica September 25, 2026

Better thermals and battery life make this iterative update nicer to use.

As Apple’s Tim Cook era draws to a close, we’re seeing more experimentation with the iPhone’s design than we’ve seen in a long time, but you wouldn’t know it from the iPhone 18 Pro. This absurdly fast, full-featured handset might be eclipsed by the hype around the iPhone Duo this year, but it’s still just as good as its immediate predecessor.

Of course, not too much has changed since the iPhone 17 Pro. There’s the new variable aperture and other camera controls for those who want to get granular with their mobile photography, a welcome addition given the iPhone’s reputation for inflexibly opinionated computational photography.

Beyond that, though, all the most important changes are under the hood: a new chip, better battery life, and much-improved thermals that both give the phone better sustained performance and make it cooler to the touch in many situations.

I think we’re seeing something of a transition for the “Pro” iPhones. They may still be the flagships in a sense, but Apple is at least for now saving its flashier design ideas for new products like last year’s iPhone Air or this year’s iPhone Duo.

The Pro phones aren’t the sexy, cool ones right now; they’re the everything-and-the-kitchen-sink, cover-for-every-kind-of-obsessive-user workhorses. I think that’s a great space for them to occupy, and this year’s iteration is no exception.

The iPhone 18 Pro mostly looks and feels like last year’s flagship. It’s a function-over-form design (at least compared to something like the iPhone Air) with good materials.

I’m not normally one to care too much about color in these phones. For my personal phone, I’ve always just grabbed whatever was closest to black. (Apple says this year’s black is the blackest yet, of course.) But I have to admit the new burgundy color of my review unit is appealing, even though it’s quite the fingerprint magnet, in a long tradition for iPhones.

The main design difference this time around is a smaller Dynamic Island, that cut-out at the top of the screen that houses the front-facing camera and sensors. Apple has achieved this by moving the IR camera underneath the OLED panel, now in the top-left corner of the screen.

A new pixel arrangement allows infrared light to pass through in that spot, while the pixels in this region operate at twice the brightness to compensate for lower density, so there’s little visible effect on the image on the display. You can tell there’s something subtly going on in that corner if you know what to look for and look closely, but I don’t think most people will notice.

As I wrote when the Dynamic Island was first introduced, the way Apple combines the per-pixel brightness and absolute blacks of the OLED panel with creative software to turn what should be something of an albatross—a big, chunky hole in the screen—into an appealing feature by displaying live activities and other information around the sensors is one of the company’s more impressive design ideas in recent years. The execution is excellent and remains so.

Now, that hole is less big and chunky, making it sensible for Apple to now show up to three live activities at once in the region, not just one. The middle one has more information, while those on the left and right are basically dots with just enough to tell you something useful.

It’s also now possible to show more information on a second live activity when there are just two being displayed; I found this even more appealing than showing three live activities.

This isn’t enough of a reason to upgrade from an earlier Dynamic Island phone, of course, but it has made a good feature a little bit better.

Let’s talk specs, performance, and the main story with this phone—heat management. For most specs, this is last year’s iPhone 17 Pro. But the A20 Pro chip has some improvements that make this one of the more notable performance steps in a while.

First up is the new A20 Pro chip. Apple has gone from a 3-nanometer process node in the A19 Pro to 2 nm here. It has a 6-core CPU with four efficiency cores and two performance cores—nothing new there. The GPU has seven cores, each with a Neural Accelerator that Apple says helps improve GPU-based AI workloads. (There’s hardware-accelerated ray-tracing support, too, though few games or apps utilize it.)

Also for local AI features (which are a big emphasis for this year’s iOS 27), there’s the dual 16-core Neural Engine.

Apple also says the A20 Pro has “the widest memory interface ever shipped in an iPhone” (naturally) with 50 percent more bandwidth. Based on what Apple has said so far about it, that seems to be mainly to improve AI performance. I’m speculating here, but given that Apple Intelligence and Siri AI features work fine on other recent iPhones, I imagine that’s a bit of padding to enable support for future AI features that won’t work on the 16 Pro or 17 Pro.

Unsurprisingly, and as the 3DMark benchmark chart below shows, that could make a big difference in graphics performance, too. It’s not like many people were complaining about the 17 Pro’s frame rates in Genshin Impact or Diablo Immortal, but hey, they definitely won’t be now.

The chip has been re-architected in a couple of ways. New chip packaging promises improved heat management, thanks in part to a design that puts the system-on-a-chip next to the memory instead of stacked on top of it.

The most notable improvement is arguably a larger vapor chamber. Last year’s iPhone 17 Pro introduced the vapor chamber as an additional cooling measure, meant to help the phone sustain good performance for longer and distribute heat more sensibly. A copper material on the display plate helps keep the display cooler, too.

Apple promises up to 40 percent better sustained performance compared to last year’s Pro and up to 100 percent better than the iPhone 16 Pro before that. That’s neat, but sustained performance wasn’t a big problem for most users before. The main benefit is that the phone feels cooler and is less likely to overheat.

In my view, the better thermals are the most welcome addition to the iPhone 18 Pro. Many of us who have tried to use our phone as a GPS on the car dashboard on a hot summer day know the frustration of features shutting down when the phone goes into crisis heat-management mode. And even in normal use, like during online gaming or web browsing while streaming video, iPhones from a couple of years ago or earlier tended to get quite hot.

It’s been quite cool and overcast in Chicago this week—fall is here at last—so I haven’t been able to test the former of those extreme cases, but I’ve used the phone enough to be able to report that there is noticeable improvement in the more day-to-day scenarios. It still gets warm in some situations, like when I read the 3DMark benchmarks, but most of the time, it subjectively seems better than a couple of generations ago.

It’s normally hard to notice the absence of a problem, but my own iPhone 16 Pro has gotten hot frequently enough over the past couple of years that the contrast has been real and felt.

We’ll leave the camera specs to the cameras section of the review, but there are a couple of other spec changes worth noting.

First off, there are further battery life improvements. Apple has long used offline video playback as one of its measures, and it says the iPhone 18 Pro can offer up to 36 hours of that on a single charge, compared to 33 for its predecessor. (It’s up to 45 for the 18 Pro Max and 39 for the 17 Pro Max.)

Subjectively, I’m impressed by the battery performance. My personal daily driver is an iPhone 16 Pro Max, which is currently sitting at 86 percent maximum capacity per Apple’s battery health panel in the Settings app.

I have no complaints; I charge it for about an hour in the morning, then do whatever I want with it (other than maybe intensive 3D gaming) with the brightness cranked up until the next morning, when I charge again.

I noticed the iPhone 18 Pro showing higher percentages when I wake up in the morning than my 16 Pro Max with similar use, which is impressive for a smaller phone—even though my 160 Pro Max’s battery has aged a bit.

In terms of other additions, Apple has put its proprietary C2 cellular modem in the 18 Pro, which uses less energy than the Qualcomm modem in the 17 Pro, so that’s part of the battery life story here, too.

And if you’re inclined to charge wirelessly rather than with a USB-C cable, the iPhone 18 Pro has wireless charging at up to 25 W.

If you’ve read my iPhone reviews before, you may recall that I am not a photography geek. This is not the review to read if you want a deep dive on optics or how well this thing will work in a professional photo shoot. (I’ll leave it to more skilled and knowledgeable people to assess the phone from that perspective, as there are already many such reviews out there.)

I’m a point-and-shooter. Thanks to both new hardware features and developments in computational photography, that’s actually where some of the more interesting and fastest-moving developments have been happening in the iPhone and its Android competitors over the past few years.

Sure, the iPhone 18 Pro is “pro” in the sense that it will be used by content creators and others who approach snapping photos or capturing videos far more seriously and creatively than I do. But really, it’s the phone that sometimes lets non-pros like me produce quasi-pro-looking images despite ourselves.

Take the new variable aperture feature, which got the most fanfare when this handset was announced. The ability to tweak this setting manually is a niche proposal, really; many people will rarely, if ever, touch it. That said, it adjusts automatically based on what’s in the scene by default, so in many cases, even folks like me will get slightly better photos.

There’s also Photographic Styles 3, the latest generation of Apple’s set of non-destructive presets for the general appearance and vibe of the photos you’re taking. Think Instagram filters, but less blunt force. Previously, Photographic Styles were basically just color balance settings, but Photographic Styles 3 allows for texture tweaks, too.

This includes four texture options: film, glow, soft skin, and standard. These options—especially the film one—allow the iPhone’s built-in Camera app to compete with some third-party apps that try to give photos warmer, more film-like looks. I won’t say it’s enough to make everyone drop those alternatives, but it’s good to have more options for those who are loyal to the main app.

Apart from these and a few other minor tweaks, it’s the same triple-48 MP rear camera system that we reviewed in last year’s iPhone 17 Pro, paired with the same front-facing 18 MP camera.

With the variable aperture and the other custom camera controls that are now accessible in the built-in Camera app (all the others are available on other recent iPhones), Apple has finally done plenty to address long-standing complaints that iPhone cameras were a little too opinionated for some users’ tastes.

Yes, these new features enable better point-and-shoot photos in some narrow situations, but user control seems to be the main pitch for the cameras this year.

This was Tim Cook’s last year as Apple’s CEO, and the iPhone 18 Pro is the quintessential iPhone of the Cook era: practical, pricey, loaded with features to cover ever more niche edge cases, and not especially bold in its design or ambitions—all to a high standard of quality.

This is the formula that has made it the world’s most popular flagship smartphone. There’s nothing wrong with that formula. Its recent predecessors were all great phones, and this one is, too.

But we all know the era of buying a new smartphone every year or two to enjoy amazing new features has passed. (Which is also great, by the way—for our pocketbooks, for the environment, for a whole bunch of reasons.) If you have an iPhone 17 Pro, there’s little reason to upgrade. Yes, we’re seeing some notable performance improvement year over year here, but I don’t think too many of us were complaining about the A17 Pro’s performance to begin with.

My daily driver is an iPhone 16 Pro, and I won’t be pulling the trigger this year, either. In fact, I think you’re still in great shape with your iPhone 15 Pro, if that’s what you have, provided your battery is still holding up.

Go further back than that, though, and all these little things start to accumulate into something enticing. That’s where we’re at, and that’s where we’ve been for a while now.

I wouldn’t go so far as to say the modern flagship smartphone is perfect in all respects; Apple and its competitors still find small ways to refine it and up the ante for specific types of users year after year, and I expect that to continue. And last year’s base iPhone 17 is still more than good enough for almost everybody.

But after almost two decades of competition and iteration, it’s at least directionally perfect. The basics are all here, and they don’t need to change. I wish the price hadn’t risen, but I suppose that’s the reality we live in right now.

If you want something new and flashy to impress your friends or to satisfy your brain with a novel experience, hold out for the iPhone Duo next month or venture into the slightly more energetic Android market. But if you just want a good phone that leverages all the latest technological progress without overdoing it for attention or progress’ sake, the iPhone Pro line is a good fit.

Xtracycle’s Swoop ASM e-bike brings an automatic transmission to cargo bikes

Ars Technica Long form August 26, 2026

A steel frame cargo bike with a unique twist: You can let it choose your gear.

The Velotric Discover M e-bike we reviewed earlier this year had a feature I found somewhat annoying: It would sporadically block much of the display with an alert telling me I should be in a different gear. While the implementation bugged me, the concept made a certain degree of sense; most e-bikes now know your cadence, how much torque you’re generating, and how that power is being translated into speed. That’s everything you need to know to determine an optimal gear.

Somewhere in the back of my mind, I thought, “If you’re so smart, why don’t you just shift for me?”

I was completely unaware that Shimano had already developed a system that did exactly that. And for the past few weeks, I’ve been using it on a $4,500 cargo bike from Xtracycle called the Swoop ASM that let me see what it’s like to hand control of my gears to an electronic brain.

The short answer is that the electronics on the Swoop really are smart enough to figure out when it should be shifting. But the system is less adept at the actual shifting process, making for rides that are less smooth than they could be when it’s active. But you can shut that feature off, and the Swoop will shine as a fantastic cargo bike.

Xtracycle got its start providing cargo trailers for mountain bikes and then branched into dedicated cargo bikes. The Swoop ASM is a long-tail cargo bike with what’s called a mullet setup: a larger tire up front and a smaller one in back. The small wheel is designed to help keep the weight held by the large rear rack a bit closer to the road. It also has a front suspension to help cushion the ride.

Notably, the bike is built with steel tubes. Most manufacturers’ lineups use a mix of either carbon fiber and aluminum because those two materials can be made into the exact same shape, simplifying manufacturing. But other materials still have their fans, as they can offer distinct combinations of weight, stiffness, and vibration dissipation.

I haven’t owned a steel tube bike since the 1990s, but the Swoop was a good reminder of why it still has its fans. It’s relatively lightweight (just under 70 lbs/31 kg) for its size, its ride is very comfortable, and it was surprisingly responsive when I stood in the pedals to accelerate away from stops. Despite its highly specialized geometry, the Swoop felt like a fundamentally good bicycle.

There are limits to how well a single frame size can adapt to different body sizes, but Xtracycle does its best to widen the comfort window. It includes a double-telescoping seat post to maximize the seat-pedal distance flexibility. There’s also a quick release on the front handlebar clamp, making it easy to tweak the angle where the grips meet your hands. I found settings that were relatively comfortable but still a bit short of ideal for my 6-plus-foot (188 cm) frame—even with the seat post at its recommended maximum, I could touch the toes of both of my feet down while seated.

Beyond that, plenty of nice touches make this a solid cargo bike. These include protective covers for the rear wheel and chain to keep clothing and limbs from accidentally getting entangled. A robust U-shaped kickstand keeps the bike stable even if you park it when fully loaded, and there’s a front cargo rack that can hold some baggage.

The rear rack can be outfitted with a large range of accessories; mine came with the default setup meant for carrying passengers. This means footrests extending out at the level of the rear hub and two handgrip bars running parallel to the bench seating. But remove a soft cover, and the metal beneath reveals a series of slots that allow a wide variety of attachments to be fitted into place.

You can also use one of Xtracycle’s bag attachments in this setup; I was provided one that ran the full length of the rear attachment and held a fair amount of cargo. Adding a second would have handled all of my typical shopping needs. (While having only one bag might seem awkward, the bike performed very well with everything I was carrying loaded on one side.)

The only problem is that this hardware makes the rear wheel extremely difficult to reach. I struggled to lock the back tire to anything, and I considered myself fortunate to not have to figure out how to deal with a flat.

All those basics make the Swoop a solid entry into the cargo bike market. What sets it apart is its use of a Shimano Cues Di2, one of the component maker’s low-end electronic shifting systems. Its mere existence surprised me, since I thought Shimano was reserving electronic shifting for higher-end component lines. But the company not only took it lower in the range; it added a couple of surprise features to its electronic shifting.

First, the basics: the drivetrain uses a single chainring on the cranks and a 10-speed rear cassette. The rear derailleur requires only a power source and control signals—no cable required. Once properly aligned with the cassette gears, it executes a perfect shift every time it’s told to. This shift includes a brief period when the derailleur over-travels to ensure the chain engages the next ring along, then drops back into the optimal location for continued cycling.

Everything in the system—the derailleur, the controllers, and the motor—takes power from a single removable battery. If the battery’s charge is good, you’re set to ride.

The mid-motor offers three levels of assist, adjusted through a controller on the left side that also includes the power button and a simple display. Shifting is controlled by the one on the right, which lacks a display. Separating the two allows each to be fairly minimalist, making it easy to find the control you need by feel.

On its own, the system worked beautifully. Shifting was fuss-free, and each change was blissfully silent. The assist worked well, and its three levels seemed to cover any needs short of going up steep hills with lots of cargo. This is not a bike that lets you skimp on pedaling in hot conditions; there’s no throttle, and even the highest setting of assist still requires you to exert some force on the pedals. But the motor definitely cuts down on the effort you have to make.

The battery, while looking fairly compact, easily handled dozens of miles without needing a recharge, which means several days of typical errands. While the battery lacks a carrying handle, it’s easy to take it out to charge it, as it pivots sideways out of the frame. When in place, it acts as a protector that keeps anything on the left side of the bike from sliding through the frame and getting tangled in the chain.

This is the first Shimano e-bike system I’ve tested, and it was just as good as you’d expect from a company that has come to dominate cycling drivetrains. Shimano Cues may be its lower-end system, but there’s no apparent skimping on the quality. And that’s before the bonus surprises Shimano has included.

Somewhere in one of the controllers, Shimano’s software gathers all the relevant information about your ride: how fast you’re going, how much force your feet are exerting on the cranks, what gear you’re in, and how fast your legs are churning (and possibly more?). And it uses that data to do a couple of interesting things.

One is what it calls Free Shift. Normally, a bike can’t shift to a different gear unless you’re turning the pedals to move the chain, which can potentially create problems. For example, you could move the derailleur down a gear but not complete the shift before stopping, meaning that the shift would be made when you start pedaling again, and the chain is under a lot of tension as you crank away from a full stop. Or you could move the derailleur several gears over without the chain following.

But the whole point of having a motor is to move the chain. So if you shift without pedaling and the bike isn’t stationary, the Cues system will use the motor to move the chain just enough to complete the shift. It does so without speeding up the bike at all.

Practically, this means that as you coast to a stop, you can simply hit the downshift button a few times, and the system will go into a low gear to make it easy to start up again without requiring you to turn the cranks. It’s … weird. Decades of cycling experience have programmed me to instinctually move my legs when I shift. Those instincts are suddenly superfluous.

It gets even weirder if you enable the automatic transmission. Shimano has included two settings, one for general riding and one for hauling cargo or passengers. When the system recognizes that you can get more out of your pedaling in a different gear, it will simply move you into that gear. That includes doing all the downshifting as you’re coasting to a stop and rolling back up through the gears again as you accelerate away from it.

Let me make that clear: You can coast to a stop without turning the cranks or touching the shifter, and you’ll still be in a different gear when you start up again.

The system is remarkably good at matching when I feel a shift is needed—Shimano’s programmers have done a fine job. Because of that, it’s pretty easy to induce a shift by altering your pedaling, as well. You can tell when it’s close, and just a bit more force will cause the system to send you up a gear. It’s kind of pointless to do so, since the buttons that shift up and down still work when it’s in auto mode, but I found myself doing it regardless.

The downside is that these shifts are not situations where instinctual actions are superfluous. To execute a smooth shift, you have to ease tension off the drivetrain by pedaling with less force, allowing the chain to slide over onto a neighboring gear with a bit less stress. Failing to do so can make for a clunky, inefficient shift and wear down components over time.

My problem with the automatic transmission mode was that I could tell when a shift was likely to come, but I couldn’t predict its precise moment. So it typically came while I was pedaling away happily, with full tension on the chain, making for a loud and awkward shift. This was especially unpleasant when accelerating away from a stop, when the bike would make three or four clunky shifts in rapid succession, each emitting a noise that told me I’d just done something I’d spent years learning to avoid. Living in a neighborhood with lots of four-way stops meant I sometimes experienced that every single block.

Shimano is not stupid, and these systems use parts that are specifically hardened to handle the added strain and wear. But it still felt bad every time I heard and felt that clunk.

The Swoop is not an inexpensive bike; at $4,500, it sits somewhere between the Trek Fetch+ 2 and the Urban Arrow Family I’ve reviewed previously. While it lacks the latter’s capacious cargo tub, the longtail form factor provides a much more bicycle-like riding experience. I’d rate its ride as superior to the Trek because of its frame and front suspension made for a more pleasant ride.

I also prefer Shimano’s drive system to the Bosch used by the other two bikes. It just felt better integrated with my pedaling, plus a bit quieter and less intrusive. The electronic shifting is a bonus—it’s not needed, but it definitely makes for a nice experience, and one where Shimano’s integration means you don’t have to worry about the status of the two additional batteries needed by many electronic systems. I don’t think I’d use the automatic shifting, but I could see where a less experienced cyclist might feel they benefit from it.

So while it’s on the pricier side, the cost seems to be in line with the features it offers. If those features are important to you, the Swoop is definitely worth consideration.

In the end, though, I’m not a huge fan of electronic shifting. I hate worrying about battery levels just to ride my bike, and I like the feel of a well-aligned mechanical shifter clicking into place. But even I have to admit that Shimano’s software does a fantastic job of shifting at the right times, and I think the system could really work well for anybody who hasn’t learned to associate a clunky-sounding shift with bad things.

A new report from Europe raises serious alarms about orbital collisions

Ars Technica Long form September 23, 2026

“I think we are going to lose the ability to use certain orbits.”

The 2013 sci-fi blockbuster film Gravity, starring Sandra Bullock and George Clooney, popularized the notion of the Kessler syndrome. In the movie, Russia shoots down a defunct satellite and creates a cloud of debris, leading to serious tension in orbit.

The movie is fantastic, a true thriller, and while some liberties were taken with the depiction of outer space, the basic premise of a cascading series of collisions rendering orbits too cluttered with debris to be usable is valid. The idea was first proposed by NASA scientists Donald Kessler and Burton Cour-Palais nearly half a century ago.

Still, the movie was science fiction, right?

Well, a lot has changed since Gravity‘s release. At the time that theatergoers were sitting on the edges of their seats and watching Bullock dodge debris, there were only about 1,000 active satellites in orbit. Today, that number is closer to 17,000, according to CelesTrak.

The preponderance of this growth has been driven by SpaceX’s Starlink constellation, which now has approximately 11,000 satellites in orbit, with many thousands more on the way. And SpaceX is not alone in the race to provide Internet from space. Amazon has launched hundreds of satellites, with thousands more to follow. Multiple Chinese Internet constellations are likewise in progress.

Then there are the orbital data centers, which may produce hundreds of thousands of satellites.

We’ve written a lot about these constellations, and they have generated a bunch of questions. Most prominent among them: Just how sustainable is all of this? Will we see the Kessler syndrome play out in real time? Here are some answers.

It depends on who you ask, so let’s start with the glass-half-empty and glass-half-full outlooks.

Starting with the pessimists: A few years ago, one of the world’s experts in orbital debris, University of Texas at Austin professor Moriba Jah, told Ars that he worries a lot about the consequences of satellites and debris in low-Earth orbit.

“I think we are going to lose the ability to use certain orbits because the carrying capacity is going to get saturated by objects and junk,” Jah said. ” I also predict that we will see a loss of human life by (1) school bus-sized objects reentering and surviving reentry and hitting a populated area, or (2) people riding on this wave of civil and commercial astronauts basically having their vehicle getting scwhacked by an unpredicted piece of junk. I predict that both those things are going to happen in the next decade.”

At the other end of the spectrum is the person almost solely responsible for the remarkable growth in satellites over the last decade, SpaceX founder Elon Musk. His attitude has largely been that space is big, and things will probably be just fine. For example, during a SpaceX-produced interview this summer at the company’s Starlink terminal factory in Bastrop, Texas, Musk said, “Space is really big. It’s not like space is gonna get crowded. Space is enormous. If you actually look at it relative to the Earth, the satellites are so tiny you can’t even see them.”

So in one way of thinking, very, very bad things are coming. In another, everything’s fine. Where does the truth actually lie?

One of the most credible sources for this kind of information is the European Space Agency, which has long studied space debris and its impacts on various orbits.

Fortunately, it just released its annual Space Environment Report a week ago. The European agency has produced such a report over the last decade to provide a transparent overview of global space activities and assess the quality of efforts to preserve the sustainability of spaceflight.

There are some striking—and concerning—changes this year. For example, the European report has dramatically increased its projections of future satellites in this year’s report after reassessing the current trajectory of large constellations.

“The notable increase in the index this year is primarily driven by the substantially larger future population resulting from the current extrapolation scenario,” the report states. “In particular, the growing influence of large constellations highlights the limitations of traditional mitigation approaches when applied to future traffic at unprecedented scales. At the same time, the results are affected by the limited availability of detailed and verifiable information on future deployment plans, operational practices, and end-of-life strategies of these systems.”

More satellites mean an increasing probability of collisions, which helps to push us toward a Kessler-like scenario.

As part of the report, the European scientists modeled a number of different scenarios. Assuming that satellite launches continue to increase—by far the most likely trend—even if operators continue to follow best practices in terms of disposing of older satellites and avoiding collisions, the orbital environment will still become significantly more cluttered.

“The extrapolation of our current behavior, which assumes the continuation of explosion in orbits at current rates, adherence by constellations to at least the minimum desirable post-mission disposal success rates, and continuation of the currently estimated post-mission disposal success rates for all other objects, leads to an unstable environment with collision rates increasing exponentially,” the report states.

In its technically precise language, the European Space Agency is essentially saying we’re on a road that could ultimately lead to something like the Kessler syndrome. Such a scenario, with a dramatic growth in constellations using best practices for satellite disposal, looks like this in terms of collisions in orbit.

It does indeed start to look pretty dicey by mid-century.

Also worth noting: The projections in ESA’s 2026 report do not include the new category of orbital data centers, as they exclude projects “still being prepared” for launch. It remains unclear whether these mega-megaconstellations of data centers in space will prove to be economically viable, but if they do, they could be the ultimate tipping point for orbital sustainability.

The European Space Agency talks a lot about the need for responsible behavior, and in managing its massive Starlink constellation, SpaceX has been responsible. The company has been effective at deorbiting satellites that lose functionality and at managing a constellation of thousands of satellites. It’s an unprecedented task that the company has learned, on the fly, to carry out at a scale no government or company has attempted before.

We know from mandatory reporting to the Federal Communications Commission that SpaceX is frequently moving satellites around in orbit, making small but precise maneuvers to avoid collisions. Five years ago, its (much smaller) constellation made about 500 such maneuvers a month. During the most recent reporting period, through May 2026, that number had jumped to nearly 35,000 per month. That comes to one maneuver every 75 seconds.

It is important to characterize these properly. Each maneuver is not a “near miss.” Rather, SpaceX has significantly lowered the probability threshold to trigger a collision avoidance maneuver. The NASA standard for maneuver is 1-in-10,000. At the outset of Starlink, though, SpaceX used a 1-in-100,000 threshold and has since become even more conservative, with a threshold of 3-in-10 million, according to a 2025 letter to the FCC.

So it’s clear that SpaceX is not operating its Starlink constellation in a cavalier manner. But it’s also clear that the company’s constellation, and those like it, are cause for significant concern going forward.

No credible experts are saying that the Kessler syndrome could happen imminently—a single collision won’t set off a Gravity-style cascade.

But space is getting more crowded, particularly orbits from 520 km to 1,000 km above Earth. A 2025 paper by Hugh Lewis and Kessler (yes, that Kessler) found that some orbital bands in this region have already reached what is known as a “collisional-runaway threshold,” which is to say that any serious collisions there may create new debris faster over time than debris would be naturally removed by the pull of gravity, down into Earth’s atmosphere.

Another concern comes from spent “rocket bodies,” upper stages from rockets that were not properly disposed of after launch. This was more common in decades past, but some launches today still do not reserve enough propellant to properly deorbit a second or third stage. These school bus-sized stages are particularly problematic at altitudes of 840 and 975 km, said LeoLabs space debris expert Darren McKnight. They are winging around uncontrolled, of course. And the higher the altitude, the longer the debris hangs around, from decades to centuries.

Finally, because there is so much stuff flying around orbit, it would be relatively easy for bad actors to start shooting missiles at satellites in low-Earth orbit, creating debris fields that could potentially wipe out communications and cause massive financial damage. The probability of Kessler syndrome becomes much higher if humans start deliberately blowing things up in space. Did we mention that Iran recently became the ninth country to put a domestically built satellite into orbit?

In the near term, it seems unlikely that space will become unusable. But it will likely become more and more expensive to operate there when considering avoidance technology, people to manage all of this, and propellant for maneuvers. And finding launch windows that avoid known debris will become more difficult.

Longer term, perhaps as early as 15 years from now but more likely longer, a Kessler-syndrome type outcome may start to become increasingly plausible.
