Aldi boss says some of rivals' loyalty discounts 'dupe' customers

BBC News Mon, 28 Sep 2026 17:45:52 GMT

Aldi's UK boss has accused rival supermarket chains of duping customers in some cases with loyalty discounts that start with "unrealistically high prices" and then drop.

Chief executive Giles Hurley said discounts are helpful "when they're real and when they show realistic reductions", but hit out at what he said were unrealistic reductions which "dupe customers".

Aldi is the only major supermarket chain that doesn't operate a loyalty scheme, which are used by millions of shoppers.

The UK's official competition watchdog investigated supermarkets' loyalty pricing schemes in 2024 and concluded shoppers "almost always make a genuine saving".

Former Asda buyer and retail consultant Ged Futter told the BBC Hurley's comments were a "a distraction from the fact is that Aldi is under pressure in the UK".

He said Aldi was "on a meteoric rise until about two years ago" but that it is "now growing behind the main supermarket pack".

"The price gap isn't as clear as it once was," he added.

Hurley, who has made similar comments on discount schemes in the past, was speaking as Aldi reported a 5% increase in sales to £19bn for 2025 from 2024.

However, operating profits had fallen slightly over the same period, which the retailer said was due to higher staff pay as well as investments in infrastructure and prices.

Hurley said the business was attracting new customers despite fierce competition across the sector.

"We are the only retailer where the price of your weekly shop is actually cheaper this summer than last summer," said Hurley

He said the business was focussed on "everyday low prices, not short-lived offers that disappear the following week".

"Promotions can supplement every day low prices when they're meaningful, when they're real and when they show realistic reductions.

"However, when promotions start with unrealistically high prices – and come down to prices which aren't that competitive and dupe customers – we would view that as loyalty that isn't supportive, that isn't transparent and doesn't help customers plan and budget."

Aldi said it had spent £340m this year on cutting prices. The German-owned chain also announced plans to open 40 new stores next year as part of a £900m investment programme and expand long-term agreements with British suppliers.

Hurley said recent droughts and global events had highlighted vulnerabilities in food supply chains, arguing that boosting domestic production should be a national strategic priority, helping to reduce the UK's exposure to shocks that can push up food prices.

Leics get partial points reprieve but stay in limbo

BBC News Mon, 28 Sep 2026 17:34:59 GMT

Leicestershire's Division One points total has risen from 111 to 119 as a result of the amended sanction

Leicestershire have had eight points of their 27-point County Championship deduction reinstated but their Division One status remains in limbo.

The original penalty for breaching pitch regulations, relating to their win against Glamorgan in August, was announced on 16 September.

The amendment to the punishment comes after the Cricket Regulator raised with the Cricket Discipline Panel (CDP) whether the 19-point penalty imposed under the County Championship's playing conditions had been taken into account when making its original decision.

The Cricket Regulator said it had "raised this issue with the CDP and Leicestershire CCC in the interests of fairness and transparency".

A section of the County Championship's playing conditions state that teams charged with producing a pitch rated as poor or below average, and the CDP upholding the charge, would receive zero points from the fixture in question.

Leicestershire took 19 points from the match against Glamorgan - 16 for winning and three bonus points - which were removed but remain the subject of appeal.

The CDP had applied an additional eight-point deduction, a further eight-point penalty suspended for a year, plus a £5,000 fine.

The latter two sanctions remain part of the amended decision but the eight-point deduction for this season has been waived.

Without the 27 points being docked, Leicestershire would have finished two points above the relegation zone.

After the eight-point reinstatement but with the 19-point penalty still in place, the Foxes are 17 points behind Essex and will be relegated if their appeal is unsuccessful.

Leicestershire had already stated their intention to appeal against the panel's decision and a statement by chief executive Emma White said the club's position is "unchanged" by the amendment.

Leicestershire to appeal against 27-point penalty

Leics on brink of relegation after points deduction

County Championship Division One table

Leicestershire's Ian Holland reacts during the defeat against Warwickshire that has left the Foxes facing relegation

In its amended decision, the panel said that "in a 162-page bundle prepared by the Cricket Regulator for the tribunal in advance of the original hearing on 12 September, there was no reference by the Cricket Regulator to the County Championship playing conditions and specifically no reference at all to Playing Condition 16.2.6".

It added that its "clear view" was that "eight points is the appropriate deduction and no more".

Confirming it was removing the immediate eight-point sanction, the panel said: "Regrettably that is the limit of this tribunal's powers given that, as both parties agree, it has no power to interfere in any way with the applicability of Playing Condition 16.2.6.

"If it had the power to do so, this tribunal makes it plain that it would have reduced the points deduction to the eight points it imposed in its original decision."

In a statement,, external the Cricket Regulator said: "Following the initial hearing on 11 September and the decision of 15 September, a question arose as to whether the separate 19-point deduction imposed under the Playing Conditions should have been taken into account by the CDP when considering the proportionality of the sanction imposed under the Pitch Regulations.

"In the interests of fairness and transparency, the Cricket Regulator raised this issue with the CDP and Leicestershire CCC. The CDP has now considered this issue and adjusted their decision on the sanction accordingly.

"The amended decision only adjusts the sanction imposed by the CDP in relation to the Pitch Regulations. It does not impact the finding that the charge for a breach of the Pitch Regulations was upheld, and it does not impact the 19-points deduction imposed as a result of the Playing Conditions."

White's statement on Leicestershire's website, external said: "The panel made clear that the latest hearing and amended decision, which relates to the sanction alone, were not appeal proceedings.

"Our position on the charge is therefore unchanged. We continue to believe it should not have been upheld and that we ought not to have suffered the points deduction we have.

"We therefore still intend to appeal, focusing upon the process and resultant evidential position upon which the panel was caused to decide the case."

Both the Cricket Regulator and Leicestershire said it would not comment further while the appeal process is ongoing.

Twelve women have been killed in one part of South Africa since July. Here's what we know so far

BBC News Mon, 28 Sep 2026 17:26:21 GMT

Police in South Africa have confirmed the discovery of the bodies of three more women in an area east of Johannesburg, bringing the total number of bodies found there to 12 in just two months.

The latest bodies were found in Ekurhuleni between Saturday and Monday morning, according to local police.

Police have made arrests in three of the cases, which do not appear to be related to the others. Nevertheless, police have said they cannot rule out the possibility of a serial killer.

The discoveries have caused widespread alarm in Ekurhuleni, particularly around Kempton Park, and come against the backdrop of longstanding concerns about high levels of violence against women in South Africa.

Here's what we know.

Case 1

Busisiwe Mahlangu's body was found in Kempton Park on 15 July 2026, the first of a string of bodies found in Ekurhuleni within a two-month period. The 37-year-old was found naked with her hands bound with cable ties.

Police arrested a suspect, believed to be her partner, two days after her murder. He has been in police custody since then and has not been linked to the other deaths that followed.

Case 2

Itumeleng Kekana, 32, was the second woman whose body was found in the same area on 3 August 2026.

The young mother disappeared in July and her body was found badly bruised, partially clothed and dumped on a bridge in Kempton Park.

No arrests have been made so far.

Case 3

Nomfesane Mjobo's body was found on 26 August, also in Kempton Park.

Few details around her death have been released but like most of the victims, she was found partially or fully naked with bruises.

No arrests have been made.

Case 4

Police confirmed the discovery of an unknown woman, in her 20s, on 7 September. The woman's body was found floating in a river in Olifantsfontain wearing only her underwear.

No further details have been shared about her death and no arrests have been made.

Case 5

Gracious Nkomo was the fifth woman whose body was discovered, again in the Kempton Park area.

Her partially clothed body was found on 10 September along a road close to South Africa's busiest airport. No arrests have been made in the 28-year-old's death.

Case 6

Elizabeth Moselakgomo was the sixth woman to be found, after a highly publicised nationwide search for her. The 38-year-old went missing while out for a daily run near her home in Kempton Park.

Her body was found badly bruised and partially clothed on 12 September. It was the discovery of her body that really raised the alarm about the spate of killings. No arrests have been made in her case.

Case 7

Police confirmed the discovery of another body just two days after Moselakgomo was found. The body was found in Olifantsfontein on 14 September, but police have withheld her name as her family has not yet been informed.

No arrests have been made.

Case 8

The body of Dineo Motapane, 38, was discovered on 15 September just two days after she was last seen alive.

Motapane's battered and partly burned body was found on the side of the road in Springs, another part of Ekurhuleni.

She leaves behind a young child. No arrests have been made in her case.

Case 9

The body of Jabulile Ntimba, in her 30s, was discovered half-naked and wrapped in a sheet on the side of a road in Boksburg on 17 September. This was the ninth body found in Ekurhuleni.

According to police, it appears Ntimba was killed because of a possible love triangle. Three people, two women and a man, were initially arrested for her grisly murder but the man was released due to insufficient evidence.

The two women have been charged with premeditated murder and defeating the ends of justice.

Case 10

The body of Ntombifuthi Nxumalo, the 10th body found in Ekurhuleni, was discovered at a cemetery in the Tembisa neighbourhood north-east of central Johannesburg on 26 September. She was found naked with serious head injuries as well as stones near her body.

This has led to police believing she may have been stoned to death.

A 36-year-old man was arrested a day after Nxumalo's death after he had travelled to another province. He faces a murder charge.

Case 11

The body of a yet-to-be identified woman was found in Springs on Sunday - the 11th body found in Ekurhuleni.

The grim discovery was made by a security company patrolling the area.

The woman was found in an open field, but no further details have been shared.

No arrests have been made.

Case 12

Boitumelo Gift Mashita was shot and killed on Monday in Tembisa Ekurhuleni. The 23-year-old woman was on her way to work when she was gunned down and her belongings were taken.

Police say her estranged husband, who they suspected of being responsible for her murder, was later found dead inside his vehicle in Midrand.

Police have not found any link between this case and the discovery of the other bodies.

While most of the bodies were found in the same area, police confirmed the discovery of another body about 39 miles (63 km) away from Ekurhuleni on 20 September.

The body of a young woman, believed to be in her 20s, was found wrapped in a duvet in a dam in Soweto, south-west of Johannesburg.

It's unclear if her murder is linked to those in Ekurhuleni.

President Cyril Ramaphosa said the killing of these women and others was a "stain on our national conscience".

South Africa has one of the highest homicide rates, with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone.

South African police statistics do not differentiate victims by gender but the South African Human Rights Commission said last week that 569 women were killed between April and June this year. This works out as an average of six women killed each day.

Police have set up a task team to investigate these murders and have offered a reward of 400,000 rand ($24,000; £18,000) for information that could lead to arrests.

Iran court upholds lashes sentence for singer who performed without hijab

BBC News Mon, 28 Sep 2026 17:15:00 GMT

An appeals court in Iran has confirmed a sentence of 74 lashes handed to a prominent singer who performed without the mandatory hijab, lawyers say.

Parastoo Ahmadi sang while wearing a sleeveless dress during a concert livestreamed on her YouTube channel in December 2024. Iran's laws ban public performances by women and require them to wear headscarves and modest clothing.

Iran's judiciary launched proceedings against the 29-year-old after the video went viral, gaining millions of views, saying the performance was "in violation of the country's legal and cultural regulations".

In June, a criminal court in Qom reportedly found Ahmadi and eight members of her band and production team guilty of charges including "offending public decency" through the publication of "obscene and indecent material".

In addition to being sentenced to 74 lashes, they were banned from audiovisual activities and from leaving the country for two years.

On Friday, the defendants' appeal was "rejected" by a higher court without a hearing, according to their lawyers.

"In our view, holding the concert was not a crime at all," one of the lawyers told the BBC. "The trial court imposed one of the harshest punishments for these charges, although fines and less severe penalties were also available."

"The Court of Appeal, despite having the option of holding a hearing, did not hold a hearing and upheld the judgment. It appears that the main reason for issuing this judgment was to deter the recurrence of similar events."

News of the initial sentence sparked widespread reaction among Iranians on social media.

"May these dark days come to an end, and may women regain the freedom to choose how they live and dress, and may artistic expression once again flourish in our precious homeland," exiled singer Googoosh wrote on Instagram at the time.

Musician Hossein Alizadeh meanwhile said he was "willing to take 70 lashes in Parastoo Ahmadi's place".

Human rights activists also condemned the sentence, with Amnesty International warning that "flogging constitutes cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment, and violates the absolute prohibition on torture and other ill treatment".

In January 2024, Kurdish-Iranian activist Roya Heshmati was flogged 74 times after being convicted of "violating public morals" over a photo on social media that showed her without the hijab.

She said a female officer forcibly placed a scarf on her head at a prosecutor's office in Tehran before a male officer whipped her shoulders, back, hips and legs, according to Kurdish rights group Hengaw.

Under Iranian law, which is based on the country's interpretation of Sharia, women and girls above the age of puberty must cover their hair with a hijab and wear long, loose-fitting clothing to disguise their figures.

In 2022, protests swept across the Islamic Republic following the death in custody of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman who was detained by morality police in Tehran in September that year for allegedly wearing her hijab "improperly".

Women burnt their headscarves or waved them in the air at the nationwide demonstrations against the clerical establishment, during which hundreds of people were killed in a crackdown by security forces.

Since then, many women and girls have stopped covering their hair in public altogether in open defiance of the dress code. Authorities have responded with periodic waves of arrests, warnings, business closures and other measures.

When discussing hijab enforcement earlier this month, conservative politician and Expediency Council member Gholamali Haddad‑Adel - who is also the father-in-law of Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei - said that Iran's war with the US and Israel meant authorities "cannot engage on this front as much as we should for the time being".

The war began at the end of February, only weeks after Iranian security forces had violently repressed another wave of mass protests sparked by the country's economic crisis, killing thousands of people.

Andy Burnham wants to fix social care - what are the options?

BBC News Mon, 28 Sep 2026 13:58:02 GMT

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he wants major reform of social care in England to create "a system that works on NHS principles" and where "everyone contributes, everyone is covered".

"There is free personal care elsewhere in the UK. I don't think it's right that people in England don't get the same", he told the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg.

The prime minister has asked Baroness Casey to conduct a review on the "best way of doing it" and she has been asked to report by April 2027.

Casey will also look at how to pay for any reforms.

BBC Verify has looked at four options for approaching social care reform and how much they could cost.

Some people face extremely high costs for care at the end of their life.

It has been estimated that around one in seven people aged 65 and over face lifetime care costs of more than £100,000.

One proposal is to cap these costs with the government picking up the bill above a certain cash threshold.

In 2011 a commission headed by the economist Andrew Dilnot proposed a lifetime cap of £35,000.

Dilnot estimated his proposed reforms would cost between £1.3bn and £2.2bn a year. The cost today would be higher due to inflation and the ageing population.

The Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition government, led by David Cameron, accepted Dilnot's recommendations.

But after the 2015 general election, which delivered a Conservative majority, Cameron delayed the implementation of the cap to 2020 over what he said were pressures on the public finances.

In 2017, when Theresa May was in No 10, the Conservatives' general election manifesto proposed a different way to reform social care.

This would have included the value of an individual's home in the means test used to decide what state funding they could get for care in their own homes.

It did not, initially, include any cap on lifetime care costs, with the manifesto saying this was more "equitable" than the Dilnot plan.

The May plan was branded a "dementia tax" by opponents and eventually dropped.

In England people can currently qualify for local authority financial support in a residential care home if all their assets - including their home - are worth less than £23,250.

This is known as a means test - where the level of financial support a person gets is based on the value of their assets and savings.

Some have suggested this threshold should be raised significantly so that many more people would qualify for means-tested support.

Boris Johnson's Conservative government in 2021 planned to raise the means test threshold to £100,000.

The annual cost of Johnson's reforms would have been £1.8bn a year over three years - although this was expected to rise over time as more people qualified.

The Johnson government planned a new Health and Social Care levy to pay for the package, but this was eventually scrapped by his Conservative successors as prime minister, because they wanted to keep taxes down.

An alternative approach is to ensure that everyone who is eligible, based on their needs, should get state-funded personal care that is free at the point of use.

This would be provided free regardless of an individual's means and whether it was received by an elderly person in their own house or a residential care home.

Scotland has implemented such a system.

However, it's important to note that personal care takes in things like helping frail elderly people wash and dress and go to the toilet.

But it does not include accommodation, food and everyday living costs which are subject to means testing.

The Health Foundation think tank estimates that implementing a Scottish-style system in England would cost £7.5bn a year by 2036.

Like Scotland, Japan and Germany have systems which base entitlement to personal social care mainly on people's care needs rather than their ability to pay.

Japan and Germany though have a mandatory long-term care insurance system which is funded through contributions from workers and employers.

Both countries also do not usually cover the full cost of personal care so individuals are responsible for some of the expenses.

Some have suggested that the government should set up a national care service in England, similar in ambition to the NHS.

This would mean all personal care would be free at the point of use while establishing national standards and care entitlement criteria.

The Health Foundation has estimated the cost of creating a universal and comprehensive social care system in England would be around £19bn a year extra by 2036.

When Andy Burnham was health secretary in Gordon Brown's Labour government in 2010 he produced a plan for a national care service.

It was suggested this would be paid for through a compulsory contribution from people's estates after they'd died.

But the idea was branded a "death tax" by Labour's opponents. The party lost the 2010 general election and its proposals went no further.

In the 2024 general election Labour again proposed a "national care service" without providing details or how it would be funded.

And after the election then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer effectively kicked the issue into the long grass by commissioning Louise Casey to investigate social care reform and report back in 2028.

It's worth bearing in mind that the four approaches above are not mutually exclusive.

Previous reform proposals have often combined more than one of them - such as a cap on lifetime costs and a more generous means test.

Burnham told the BBC that any changes would have to be "done carefully, without putting extra strain on the public purse".

One option - suggested by former Labour Treasury minister Darren Jones - is to get rid of the triple lock on the state pension. This guarantees that the pension rises every year by whichever is the highest of inflation, average earnings growth or 2.5%, to pay for a new system of social care.

But the long-term revenues from such a move are uncertain, because the cost of the triple lock depends on the future volatility of the growth of earnings and prices.

The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) has estimated that keeping it in place could cost "anywhere between £5bn and £40bn per year."

The Resolution Foundation think tank has estimated that scrapping the triple lock now and replacing it with a simple earnings link would save the government only around £650m a year by the end of the Parliament.

That would be well below the estimated annual cost of most social care reform options.

Lithium-ion battery caused fire that killed mum and 3 children

BBC News Mon, 28 Sep 2026 12:13:31 GMT

A house fire that killed a mother and her three children was caused by a lithium-ion battery.

Elisha Brabin, 36, and her children, Leo, 16, Ellis, eight, and Prudence, seven, died after a blaze "spread rapidly" inside a house on Stone Square in Bootle, Merseyside, in the early hours of 22 September.

Following an investigation with Merseyside Police, Merseyside Fire and Rescue Service (MFRS) said the fire was caused by an electrical event linked to a lithium-ion battery, which are used in e-bikes and e-scooters.

Kev Johnson, of MFRS, said: "This tragedy highlights the very real risks posed by lithium-ion batteries, which we confirmed as the source of the fire."

Six fire engines were at the scene at the height of the blaze at the semi-detached property, at 03:45 BST.

MFRS said four people "showing no signs of life" had been found in an upstairs bedroom.

A man was taken to hospital suffering from burns.

"This is a devastating incident, and our thoughts are very much with the family and friends of the mother and children who lost their lives and those who were injured," Johnson said.

He commended the efforts of staff and NWAS colleagues "who made every effort to provide a different outcome".

"Sadly this was not the case due to the speed and intensity of the fire," he said.

MFRS has not confirmed what the battery was being used for, but they are often found in e-bikes and e-scooters.

The fire service said there had been 150 fires linked to lithium-ion batteries on Merseyside between April 2023 and August 2026, and five fatalities linked to the batteries.

Johnson said: "We're urging people to follow the manufacturer's instructions - only using batteries and chargers which have been supplied with the vehicle or approved by the manufacturer, as anything else can pose a huge fire risk.

"It's also important to know and recognise the signs that your lithium-ion battery may be failing – if it is swelling, making unusual sounds, has a strong smell, is failing to charge, or is smoking, please stop using immediately."

Paying tribute, Ms Brabin's relatives said she was a "devoted and loving mother who lived for her children".

They said the family had been left "heartbroken" and their "unimaginable" loss would be "felt forever".

They also said "our beautiful babies, Leo, Ellis and Prudence, were loved beyond measure" and they were "devastated by the loss of Elisha, Leo, Ellis and Prudence".

"They have all been taken from us far too soon," they added.

Three dead, including child, in Channel crossing attempt

BBC News Mon, 28 Sep 2026 12:06:52 GMT

A 10-year-old child and two 30-year-old women have died after a small boat that was attempting to cross the English Channel got into difficulty off the northern coast of France, local authorities have said.

Officials responded to a distress call from the boat, which was carrying 105 people, after it departed from the Blériot Plage in Sangatte on Monday morning.

Three passengers were treated on board but were later confirmed dead by an emergency medical team flown out by helicopter, the French Maritime Prefecture of the Channel and the North Sea said.

Pas-de-Calais prefecture said its initial findings suggested the deaths were caused by trampling but an investigation has been launched to determine the exact cause.

Of the 102 other people on board, nine were treated by emergency services upon their arrival in the port of Calais, the prefecture said.

François-Xavier Lauch, prefect of Pas-de-Calais, blamed the incident on smuggling networks, which he said expose vulnerable people, including children, to the deadly risks of crossings.

The prefecture described the boat as a taxi-boat, which requires migrants to wade out onto the water to board.

Three other people died after similar taxi-boat departures last week, French authorities said.

Monday's deaths take the total number of migrants who have died so far this year to 20, according to Pas-de-Calais prefecture. For the same period last year, it said the number was 21.

Thousands of migrants attempt the perilous journey from France to the UK every year. In doing so, they cross one of the most dangerous and busiest shipping lanes in the world.

More people attempt the route in the summer months when the weather is warmer and when seas are calmer.

The UK recorded the highest number of migrant arrivals so far this year on Wednesday - with a total of 781 arriving in 10 small boats, according to Home Office figures.

Two boats also reached UK shores last week without being intercepted by UK authorities, at Folkestone and Samphire Hoe in Kent.

In July last year, France and the UK agreed on a "one in, one out" returns deal, which was designed as a deterrent to stop boats from crossing the Channel.

The deal allows the UK to return some small boat arrivals while agreeing to take in the same number of people from France who are believed to have a legitimate claim to come to Britain.

In August the UK government said it was making progress in tackling small boats, with the percentage who had made the journey in 2026 much lower than for the same period in 2025 but added it needed to "push further and harder in order to eradicate this vile trade".

So far, 2026 has seen 18,609 people successfully make the Channel crossing, which is 42% lower than the same period in 2025 when 32,188 had crossed in small boats.

How to find your perfect pillow - according to an expert

BBC News Mon, 28 Sep 2026 09:45:37 GMT

"I am one of those people," says Dr Chris McCarthy. "I do take my pillow with me."

You may have seen those people at the airport - a pillow stuffed under an arm as they drag their suitcases to check-in.

Or you might be one yourself - attached to a pillow that's soft enough to settle into but robust enough that it's not bunched into a ball by morning.

McCarthy insists he's not being fussy. He's a top physiotherapist and knows the wrong pillow can be a pain in the neck.

He doesn't take his abroad, but as soon as he gets to his hotel he starts "faffing about" with the pillows - and he's got a tried and tested trick to make even the most lacklustre one fit for sleep. Here's his guide to choosing the perfect pillow for you.

McCarthy, an associate professor at the Manchester School of Physiotherapy, says the right pillow will depend on what position you sleep in.

He tells the BBC's Sliced Bread podcast that most people fall into one of three categories of sleeper: side, back or front.

McCarthy discourages front sleeping as your neck is turned one way for a long period of time.

"Inevitably a muscle or ligament gets stretched and a bit irritated," he says. "If there's one thing there's a really good consensus on... in the physiotherapy world about treating spinal pain, it's don't sleep on your front."

When choosing a pillow, back sleepers should consider the flexion at the top of their spine, a curving that increases naturally in many people as they age.

If you have a bigger bend "it means you need a slightly thicker pillow than someone who's got a very flat back," says McCarthy.

For side sleepers the key measurement is the width of your shoulders. In general, the broader you are the thicker the pillow you will need. But you also need to consider your mattress.

McCarthy says how much you sink into your mattress "makes a huge difference in the subsequent height you then need from the pillow".

"Broad shoulders need a thick pillow [if] you're on a very firm mattress," he explains.

"If you're on a softer mattress, then you need a thinner pillow because your shoulder sinks into the mattress [more]."

This is less of an issue for back sleepers as they don't sink into the mattress as much as side sleepers do.

If your pillow feels too flat, McCarthy suggests placing a folded towel underneath and changing the number of folds to adjust the height. Then you can make a rough measurement to help you pick a new one.

Specialist pillows are often advertised as contoured, ergonomic or orthopaedic - but McCarthy says their effectiveness isn't completely proven.

"There is a little bit of fairly scrappy evidence to suggest that having a little bit of a higher front of the pillow, which goes into the neck area... does help [side sleepers]."

To see if a higher front helps you sleep better, you can try McCarthy's towel trick by rolling it and placing it underneath your pillow.

He urges side sleepers to pick a position that keeps their back straight.

For back sleepers, some manufacturers advertise a pillow with a dip in the middle that is raised at the sides. It does put people into a good sleeping position, says McCarthy, but some of his patients have found them "a bit claustrophobic".

Someone who has a large and heavy head also needs a thicker and firmer pillow, he adds.

Feather and down can keep you cool on warm nights because they wick away heat from your head, says McCarthy.

But they can change shape during the night, particularly if the sleeper moves around a lot and the pillow can end up bunched towards the headboard.

"What starts off as a nice, flat, supported surface becomes a wedge and so your neck is then kinked up."

Hollow fibre and microfibre fillings can hold shape better though they generally don't wick away heat as well, says McCarthy.

Some are made with a firmer material in the lower half of the pillow, which help retain the shape during the night.

McCarthy bought his foam pillow, which has tubular spaces for ventilation, five years ago for about £50. As a side sleeper, he adjusts its height using a folded towel laid underneath it.

He says choosing the right pillow is very much "horses for courses" and encourages people to utilise the trial period some manufacturers offer customers.

"There just isn't a one-off design that is perfect for everybody or every position, I'm afraid," he says. "You really have to personalise it."

British chess prodigy, 11, becomes youngest woman grandmaster

BBC News Mon, 28 Sep 2026 09:11:30 GMT

A British child chess prodigy has become the youngest player in history to earn the woman grandmaster (WGM) title.

Bodhana Sivanandan, 11, from north-west London, secured her third and final WGM norm - a certified title-level performance - while representing England at the 46th Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, the International Chess Federation (Fide) confirmed.

Speaking to Fide, Sivanandan said she was happy about the achievement but wanted to "keep making history".

It is the latest milestone in a remarkable rise for the schoolgirl, who has already become Britain's youngest women's chess champion and the youngest person to represent England internationally in any sport.

Sivanandan, from Harrow, played all 11 rounds on England's top board - a position assigned to the team's top player - and finished the tournament with eight points.

She had already passed the 2300 rating threshold required for the WGM title before securing her third and final norm.

She told Fide in an interview on Sunday about making history: "I'm happy to do it, but I want to keep going and keep making history as well, instead of just stopping here."

Kateryna Lagno, who has represented both Russia and Ukraine, previously held the age record for the WGM title, having achieved it aged 12. Hou Yifan, from China, also achieved the title at 12 and remains the youngest woman to have earned the higher, open grandmaster (GM) title, which she achieved aged 14.

Woman grandmaster is the highest woman only title a female player can attain and the rank is held for life.

Sivanandan's success in Samarkand also earned her a second International Master (IM) norm, taking her another step towards the higher title.

Players normally need three qualifying norms and a rating of at least 2400 to become an international master. Sivanandan now has two IM norms.

The international master title, open to both sexes, ranks higher than Sivanandan's current accolades - the woman grandmaster and woman international master titles.

Speaking to Fide about her love of the game, she added: "I like travelling and also because I do full-time school as well, it links to loads of school subjects, so it's really useful there as well."

Her father Siva previously told the BBC he had no idea where his daughter got her talent from as neither he or his wife, both engineering graduates, are any good at chess.

Her rise through chess has been rapid. After teaching herself to play during the coronavirus lockdown, she entered her first tournament at Harrow Chess Club in July 2021.

A year later, aged seven, she won all 24 of her games at the European Schools Championship.

In 2023, she became the youngest person to avoid defeat against a grandmaster in a competitive game at the European Rapid and Blitz championship in Croatia. The following year, aged nine, she was selected to represent England at the Chess Olympiad in Budapest.

The English Chess Federation said that selection, when she was nine, made her the youngest person to represent England internationally in any sport.

Last year, aged 10, Sivanandan became the youngest female player to defeat a grandmaster when she beat Peter Wells at the British Chess Championships.

In July this year, she earned her first IM norm at the Dole Open in France, becoming the youngest girl to achieve one, aged 11 years and four months. She also defeated grandmaster Marc'Andria Maurizzi, becoming the youngest girl known to beat a player rated above 2600 in a classical game.

You need £17,000 for a first home - here's how to save it

BBC News Mon, 28 Sep 2026 08:21:54 GMT

If buying your own home is the finishing line, then saving up the money to get there is a marathon.

The "Your First Home" scheme, announced on Saturday, aims to help first-time buyers in England get on the housing ladder with a small deposit.

Currently a 5% deposit on the average UK house price of £272,000 plus moving costs and legal fees - will set you back about £16,850, according to financial information service Moneyfacts.

That's daunting, but here are four ways that experts say you can at least make a start on saving for a deposit.

Depositing an amount you can afford into a regular savers account the day after you are paid is a good way to start, suggests Anna Bowes, savings expert at financial advisers The Private Office.

"It becomes like another bill, but one that you can benefit from in the future," she says.

The type of account that's suitable depends on your circumstances.

Some of the ones that pay the highest interest are only accessible if you hold a current account with the provider, she says.

Other considerations are whether you can lock the money away for longer, to receive a better savings rate.

If you don't have a buffer of other savings, then experts say an easy access account gives you the chance to dip into the money to pay an unexpected bill.

You can save up to £4,000 a year in a Lifetime Individual Savings Account (LISA) and the government guarantees a 25% bonus. So, if you put the full amount in then the government will add £1,000 a year.

But there is a catch, that has left some people out of pocket.

Money saved in a LISA can only be used to buy a first home up to the value of £450,000 - a threshold that has not changed since 2017.

The only other time you can withdraw the money is after the age of 60 or in the exceptional case that you are terminally ill with less than 12 months to live.

Withdrawal under any other circumstances means you get hit with a penalty - so you could get back less than you put in.

Ministers are planning to replace the LISA with a new First Time Buyer ISA, but there are no clear details yet about how it will work.

The earlier you start saving the more you can build up thanks to the magic of compound interest. In short, interest is added on a larger and larger pot as time goes by.

Bowes says that saving £50 a month from the age of 20 would give you about £41,000 in 30 years' time when you hit 50, assuming interest of 5% is paid a year.

Start 10 years later, and you'd need to save more than double - £101 a month - to have the same amount at the age of 50.

Investing in stocks and shares is another option, but the value of investments can go down as well as up.

An increasing number of lenders are offering mortgage deals with little or no deposit required.

David Hollingworth, from L&C, points to mortgages that have deposits starting from £5,000 and allow people to borrow up to 98% or 99% of the property purchase price.

They might not always be the best option, and not everyone will be eligible.

And, of course, some first-time buyers turn to their parents for help.

Again that's not available to all, but a survey by the Nationwide Building Society suggests that more than half of parents who charge their adult children rent are putting some or all of the money towards helping their child save to buy their own home.

Award winner to fourth choice - what has gone wrong for Ramsdale?

BBC News Mon, 28 Sep 2026 08:10:08 GMT

Aaron Ramsdale has not played a competitive game of football for five months

In April 2023, Aaron Ramsdale was within touching distance of winning the Premier League with Arsenal.

But the goalkeeper made a costly error for the Gunners to give away the opening goal in a 3-3 draw with Southampton at Emirates Stadium which contributed to the demise of Arsenal's 2022-23 title bid.

If Arsenal had won that game, the title would have been in their hands. Instead, the draw handed the initiative to Manchester City, who took full advantage.

It was a mistake which perhaps also signalled the beginning of the end for Ramsdale under Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta.

Four months later, the north London club brought in David Raya from Brentford and the Spaniard quickly claimed the number one spot.

And in a somewhat unfortunate poetic twist, it is the Saints where Ramsdale finds himself completely out of favour three years on as the fourth-choice goalkeeper at a Championship club.

From an England international on the cusp of greatness, Ramsdale is now in the almost unthinkable situation of being without senior football this season in the prime of his career at the age of 28.

So why has Ramsdale had such a fall from grace and where have things gone wrong?

Aaron Ramsdale made 89 appearances for Arsenal and kept 32 clean sheets

Questions were raised among the Arsenal fanbase when the club paid £24m to sign Ramsdale from Sheffield United in August 2021 after the Blades had been relegated from the top flight.

But he quickly won supporters over by producing a string of excellent saves in his debut season, perhaps most notably against Leicester City when he denied a James Maddison free-kick at full stretch - a save which Peter Schmeichel described at the time as "the best I've seen for years".

After ousting Bernd Leno, his efforts helped Arsenal finish fifth in 2021-22, improving on an eighth-placed finish the previous year.

The following season, Ramsdale was a vital cog in Arsenal's spine as they launched a surprise title challenge, only to be outdone by an imperious Manchester City side.

Despite his blunder in the draw with Southampton - which was one of several results that dented Arsenal's title hopes - Ramsdale made the Professional Footballers' Association (PFA) team of the year and was also named goalkeeper of the year at the London Football Awards.

But Ramsdale quickly fell behind Raya in the pecking order in 2023-24 and lost his starting berth after just four league games.

And in one of the only two other Premier League matches he did play that season against Raya's then parent club Brentford, Ramsdale made another mistake to allow Yoane Wissa to put the Bees ahead.

Arsenal recovered to win that game 2-1 in March 2024. But Ramsdale never played for the club again.

He was sold to Southampton for £25m in August 2024 after returning from Euro 2024 with England, having been an unused sub throughout the competition in Germany.

Clubs have paid a combined £74m in transfer fees for Aaron Ramsdale, who has five England caps

At the time of Ramsdale's signing, he looked to be the perfect goalkeeper and a coup for Southampton.

Russell Martin's side had just won promotion and were hoping to implement a style of play in the Premier League that had brought them such success the previous season.

Ramsdale ticked all the boxes as a goalkeeper who had ability with his feet to complement Martin's preference to build up from the back.

His previous spells at Sheffield United and Bournemouth also justified his addition as someone whose stock had continued to rise despite being involved in relegations.

Ultimately, though, the move to Southampton did not work out as planned.

He made 30 league appearances for a Saints side which finished bottom of the Premier League with just 12 points - the second-lowest ever points tally in the competition - and conceded more goals (66) than any other goalkeeper in 2024-25.

That is not to say Ramsdale was to blame in a Southampton side which performed poorly across the board, with some fans at the time in fact praising him for keeping the score down in games.

It would, however, be the fourth relegation Ramsdale had suffered, having already done so with Chesterfield, while on loan in 2017-18, the Cherries in 2019-20 - although he was named player of the year for Bournemouth that season - and then the Blades.

Aaron Ramsdale and Asmir Begovic both signed for Bournemouth in 2017

After signing from Sheffield United in 2017, Ramsdale was an understudy to experienced goalkeeper Asmir Begovic at the Vitality Stadium for two years before his breakthrough.

"First of all, Aaron's a fantastic goalkeeper," Begovic told BBC Sport.

"We first worked together about nine years ago and since then he's been on an incredible ride where he's performed at the highest level.

"I remember my remit when I came into Bournemouth was to mentor and set a tone for some of the younger goalkeepers, one of which was Aaron Ramsdale.

"There's many different factors that go into it but I think it's been unfortunate that maybe a few things haven't aligned for him [at Southampton]."

Southampton's relegation prompted Ramsdale to seek top flight football once more and he moved to Newcastle United on loan for the 2025-26 campaign.

But again, what was supposed to be a move to help re-establish his career at the highest level did not come to pass.

Ramsdale kept just two clean sheets in 23 appearances in all competitions for the Magpies, featuring only 12 times in the Premier League - and neither he nor Nick Pope could make the number one spot permanently their own.

He also had the unfortunate experience of letting in seven goals in one game in a 7-2 defeat by Barcelona in the Champions League last-16 - the most he has ever conceded in a single game.

Follow Southampton content on BBC Sounds

Pre-match, post-match and topical Saints content

Subscribe and listen for everything you love about the Saints

Aaron Ramsdale, back right, has not made any of Southampton's 10 matchday squads this season in the Championship or EFL Cup

Southampton boss Tonda Eckert has seemingly made it clear Ramsdale is not part of his plans this season, with Daniel Peretz his number one, George Long the second choice and Jamie Jones returning to the club as mainly a training goalkeeper.

"The reality is that Rambo's story with the football club started before myself," Eckert told BBC Radio Solent.

"We've had honest conversations from the first day of pre-season until the very last day of the transfer window.

"The expectations for him are clear to support the team in the best way and he's been very professional in doing that so far."

Despite his exclusion so far this season, Ramsdale is said to have a good relationship with Eckert, the coaching staff and the other goalkeepers - and has an affection for the club.

Ramsdale also believes there is a route back into the first team for him at St Mary's and is willing to fight for his place until at least January, when the winter transfer window opens.

He had offers on the table in the summer to go on loan to clubs in England, Spain and Italy but declined, with his current ambition to try to help Southampton win promotion back to the Premier League and play in the top flight.

As well as being a popular figure in the dressing room and well-liked by Saints supporters, Ramsdale also had personal factors to consider for what would have been a move to a fourth club in four years.

His wife recently gave birth to their second child and the family are settled in the area, with Ramsdale only wanting to change clubs if it was the right opportunity.

Begovic says his former team-mate will be finding his current lack of playing time "very difficult and frustrating".

"I had a few spells where I was frozen out at a club for a short time but I can't really relate to Aaron's situation," he added.

"I can imagine there will be some factors that are out of his hands. In the meantime he'll have to make sure that he trains well and stays fit and be ready if an opportunity comes up to play.

"He has to be ready for the long term and if the chance to move elsewhere comes up, he's ready.

"I'd love to see Aaron playing again and hopefully it happens in January but I'm fully aware that it won't be a straightforward situation."

Angela Scanlon takes over Sara Cox's drivetime slot on Radio 2

BBC News Mon, 28 Sep 2026 08:05:20 GMT

Angela Scanlon is to take over BBC Radio 2's drivetime show after Sara Cox moved to the breakfast slot.

The Irish personality said it was "properly exciting" to be hosting the station's 16:00-19:00 show every weekday from November.

She said: "Millions of people, all having completely different days, piling into the same conversation for a few hours - what a strange and lovely thing!"

Scanlon, who hosted a Sunday early morning programme on the station from 2018 to 2021, was among a number of people who filled in after Cox vacated the drivetime slot in May, including Joel Dommett, Jason Manford, Ellie Taylor, Alex Jones and Gary Davies.

Scanlon is also known for The One Show, This Morning, Your Home Made Perfect, The Apprentice: Unfinished Business, and for taking part in Strictly Come Dancing in 2023.

"Every weekday, I'll be in your ears, your cars and your kitchens - on the school run, on the way home, or standing at the hob wondering what on earth to feed a small but hungry mob," she said.

"I want all of it: the stories, the opinions, the chaos, the tiny triumphs and the things you probably shouldn't admit on national radio."

Radio 2 controller Helen Thomas described Scanlon as "incredibly warm and quick witted and proved to be extremely popular with the Radio 2 audience this summer".

She added: "Drivetime is such an important show in terms of ensuring people get home and start their evenings in a positive and upbeat mood, and I'm delighted Angela will be taking up the reins in November.

"I'd like to extend my thanks to all the hosts who have presented in this slot since our Sara moved on up to Breakfast."

Scanlon also hosted the Virgin Radio weekend breakfast show after Graham Norton's departure in 2024, and co-hosts the Get A Grip podcast.

Meanwhile, Radio 2 has also announced that Ben Earle will present the station's weekly country music programme following the departure of longtime host Bob Harris.

"Whispering" Bob, who presented the show for 27 years, announced his departure in June, weeks after revealing his prostate cancer has spread to his spine.

Earle, one half of British country group The Shires, has also fronted a weekly show on Absolute Radio Country for the past five years.

Carer at home investigated by BBC struck off for threatening elderly man

BBC News Mon, 28 Sep 2026 05:18:57 GMT

A carer who was secretly filmed mocking and threatening an elderly bedbound man with dementia has been struck off.

Amina Sani was found to have threatened the 81-year-old with police and threatened to hit him when he became distressed and lashed out at the prospect of being showered against his will.

The Nigerian worker went on to carry out the man's intimate personal care while a cleaner held his arms down.

The incidents at Castlehill Care Home in Inverness on 10 April last year came to light after the resident's daughter installed a secret camera in his room due to concerns over his care.

The footage was later featured in a BBC documentary into care standards at Castlehill, in which families accused the home of "cruelty" and "neglect".

Sani's legal representative told a Scottish Social Services Council misconduct hearing that she had not been trained properly in what was her first job in the UK.

Namatirai Chipere said her client was a victim of problems in the social care system herself.

However, hearing chairman Iain Burke said the incidents were a "significant abuse of trust and power" for which she had shown no insight or remorse.

He said her attitude and behaviour were "fundamentally incompatible" with registration as a social care worker.

In a statement, the home's owner - Morar Living - said it acted promptly when concerns were brought to its attention.

It said there was "no truth" in Sani's claim that she was not trained properly.

Castlehill, now renamed Morar Highland, was graded "good" in its most recent care inspection.

The panel was shown video footage covering a period of more than 20 minutes, in which Sani repeatedly tells the man that he was to be showered.

He can be heard screaming "no" and "leave me alone", before swearing at Sani and another carer.

The pair can be seen laughing during the encounter.

During evidence at the hearing, the man's daughter Su Christie, said her father, a former merchant navy crewman, had a lifelong fear of showers due to a childhood trauma.

Following the judgement, she said: "You could tell by the things he was doing, the things he was saying, that his distress was growing and growing throughout that interaction and there was no attempt to bring him down or de-escalate him whatsoever.

"He didn't know what was going on. He's a confused 81-year-old man living with dementia. He was frightened.

"It was devastating, utterly devastating. I was in shock because, although I knew there were issues, I didn't expect to see that. It was very distressing to watch."

The panel ruled Sani told Christie's father: "We will call the police and they will take you to court" and, referring to a male cleaner, "do you think that man is going to hit you?" or words to that effect.

She also pulled his duvet off without any warning, causing him to become distressed and agitated.

Delivering the panel's judgment, the chairman said: "We agree with your solicitor's submissions that you were let down by your employer, and there is little doubt that there was institutional failure.

"None of the failures you have highlighted absolve you from your personal responsibility as a registered social care worker.

"It is clear throughout the video clips that you did not show any kindness or compassion to the resident. At one point you and your colleague can be seen laughing in response to something the resident says or does.

"It does not appear to us to be laughing with the resident, but it appears more disrespectful in nature. We find that the resident suffered harm and you did not respect his dignity."

Burke added that the panel felt Sani's treatment of the man was "not something that could be remediated with training" as it reflected her attitude.

It also noted she failed to use any de-escalation techniques.

In closing submissions, Sani's legal representative said her client wished to apologise to the family.

Christie, who moved her father into a new home shortly after the incident, said: "I think it was the right decision.

"Whilst the panel did comment on institutional failures, this hearing is about her own personal accountability. And I think it sends the message that personal accountability matters.

"In a care setting, people living with dementia, like my father, should be treated with respect, dignity, and patience and courtesy. They should be treated as human beings and that's all I was asking for."

A hearing to decide sanctions over the behaviour of carer Oluwabunmi Salami, involving the same man, continues.

Earlier in the hearing, Salami admitted allegations that she raised and lowered the man's bed without warning, causing him distress.

A spokesperson for Morar Living said: "There is no truth in Amina Sani's claim that she was not trained properly by Morar.

"When concerns were brought to our attention, Morar Highland acted promptly, including suspending employees where appropriate, undertaking formal investigations and taking action in line with the findings.

"We made the relevant referrals to the Scottish Social Services Council (SSSC) and, where required, to the Protecting Vulnerable Groups (PVG) Scheme.

"The safety, dignity and wellbeing of our residents remains our priority, and all concerns regarding staff conduct are taken seriously and acted upon appropriately."

Thousands of illegal ghost plates on cars revealed by new cameras

BBC News Mon, 28 Sep 2026 05:02:30 GMT

Thousands of illegal registration plates on cars and other vehicles have been detected by a new camera system currently being tested on motorways in south-east England, BBC Panorama can reveal.

These plates have been adapted to avoid their details being identified by automatic number plate recognition (ANPR) systems, which are used to enforce speed limits and low emission zones as well as to track criminals.

Illegal plates are putting the public at risk and are far too easy to get hold of, according to one former government advisor.

We have spoken to families who say their lives have been devastated by road deaths where illegal plates were involved.

Filming undercover, we also discovered how easy and cheap it is to buy plates without any background checks.

The minister responsible for vehicle registration across the UK has told us a national plan has now been instigated to understand how widespread the problem of illegal number plates is, and what can be done about it.

The UK has one of the largest networks of ANPR cameras in the world, with 14,000 sites capturing 100 million number plates each day. Many experts believe this system is failing to keep up with tactics used by some drivers determined to avoid recognition.

These tactics include deliberately using false plates that clone the number of another vehicle - and so-called ghost plates, where special plastic is used to make all or part of the registration number unreadable by most motorway cameras.

One of the main providers of ANPR technology, MAV Systems, has been testing a new camera capable of identifying and reading ghost plates.

At one test site, just outside London near the Dartford Crossing, it has recorded an average of more than 1,000 of the ghost plates a day over several months.

Two other sites have been running for almost two years. At one, near the M25, detections have risen from 1,000 a day to nearly 2,000 a day - while at the other, near the Eurotunnel at Folkestone, the system is flagging more than 400 a day.

Sharon Gannon's son, Jason Wallis, died in a crash where hidden registration plates were involved. She believes being invisible to ANPR cameras emboldens drivers to take deadly risks.

Wallis was killed in Buckinghamshire in 2023. He and his brother-in-law, Lewis Baker, had been riding their motorbikes at high speed when they both crashed into a car. The car driver was not hurt.

Baker survived and was later jailed for 15 months for dangerous driving. In court, he admitted using a device to hide his number plate from public view. He also said he and Wallis had ridden at high speed more than 100 times.

"It has broken us all," Sharon Gannon says of the effect the crash has had on her family.

In another case, from 2025, 81-year-old Graham Slinn was killed on a pedestrian crossing when a car with cloned plates hit him at high speed.

The 20-year-old driver, Cain Byrne, who was driving without a licence or insurance, had also inhaled nitrous oxide minutes before the collision. He was identified after police trawled through hours of CCTV footage. One camera even caught the moment he had put the illegal plates on his car.

Byrne was jailed for 11 years and six months for causing death by dangerous driving, driving while disqualified and driving without insurance.

The victim's daughter, Nicola Timmis, says cloned plates are like a "gateway drug" which allow drivers to take more dangerous risks.

"It seems like it's harmless, but then one thing leads to another, leads to another, and before you know it, it's somebody dead," she tells Panorama. "It is not a victimless crime."

Both cloned and ghost plates look like normal vehicle registration plates when viewed by the naked eye.

In the case of cloned ones, at least two vehicles are on the road with the same letters and numbers - with only one of them being legal.

Ghost plates, on the other hand, show correct details for the vehicle - but they are made up of reflective materials which are difficult or impossible for most ANPR cameras to read.

Cloned and ghost plates undermine the police's ability to track organised criminals, says Tony Porter, a former senior counter-terrorism officer who has advised the government on surveillance cameras.

"The police need an effective ANPR system that doesn't have weaknesses [and] doesn't put the public at risk," he says.

While passports have security features such as watermarks and electronic ID chips, Porter says, "we tolerate a £10 number plate with no security mechanism on it".

In the UK, there are more than 34,000 businesses registered with the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA) to supply number plates.

Anyone can currently become a registered number-plate supplier by filling in a quick form and paying a one-off fee.

Panorama secretly filmed at a market in Essex to find out how easy it is to buy a plate in breach of the rules.

Two out of three businesses we approached there offered ghost plates which they said could help avoid cameras policing London's Ultra-Low Emission Zone (Ulez) cameras.

One of them allowed us to buy a plate without asking for either ID or proof that we were allowed to use the registration - both of which are required by law.

Instead, we handed over £40 in cash and, eight minutes later, we had a brand new number plate. Buying a ghost plate is not illegal in itself, but it would be against the law to put it on a vehicle and drive with it.

Just two number plate suppliers have been prosecuted and forcibly removed from the DVLA register since 2020, a Freedom of Information request by Panorama has discovered. Only six DVLA officers are tasked with inspecting and auditing the thousands of registered suppliers in the UK.

The DVLA said in a statement that it was "cleaning up the register, strengthening compliance and enforcement" and that it continued to work closely with police and Trading Standards to "tackle suppliers who break the rules".

To witness the scale of the problem, Panorama joined the police and DVLA at a location on the edge of Birmingham and West Bromwich to see a roadside operation checking for illegal number plates and other issues.

Not long after we arrived, officers stopped a van. Specialist infrared goggles - which see number plates the way ANPR cameras do - revealed it was displaying a ghost plate. The driver received a £100 fine but said he was unaware the plate was illegal.

The police and DVLA then visited the plate supplier, where staff denied selling ghost plates. But, using the goggles to view the supplier's stock, Panorama identified two ghost plates displayed on a wall alongside several legal ones.

Police also discovered the supplier kept ghost letters and numbers separately on a shelf, which they said suggested "some level of intent".

The supplier, which told Panorama it did not manufacture the letters it used to make plates, received a warning letter, although a prosecution is still being considered.

Police forces want to see tighter licensing and regulation around who can issue a number plate, says Chief Constable Tim Forber, the UK's policing lead on ANPR.

"Not a week goes by where we don't see an example of someone on cloned plates involved in serious and organised crime," he adds.

There is a problem that needs tackling and a more robust system may be needed, according to Justin Madders, the minister in charge of UK vehicle registration.

He says the government recognises this and is creating a national centre to crack down on illegal number plates, bringing together police forces to share intelligence and trial new technologies to improve road safety, tackle organised crime and drivers attempting to dodge fines.

"I don't think we can rule anything in or out at this stage," he adds.

Additional reporting by NJ Convery

Felled Sycamore Gap stump has 'encouraging' growth

BBC News Mon, 28 Sep 2026 05:01:06 GMT

The stump of the iconic Sycamore Gap tree is showing "encouraging" signs with a thick ring of new shoots growing around it, three years on from its illegal felling.

The landmark on Hadrian's Wall in Northumberland was targeted on 28 September 2023 by Daniel Graham and Adam Carruthers, who travelled during a storm from their homes in Cumbria to cut it down.

Their actions sparked widespread outrage and the pair were later jailed for criminal damage to the Victorian-planted tree and Roman wall.

Site owners the National Trust fenced off the stump to see if it would recover, with general manager Andrew Poad saying he is "filled with hope by the way nature is taking its course".

He said: "These flourishing shoots are really encouraging and show the special measures we've taken, including reducing soil compaction around the roots and limiting human disturbance, are paying off."

Poad said the trust was grateful to visitors supporting their efforts to give the tree "the best possible chance to thrive".

He added: "We're monitoring the tree closely and, over time, our rangers will manage it depending on how it develops."

After the tree was felled, seedlings were kept in a secret National Trust centre to help preserve the legacy of the much-photographed landmark.

Saplings were then donated to community groups and charities around the country, with art projects launched to highlight nature's importance and condemn the illegal felling.

Graham and Carruthers were jailed for four years and three months in July 2025 for their roles in chopping down the tree with a chainsaw.

The pair, who were 39 and 32 at the time of their conviction, filmed themselves in the act and took a wedge of trunk away as a trophy.

Graham, a groundworker from near Carlisle, and Carruthers, a mechanic from Wigton, never explained the motive for what prosecutors called a "moronic mission", but sought to blame each other during the trial.

The tree was planted in the late 1800s and became a much-loved visitor destination and landmark at the former frontier of the Roman Empire.

It found global fame after featuring in a scene of the 1991 film Robin Hood Prince of Thieves, starring Kevin Costner, and was popular with photographers and artists.

Blood test could gauge if a baby has a dangerous infection in 15 minutes

New Scientist September 26, 2026

A blood test could determine whether a feverish baby has a bacterial or viral infection in 15 to 20 minutes. This would help doctors gauge whether the infection is serious or may pass without treatment, which could prevent unnecessary use of antibiotics.

When babies are brought into hospital with fever, they “are considered high-risk until proven otherwise”, says Tommaso Bellini at the Giannina Gaslini Institute in Genoa, Italy.

Severe meningitis outbreak caused by bacteria that took genes from microbiome

A fever can be the result of several things, including infection by viruses or bacteria. These different types of pathogens require different medications. Furthermore, most common viruses are fairly benign, while bacterial infections are generally more dangerous, says Bellini.

Advertisement

Existing tests to gauge infection type take at least a few hours, so babies with fever are often given antibiotics against bacteria as a precautionary measure. But only about 15 per cent of them actually have a serious bacterial infection, says Bellini. This unnecessary use of antibiotics helps drive the spread of bacterial resistance.

To develop a test that determines infection type, Bellini and his colleagues followed 85 babies, all younger than 90 days old, who were brought into emergency rooms with fever after previously having no serious health concerns. The team took blood samples and tested for two proteins: CD64 and CD169.

Previous studies have shown that these proteins become more common in certain blood cells when the body responds to infections. CD64 is made at higher levels in response to bacteria and is found on the surface of white blood cells called neutrophils. CD169 rises in response to viruses and appears on the outer membranes of monocytes, another type of white blood cell.

Free newsletter

By comparing the levels of both proteins in neutrophils and monocytes, the test correctly identified all 15 cases of bacterial infection, 44 incidences of viral infection and 26 cases of no infection. Bellini presented the results at the European Emergency Medicine Congress in Paris, France.

The results came through in 15 to 20 minutes in a lab, says Bellini, who is trying to develop a version that can be used as quickly in hospitals.

This builds on several years of research to develop a CD64/CD169 test. Fabrice Malergue at Beckman Coulter Life Sciences in Marseille, France, has spent much of the past decade working on it. In 2021, his team found that CD64 and CD169 levels reliably distinguish between bacterial and viral infections among adults in an emergency room.

Heartland virus and Bourbon virus, which are transmitted by lone star ticks, have killed at least seven people in the US

Other groups have since replicated that finding, found ways to perform the test more quickly and easily, and demonstrated that it works in children. Performing the test on babies in a hospital setting is a significant advance, says Malergue. It was crucial to investigate the test in this age group because their immune systems are still developing, which meant “some people had doubts about the capacity of these [CD64 and CD169] markers to arise”, he says.

Malergue says one of his collaborators used the test in Martinique during an outbreak of dengue fever, which is caused by a virus and is usually mild. The collaborator found that some people actually had a bacterial infection called leptospirosis, which is life-threatening without antibiotics.

Bellini now hopes to assess the test in a trial of 300 to 500 infants at multiple hospitals. Meanwhile, Malergue and his colleagues have developed a benchtop machine that can quickly analyse finger-prick blood samples to determine whether an infection is viral or bacterial, which is approved for research use.

Scientists can’t stop using AI, even when forbidden from doing so

New Scientist September 28, 2026

Banning researchers from using AI to assess the merits of scientific papers doesn’t make much difference to the conclusions the reviewers reach – in large part because many of them ignore the prohibition and use AI anyway.

A team led by computer scientists at Microsoft Research ran a large randomised experiment during the 2026 International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), one of the world’s biggest AI conferences, which took place in Seoul, South Korea in July.

Some 24,661 papers were submitted to the conference, requiring oversight from 17,886 reviewers. When researchers submitted their work, they could choose how it would be reviewed. The first option was to have it assessed by reviewers using a conservative policy that entirely banned the use of large language models (LLMs) to help with reviewing. The other option was to have the assessment performed by reviewers using a permissive policy that allowed the use of LLMs to help understand papers, check related work and polish reviewers’ own writing, but not to judge the merits of a paper or draft a review of the work.

Advertisement

Scientists prefer feedback from ChatGPT to judgement by peers

The team led by Microsoft Research scientists discovered that papers reviewed under the two policies had almost identical acceptance rates – 27 per cent under the stricter policy and 26.5 per cent under the permissive one – while average review scores were 3.31 and 3.32 out of 6, respectively. Reviewer confidence was also virtually unchanged. Reviews written under the permissive policy were around 5.5 to 7 per cent longer, and were rated as slightly higher quality by experts, although a reviewer-by-reviewer comparison found no meaningful difference.

The reason for that lack of difference became clear after an anonymous survey of 1486 of the reviewers who took part in the exercise. There, 22.5 per cent of reviewers who were instructed not to use AI admitted to using an LLM anyway. “Self-reported non-compliance of 23 per cent is definitely higher than what I was anticipating,” says Miro Dudík at Microsoft Research, who was involved in the study and was also one of the conference organisers.

Those who used AI when told not to did so to brainstorm feedback, draft review text, read the papers and summarise their strengths and weaknesses. “Our post-conference survey reveals some reasons why reviewers might end up violating policy, like large reviewing workloads and insufficiently clear rules,” says Dudík.

Subscriber-only newsletter

“This study shows that banning AI in peer review is very difficult to enforce,” says Kayvan Kousha at the University of Wolverhampton, UK. “Because of the workload of academics, there is a temptation” to use AI, says Kousha.

In a separate part of the study, the researchers analysed the reviews using Pangram, an AI text detector. They found that only 52.2 per cent of reviews under the conservative policy were classified as fully human-written, compared with 37.0 per cent under the permissive policy – though the researchers warn AI text detectors aren’t perfect.

“I believe our work has relevant insights for other computer science conferences – and potentially venues in other fields as well – that are facing similar challenges,” says Sunnie S. Y. Kim at Microsoft Research.

arXiv DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2609.19420

A record El Niño climate phase will unleash unprecedented heat and extreme weather, and the UK food system is vulnerable, climate minister Katie White told New Scientist.

At the same time, she pushed back against “panic and fear” after environment minister Angela Eagle told Britons they should “store a bit of food that can keep you going for a while” in case of El Niño storms and flooding.

The collapse of the AMOC would be catastrophic. How will we know when it’s coming?

“Look, am I going out and buying loads of extra beans? I’ve always got a few cans of beans, but that’s mainly so I’m ready for when I’ve not had a chance to go to the shop,” said White. “So I’m not going out and doing that.”

The UK Met Office, the national weather service, has warned that the UK is likely to face an unusually warm, wet and stormy autumn and winter due to El Niño, which occurs every two to seven years. While late winter in the UK has often been cold and dry during El Niño, the current event is so strong that it could remain warm and rainy into spring.

If fields become too muddy, tractors may not be able to sow crops like winter wheat, as happened in the 2023-24 El Niño, or the plants could fail to sprout. Continued wet weather could undermine spring barley. Farmers could be forced to spend more on livestock feed and housing, raising meat and dairy prices as well.

Closer to the tropics, crops like rice could fail due to heat, drought and weakened monsoons. “We will have a wetter start to this winter… On the back of a very dry summer, that is difficult,” said White. “The food system is vulnerable.”

Large countries including China, Brazil and Germany have been building up stores of key foods like wheat, rice, corn and sugar. But the UK doesn’t keep substantial public food reserves.

White argued that the UK would be better off helping local farms and groceries to become more resilient to climate shocks. A task force she established that includes military experts and scientists will meet in October to scrutinise readiness for climate security threats, including to food.

“I don’t think we need to be in a position of grain stores, but I do think we do need to be looking at where the vulnerabilities are in the food system and how we support local production in the most sustainable way,” she said. “That’s going to be working with farmers and also on local supply chains.”

5 graphs that show how the record-breaking El Niño will affect the world

Farmers will probably have to plant more weather-resistant varieties or different crops entirely, according to Monika Zurek at the University of Oxford. The UK also needs to reduce its reliance on imports for 40 per cent of its food. But “grain storage is definitely part of the answer” as well, she says.

El Niño flooding could also threaten housing and infrastructure, and these risks will continue as climate change makes most of the world warmer and wetter. The UK should not only build anti-flood engineering works such as the Thames Barrier, but also restore ecosystems like wetlands to absorb excess water, said White. Extreme heat, which killed at least 35,000 people in Europe this year, is likely to bake the continent again next summer.

The long-term solution is for the UK and other countries to reach net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050, she said, a goal that right-wing parties have been increasingly attacking in the UK, the European Union and the US.

Yet the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, which White is a part of, is reportedly set to approve the Jackdaw gas field off Scotland, and may consent to the Rosebank oil field as well.
