Scale of City’s punishment is the only story but Premier League must bear some responsibility

The Guardian Mon, 28 Sep 2026 19:30:19 GMT

Manchester City have come out fighting against the guilty verdict but the Premier League faces questions of its own

Nothing is over, nothing is done. Or at least not judging by the bravura, balls-out confidence of Manchester City’s chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak, who remains convinced the past three days of whiplash are simply the drumroll before the big reveal, prelude to some clinching piece of evidence that will swish away the initial finding of guilt on the Premier League’s 100-plus charges.

This appears to be the official City position right now. Rope‑a‑dope litigation. Scooby‑Doo justice. A verdict that is simply exposition, buildup to that moment where we finally get to rip off the zombie mask and reveal the cranky old amusement park owner underneath, with his bulging ring‑binder full of irrefutable evidence of City’s innocence.

This is certainly one way of going about things. Lord Pannick KC, Mystery Machine Chambers. Come for the legal expertise. Stay for the unfathomable brinkmanship.

That great escape may still present itself in more nuanced ways, most obviously in the question of what the actual punishment is here. But even in the current in-between days this feels like the end of an era. The greatest decade in the history of nation-state football projects is over. They’re selling Pep wigs in Woolworths. And we have failed, barring that promised deus ex machina, to paint it sky blue.

So what next? It is understandable there should be a great deal of confusion. This has never happened before. It is without precedent. The common assumption is that events will unfold like this: sanctions first, perhaps as early as midweek. Then an appeal. Then whatever comes next. But someone is suing someone. And it won’t be cheap or quick.

For now, the scale of City’s punishment is the only story in town. A verdict means nothing without the hammer of actual consequences. The triumphalism of those who seem personally invested in seeing City fail could still turn out to be premature.

There are many suggestions of how this may play out. Among the more lenient is a combination of a major fine, a one-season points deduction and a transfer ban. In other words, punishment that looks like punishment but isn’t really. Everyone feels vaguely vindicated. We carry on.

There is the suggestion of political pressure applied by City’s owners, as reported most recently by Bloomberg, with the idea floated that the United Arab Emirates government wishes to see its investment protected as a quid pro quo for its trading partnership with the UK. This is not actually a conspiracy theory. It’s how the world works. Politics is real. Football is not.

At the other end of the scale is a suggestion the Premier League will press for major sanctions as a means of heading off a disastrous round of internecine litigation, club-on-club action that would risk torpedoing the thing we’ve all been watching for the past 15 years. Yes: truth, fair play, stolen glory. But won’t someone think of the brand?

Here is one small suggestion. If the verdict does hold up, the punishment handed down should include a lengthy ban on City having any kind of sponsorship. This would at least speak to the core of the charges, the allegation that state-owned companies were used to funnel in direct investment. It would force City to grow their revenue by more standard means. It may even have a beneficial effect.

Not that anyone is talking about compromise yet. One of the most notable aspects is how utterly entrenched aspects of City’s fanbase seem to be on this. Facts are malleable, principles relative. Everything must be bent to your interests.

There is a very important distinction here. It is entirely legitimate to question the existing rules. Maybe outside investment should be allowed. Spending your own money on your own property, pumping funds into the system, adding not taking: this seems not just reasonable but commendable. How can it be a crime?

This is to wilfully misunderstand the equation. If everyone else is obeying the rules, if the entire culture is based around competitiveness, then this becomes not just deceit and deliberate cheating, but a trashing of the basic idea of sport.

And, in the end, this affects people’s lives in tangible ways. Not just hopes and dreams, but employment, wellbeing, the goals you work for all your life. How many families have been uprooted, incomes affected, moments of happiness scrubbed by outcomes that might have gone the other way?

This is the state of cognitive dissonance described in al-Mubarak’s statement, which is also the only official comment by any party so far. It is not surprising there should be zero acknowledgement of any culpability, or even legitimacy to the charges. Hang on to a rising balloon and you face a difficult decision. Let go before it’s too late or just keep getting higher. Al-Mubarak is in a difficult position here, frontman for a propaganda project that has spectacularly crashed. Faced with this he has trebled and quadrupled down, and in the most tribalist way.

“This club matters to me,” al-Mubarak begins, a club executive who is, as things stand, guilty of destroying that club’s future prospects. There is dark talk of “media reporting”, with its implication of lies and fake news, as though this is all just another structural obstacle in the way of the true victims here, inherited dictatorial billionaires.

“Here’s what I said to my family,” al-Mubarak goes on, weirdly dragging his own relatives into the picture, before offering once again the most intriguing element, the suggestion there is some key detail here, some game-changing element City are desperate to get out, but which has so far been prevented from entering a properly constituted legal tribunal. “There are so many things that I would like to be able to share with you to help you understand why we feel so confident.” This is not a standard line after being found almost unanimously guilty.

So what is he getting at? Part of the problem is the rush to demonise only one side, to see simply bad guys and good guys. In reality, it seems likely the written judgment will heavily criticise the Premier League’s governance.

Rightly so. These charges have been doggedly pursued, but what about, well, everything else? How did an organisation that maintains its serial champions have been cheating for a decade and a half allow this entity into its competition in the first place? How did it fail so completely to regulate it?

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

How about, to choose one example, Roman Abramovich, the Kremlin-connected oligarch on whom the British government overnight imposed sanctions as an unfit person, whose own irregularities are well documented? The Premier League has always basically been a TV rights agency masquerading as a regulator. As long as the show rolls on, well, the show rolls on.

This is the only real conclusion to be drawn from any of this. Some kind of governance is being effected here. But this remains a leaking, lurching pirate ship of an organisation. In any sane version of the current timeline there would be pressure for a complete reconsideration of how and why the Premier League exists.

One thing was obvious years before the current state of emergency: countries should not own football clubs. Sovereign wealth funds should not own football clubs. There is an irreconcilable conflict of objectives here. All is fair in foreign policy. Countries will spy, steal and misdirect to gain influence. It is pretty much a patriotic duty to do these things.

But you really don’t need to invite that level of supra-judicial chicanery into your delicate cultural treasure of a sport. What did anyone think was going to happen here? What would the people of the Netherlands think if the UK government bought AZ Alkmaar and began pumping in funds via sponsorship deals with National Rail and the Highways Agency, all the while promising to play fair? This is what the Premier League has permitted. You don’t really get to act surprised when it goes a bit wonky.

It is also important to remember that English football hovers like a locust cloud over every other league. The reeling-in of talent and expertise is hugely destabilising. How are you supposed to feel in Germany or Belgium about the fact City and Chelsea have between them spent more than £3bn on transfer fees, all of which is now tainted, apparently put into circulation by something other than a legitimate sporting project?

There is a fair case for Uefa to seek recompense, even to withdraw its patronage until this bandit league gets its own house in order. This won’t happen, because of eyeballs and income flows. But this is down to the balance of power, not any sensible idea of procedure or morality.

What next, then? It is hard to see how a combined 89 charges of failure to provide accurate information or to cooperate with an investigation can be overturned on appeal. But it is also far from impossible. City’s bullishness is presumably based on information from their legal team. The next stage after appeal would be the high court, where different rules on evidence and the law may apply. Perhaps the long game is to get to that stage. It may even work, as it did at the court of arbitration for sport with the Uefa case. Or maybe they’re just planning to spin it out until everyone goes broke, dies or gets into esports.

But in the end, why would you do this? What do you actually want from football? Is proving to the last decimal point that this is all technically admissible really a desirable outcome? The level of sustained, destructive aggression is telling in itself. As are the potential macro-implications.

Most obviously, this case speaks more widely to the way money and power flow in and out of Britain. One version of the endgame is that City’s owners could be forced by the football regulator to sell up. Manchester City are a vast going concern. Imagine the wider shockwaves if this were to happen.

To take one example, a significant amount of the UK property market’s enduring rock‑solid value is built on the idea of inviolable property rights, safety in ownership. Where better to park your funds than a place where the rule of law seems to work for and not against you? London alone is said to have more than £4bn worth of value bound up in dark money. Imagine the ripple effects if a decision on a set of sporting regulations ends with a sovereign state being ordered to forfeit property. Never mind the abrupt lurch into negative equity. It’s enough to make you feel a little pride once more in the power of the wig and the rulebook.

More directly, this remains an existential threat to the league. Not least in the depth of ill-feeling. City’s owners clearly have a deep hostility towards their fellow Premier League members, who are being portrayed as partial and culturally biased. Why would you want to remain part of this organisation? Why would you make any effort to protect it?

Nothing is over, nothing is done. All that seems certain is that this would probably be a good time to hoist the death’s‑head flag and get that old Super League ship rolling again. There might just be a few more takers this time.

The Guardian Mon, 28 Sep 2026 19:07:45 GMT

Former journalist and honorary life president of Norwich City FC died peacefully at home on Monday

Michael Wynn-Jones, the journalist and husband of the TV chef Delia Smith, has died at the age of 85.

Wynn-Jones was honorary life president of Norwich City football club, which said everyone at the club was “deeply saddened” by his death.

The club said in statement: “Michael died peacefully at home on Monday morning, aged 85. He will be greatly missed. His family are grateful for the wonderful care provided by the community nursing team at St Elizabeth hospice in Ipswich.

“Our deepest condolences are with Delia and Tom [Smith, the couple’s nephew], and with all of Michael’s family, friends and loved ones. At the family’s request, we ask that their privacy be respected at this difficult time.”

Wynn-Jones lived with Smith near Stowmarket in Suffolk and they had been married for more than 50 years.

The couple oversaw several promotions to the Premier League for the Canaries, putting the club on a solid financial footing. Smith had a more prominent, public role at Norwich City but Wynn-Jones was reportedly regarded as a trusted adviser and influential figure in the boardroom.

Darren Huckerby, a former player for the club, posted a tribute saying Wynn-Jones “stayed out of the limelight but all at Norwich City FC owe him so much”.

Wynn-Jones worked as a journalist for titles including the Daily Mirror and the Spectator and founded his own publishing company.

He began attending Norwich City games in April 1955 at the age of 13. He wrote fondly of the club’s unlikely run to the FA Cup semi-final in 1959.

Norwich City Fans Social Club said in a statement: “All of us at NCFSC are devastated to hear the news about Michael Wynn-Jones passing. Michael is a true NCFC legend and what he did for the club cannot be underestimated. We are thinking of Delia, Tom and all of Michael’s family at this incredibly sad time. Rest in peace, Michael.”

Delia Smith previously told BBC Radio 4’s Desert Island Discs that she and Wynn-Jones bonded over their passion for food and football.

She said in 2021 she rarely cooked at home, leaving Wynn-Jones to hover over the stove while she went “to the end of the garden”.

Paris magic and tradition keep the Arc in a class of its own above the latest gimmicks

The Guardian Mon, 28 Sep 2026 19:00:42 GMT

It may not be the official best race in the world but winning at Longchamp still confers a status little else can match

When France-Galop announced in June that geldings will be allowed to run in the Prix de l’Arc de Triomphe from 2027, there was an underlying sense that action was needed to maintain the race’s status as Europe’s showpiece event. The Arc was officially the World’s Best Horse Race in five of the seven years after the award was introduced in 2015, but has fallen short of rivals including the Japan Cup and the Breeders’ Cup Classic since 2021 at a time when several geldings, including the French-trained Calandagan, have been among the world’s top-rated middle-distance horses.

Yet even a brief glance through the leading contenders for this year’s race at Longchamp on Sunday offers reminders that the Arc has a heritage and mystique that will always set it apart among the championship events around the globe. The names of the winners, both equine and human, retain their currency from one generation to the next.

Daryz, the favourite, will be the first male horse to win a second Arc since Alleged and Lester Piggott in 1978 if he comes home in front this weekend. Forty-eight years on, his main rival in the current betting is Maltese Cross – who is trained by Piggott’s son-in-law, William Haggas. Next in the list is Andrew Balding, who with Kalapana, the King George winner, will attempt to bring an Arc trophy back to Park House Stables in Kingsclere, 55 years after his father, Ian, trained Mill Reef for his historic success in 1971.

There is a sense of generational shift too about the fact that Joseph O’Brien’s Oaks winner, Thundering On, is a shorter price than any of his father Aidan’s three remaining runners. And at longer odds, Criquette Head, a multiple Arc-winning trainer like her father, Alec, is the part-owner of Pearled Majesty, while Jean-Claude Rouget, a dual winner as recently as 2020 and 2023 with Sottsass and Ace Impact, will close out his 48-year career when he saddles Arrow Eagle.

An Arc winner is special in a way that cannot be summed up in a rating, and so too is the sense of anticipation that unites tens of thousands of fans – French, British, Irish, Japanese and more – as they head into the Bois de Boulogne on the first Sunday in October.

Daryz heads a list of 19 possible runners after the latest declaration stage for the Arc on Monday, and while one of those, Sunly, seems more likely to take up an alternative engagement on Saturday, John & Thady Gosden’s Friendly Soul has earned a free supplementary entry via her win in the Prix Vermeille earlier this month and could be added to the field on Wednesday.

Meisho Tabaru and Admire Terra will attempt to snap Japan’s 0-for-36 losing streak in the Arc, which stretches all the way back to 1969, while Aidan O’Brien’s initial entry has been whittled down to three possible runners: Diamond Necklace, Minnie Hauk and Benvenuto Cellini.

So the field for Sunday’s Arc is beginning to take shape, but there is still much to be resolved before the runners go to post, including the draw and the going, which remains unusually quick for this time of year in Paris.

A drop or two of rain has crept into the weather forecast for the rest of the week but at this stage, the ground still seems likely to be no slower than good. That is excellent news for Maltese Cross, but less encouraging for supporters of Thundering On, whose participation has yet to be definitely confirmed as her connections hope for some ease in the ground.

The draw for stall positions, meanwhile, will be made on Thursday morning – under “the supervision of a Commissioner for Justice”, no less - but in another attempt to add to a sense of building excitement, the outcome will be kept under wraps until an “opening ceremony” on Thursday evening, which will be broadcast live on France-Galop’s YouTube channel.

This deadline for declaring jockeys and equipment, meanwhile, has been extended to later on Thursday evening, so it is entirely possible that riding arrangements for Aidan O’Brien’s three runners will be delayed until his first-choice jockey, Ryan Moore, knows where they are drawn.

Is the gimmickry entirely necessary? Probably not. But by Friday morning, the field will be set and thousands of racegoers will be packing their bags and setting off for Paris. The Arc may not have been the official best race of the year since 2021, but for many Flat racing fans, its unofficial status as the best race anywhere remains undimmed.

Absence of violence in Drumcree does not make standoff any less significant

The Guardian Mon, 28 Sep 2026 18:37:08 GMT

Row comes amid rising division and a tendency towards cynical political posturing in Northern Ireland

Three decades ago, it took the deaths of three Roman Catholic children – the Quinn brothers, Jason, nine, Mark, 10, and 11-year-old Richard – in a petrol bomb attack to bring an end to the Drumcree dispute. “No road is worth a life, let alone the lives of three little boys,” the Orange Order’s County Armagh chaplain said at the time.

It is perhaps extraordinary to think that this could ever have needed saying – but that was then. Northern Ireland is very different place today.

Passions are running high, but the attempt by 35 members of the Protestant Orange Order to walk down Garvaghy Road, a main thoroughfare in a predominantly nationalist part of Drumcree in Portadown, County Armagh, did not lead to violence on Sunday or Monday.

Faced with thousands of members of the nationalist community standing in their way and a police line ordering them back, Orange Order district master Nigel Dawson concluded: “There’s no point getting wet unnecessarily,” as he instructed members of the order back inside the church hall to shelter from the rain.

Every half-hour on Monday, the Orange Order members walked up to police lines only to be turned back by Supt Brendan Green, but the process was peaceful and respectful.

The blessed absence of the old ways does not make what is happening at Drumcree any less significant, however. History doesn’t repeat itself, and although hope and history sometimes rhyme, more often we hear echoes of history returning to us.

The divisions and tendency towards cynical political posturing in Northern Ireland, papered over by the 1998 Good Friday agreement – when all sides were exhausted by the hate and misery of the three decades of Troubles – have been all too evident of late.

This particular dispute can be reasonably argued either way. The independent Parades Commission has ruled that the march down the Garvaghy Road is permissible. The marchers are simply taking advantage of their rights, it may be said. But is it really necessary to take this road after 28 years of the march being banned? Who is served by the provocation?

The detail of the argument is perhaps less important than the fact that it is happening, and what that says about Northern Ireland today, and what it may mean for the future.

On the nationalist side, there has been growing and bristling self-confidence about the prospects of a border poll on a united Ireland. This was only inflated by Donald Trump’s recent suggestion that a unified Ireland should happen sooner rather than later. “The days of unionist supremacy and domination are gone,” said the first minister, Michelle O’Neill of Sinn Féin, on Monday after appearing herself in Drumcree. “We will not be going backwards.”

The numbers gathering from the nationalist community, some of whom were bussed in from Belfast and Derry, appeared to surprise the Police Service of Northern Ireland. It was a moment of unity within an often fractured nationalist community.

Those in attendance included Colin Duffy and his brother Paul, who were both acquitted of terror charges in 2015, along with the SDLP party leader Claire Hanna, a vehement critic of those who reach for violence as an answer.

Meanwhile, for the unionists, the changed relationship with the rest of the UK brought about by the Brexit deal and changing demographics has arguably engendered a distinct lack of confidence about the future.

Gavin Robinson, the leader of the Democratic Unionist party (DUP), the largest unionist party, claimed on Monday that “standards have been shattered” by the presence of the first minister with the protesters in Drumcree.

When O’Neill and Mary Lou McDonald, the leader of Sinn Féin in the Republic of Ireland, arrived at the protest, it was to chants of “bring it down” and “fuck Stormont”, in reference to power-sharing arrangements in Northern Ireland, structured to make unionists and nationalists work together.

“How we can go forward when there is such a level of disdain for the simple fundamental democratic principles of society?” asked Robinson of the attempt by the first minister to block a lawful march.

It is likely that the prospect of elections for the Northern Ireland assembly next year, and the need to rally the faithful to their respective cause, is not helping to calm the rhetoric.

In Stormont, the speaker, Edwin Poots, a former leader of the DUP, condemned the first minister for her “gross discourtesy” and “contempt” in not coming to answer an urgent question about the crisis.

In this context, there is concern that even if Sinn Féin’s leaders, with the crowds’ chants ringing in their ears, do not walk out of the Northern Ireland executive, that the DUP could well do so.

After a prolonged period in which agreement on a budget for Northern Ireland’s collapsing public services has not been found with Westminster, such further fracturing risks a whole new level of instability.

The Northern Ireland secretary, Chris Bryant, spoke to Breandán Mac Cionnaith, from the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition, on Monday. The possibility of mediation was discussed, Mac Cionnaith said. Speaking in the Republic, Micheál Martin, the taoiseach, called for cool heads. “No one wants to go back to the past divisions, to past trauma that we experienced at Garvaghy Road, Drumcree, in the past,” he said. “I would say to Sinn Féin and to everybody else: time to dial back now and time to engage in dialogue, and to work this out in a sensible, community-based way.”

The Guardian view on the Drumcree parade: ghosts from the past have brought Stormont to the brink

The Guardian Mon, 28 Sep 2026 17:44:41 GMT

A reckless decision to authorise an Orange Order parade with a notorious history has deepened the political crisis in the Northern Ireland executive

The last time that the Orange Order successfully marched from Drumcree parish church down the Garvaghy Road, a mainly Catholic part of Portadown, it required a British army presence and a lockdown of locals forced off their own streets. The 1997 parade was preceded by loyalist death threats and followed by nationalist riots, in which more than 160 people were injured. The lengthy track record of lethal violence and disorder associated with the march led the Parades Commission – established the following year as part of the peace process – to ban it.

On Sunday, however, in scenes that rolled back the years in deeply unwelcome fashion, the old traumas and hostilities were recklessly allowed to resurface. Unfathomably, after a routine decision to renew the ban this year was challenged on procedural grounds, the commissioners reversed their ruling late last week and permitted a march to go ahead on a limited scale. The entirely predictable result was a tense standoff and a political crisis in Stormont, after protesters blocked the Garvaghy Road route until the early hours of Monday morning.

Facilitating the parade – a decision witheringly criticised by the Irish taoiseach, Micheál Martin – was a grievous unforced error on the part of the Parades Commission. Police advice that it was unlikely to provoke disorder was tin-eared, given the context. Orange Order parades now take place without incident across Northern Ireland each summer. But Drumcree’s notorious history makes it prime territory for unionists seeking to reignite a culture war and provoke a response.

Thankfully, violence was averted. But the continuing fallout of a needless episode has dangerously exacerbated tensions in the deadlocked Northern Ireland executive, as it approaches a final Westminster deadline for agreeing a budget. Unionist demands for a police investigation, on the grounds that the Sinn Féin first minister, Michelle O’Neill, broke the law by attending the protest, are indicative of a polarising political climate that bodes ill for the future.

Depressingly, in the short term that may suit both Sinn Féin and the Democratic Unionist party (DUP). After being damaged by internal scandal and spectacular misjudgments over Brexit, the DUP is attempting to shore up its base and see off a challenge from the still more hardline Traditional Unionist Voice party. Sinn Féin’s support has also been slipping amid stasis at Stormont and calls for a faster push towards a united Ireland.

As division and acrimony deepen, the desire of most voters for a functioning executive seems dismally low on the list of priorities. The Drumcree standoff was the worst possible way to begin a crunch week of talks over a budget that should have been set six months ago. On Sunday, the new Northern Ireland secretary, Sir Chris Bryant, flew to Belfast to meet political leaders and members of the Garvaghy Road residents’ association. He already looks to have one of the most challenging jobs in Andy Burnham’s cabinet, as cross-party relations in the assembly break down and fears of a DUP walkout mount.

Calling for “calm on all sides”, the prime minister has stressed the need to preserve the gains made since the Good Friday agreement. That is the right message. But disastrously wrong calls on Drumcree, from bodies that should have known better, have now brought Stormont to the brink.

The Guardian view on Britain’s new chancellor: his purpose must be to protect living standards

The Guardian Mon, 28 Sep 2026 17:44:08 GMT

John Healey has offered a vision, but an energy shock will mean households and businesses need to be offered help in the budget

In his first speech to Labour party conference as chancellor, John Healey offered prudence with a purpose in a speech stylistically redolent of his former boss Gordon Brown. Mr Healey made fiscal credibility the condition for his goal of turbocharging apprenticeships for young people, funding for unions to reskill workers and spending on defence to create manufacturing jobs. The speech’s imagery was canny: miners, shipyards and submarines give “reindustrialisation” a recognisable Labour history. He also faced the future with a clever line about British workers “harnessing AI, not being outrun by it”. His message was that the “politics of hope” will be earned through “fiscal discipline, good work and through strong industries”.

The new Labour chancellor sounded like New Labour when he claimed that it was “not progressive to allow a bigger and bigger benefits bill”. What was lacking was a plan for care work, public services and the energy transition. Mr Healey clearly has a story about the supply of properly trained workers and another one about revitalising industry, but he offered little explanation of how enough good jobs will be created across the wider economy. Labelling a defence contract “industrial renewal” does not prove it is the best use of state capacity.

Worldwide economic shocks and trade tensions, Mr Healey warned, are being felt hard at home – from prices at the pump to monthly mortgage payments. Andy Burnham offered the public “breathing space” when he entered Downing Street – with a £150 warm‑home discount for 6m low-income households and an electricity VAT cut worth £45 for bill payers. But with no end in sight to the war on Iran and the resulting disruption to the strait of Hormuz, that will not be enough. Energy bills are forecast to rise by as much as 26% in January. One projection sees a typical household’s bill jump by £442 to £2,165. Petrol is at its highest price since the summer of 2022, while diesel is approaching its all‑time high.

What was left unsaid by Mr Healey was far more important than what was said. He made no promise of additional support for individuals and businesses in the forthcoming budget. But with a price shock imminent, surely this is the real purpose behind his prudence. Mr Healey has tied his hands with his predecessor’s fiscal rules. The self-imposed restraint limits the chancellor’s ability to respond to an energy shock.

According to City economists, Mr Healey has only around half the £24bn headroom that the Treasury had earlier this year. Fuel duty is set to start rising from January – but leaving it at current levels until the end of this parliament would cost roughly £3.6bn. In June, the Trades Union Congress proposed covering two-thirds of households with targeted help that would cost £6bn. Such schemes would use up most of the headroom, even before offering business reliefs.

Mr Healey is choosing the size of the buffer as his test of credibility. But he must also protect living standards. Having criticised Tory austerity in his speech, it’s hard to see how he could announce large-scale departmental cuts. The size of the headroom that the chancellor is prepared to tolerate will determine whether his budget looks like taxing to fund a modest energy rescue package, or borrowing for a larger one.

Five UK nationals arrested near RAF Fairford released on bail

The Guardian Mon, 28 Sep 2026 17:31:14 GMT

Police say alleged offences could have been committed ‘knowingly or unknowingly’ on behalf of a foreign state

Five men arrested over a suspected bomb plot at RAF Fairford have been released on bail as police investigate why they were so close to the airbase in three vans with suspicious material in the back.

The five suspects were revealed to be British men, all in their 20s and from London. They had been arrested in the Gloucestershire countryside early on Sunday morning on suspicion of explosives offences and preparing an act of terrorism, with an Iranian link a key line of inquiry.

Their release on police bail suggests detectives believe it is unlikely they were on the brink of a mass casualty attack by exploding a bomb close to the base, sources said.

An Iranian link is still under investigation, as is whether any of the five were paid to gather in the village of Whelford, two miles from RAF Fairford.

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, called a meeting of the government’s crisis committee Cobra over the events and Iran’s possible role.

An initial examination of the vans led police to suspect they carried explosive materials, with assessments made as to whether they were viable improvised explosive devices.

The head of UK counter-terrorism policing, the assistant commissioner Laurence Taylor, said the release of the men on bail did not mean the investigation was over and that they were subject to “stringent conditions”.

He said: “I know there is significant interest in whether the current geopolitical context has a bearing on this incident. At counter-terrorism policing we are working within this context every day, and at this stage we are keeping an open mind in this investigation.

“We have, as you would expect, ensured that our protective security advice and posture remain commensurate to the threat. But be assured, we are considering this from every possible angle. Including, that this may be activity committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state.”

Iran is suspected of using proxies in the UK, in incidents ranging from alleged arson attacks against Jewish targets to men flying a basic drone near the Israeli embassy.

Taylor said: “Often this threat becomes visible to us as criminal activity, often at a small scale and committed by individuals whose primary aim is not terrorism but a quick financial gain. It can be harder to spot, and to that end I would ask the public to remain vigilant and report anything suspicious to police.”

Donald Trump claimed on Sunday that the men “were looking to do big damage” at the base, used by the US air force, which was taken as revealing a serious terror plot.

On Monday, the US president expressed surprise that the suspects had been bailed. He said: “I would not have released them.”

Taylor said: “I can confirm that following extensive interviews and inquiries, the five men who were arrested are being released on police bail this afternoon. They absolutely remain under investigation as we explore multiple lines of inquiry.”

Police said the five men were all from London, one aged 23, three aged 24, and one aged 25. They were arrested after a farmer driving home from a party spotted them. She said she believed they were wearing balaclavas and they ran away when her headlights illuminated them. She then called the police.

Trump also suggested the plot was known to the US authorities. But British sources suggested the specific activities of the men were unknown.

The base had been at its highest state of alert, called delta, for several days beforehand because of a general threat, with extra security measures.

The farmer said she was surprised it had been left to her to disrupt the activities of the men.

In a round of broadcast interviews, the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said the woman had only a “partial picture” of the events.

About 85 households in the Cotswolds village of Whelford were evacuated early on Sunday morning to a leisure centre, with a 400-metre cordon placed around the white vans as bomb disposal robots examined them.

At the Labour party conference, the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said the evacuated residents should shortly be able to return home.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps had made threats against RAF Fairford in July.

Iran’s embassy in London denied any involvement in the events in Whelford. It said: “The embassy of the Islamic Republic of Iran in London categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran to arrest of five suspects in the vicinity of RAF Fairford base.

“The circulation of such fabricated speculations, particularly in the aftermath of the criminal acts of aggression committed by the United States and the Israeli regime against the Iranian people, will serve no purpose other than to fuel Iranophobia propaganda in the UK.”

Reality pays a visit to the Labour party conference, but it’s the ‘Hope Again’ that kills you

The Guardian Mon, 28 Sep 2026 17:20:44 GMT

Most MPs are clinging to this year’s Beckettian slogan, but the chancellor brought his own brand of despair

UK politics live – latest updates

It could be just me, but I’m beginning to find that all this “hope” stuff is getting me down. Everywhere you go at the Labour party conference, you are being urged to “Hope Again”. It’s on the screens in the main hall and on banners in the exhibition area. It’s on T-shirts, balloons and coffee mugs. It’s all just a bit much. Overkill. You now bump into Labour MPs who are visibly collapsing under the strain of having to walk around with an optimistic perma-grin. And the conference is only into its second day. Come Wednesday they will all be on intravenous Valium.

What does “Hope Again” even mean? Is it an instruction? Have we all been hoping in a highly unsatisfactory way so far? Are we being sent back to hope school to learn how to be more upbeat? In which case, I rather think these remedial classes in hoping will be wasted on me. I’ve always been a bit miserable. It feels a bit like someone going round and telling you “Smile. It may never happen.” Or to “Keep calm and carry on.” There are also distinct echoes of Samuel Beckett: Fail again. Fail better. Only in Liverpool it’s: Hope again. Hope better.

You also can’t help feeling that all this talk of hope is wasted on John Healey. He is a man with a naturally low-energy vibe. Someone in touch with the darker, more depressing side of his own personality. A man after my own heart.

As someone with the touch of Harry Potter’s Dementors, ready to suck the joy out of any occasion, he knows that anything that can go wrong almost certainly will go wrong. Anything good is merely a transitory, illusory state. Take Healey to the football and he will show you a bad time. His home team of Rotherham might go 2-0 up in the 88th minute and John will assure you they’ve peaked too soon – they are nailed on to lose 3-2. I speak from experience. I’ve done it myself. John, meet John.

Luckily for me, no one is expecting me to be a ray of sunshine. That’s way above my pay grade. Unfortunately for Healey, optimism was precisely what he was required to deliver in his first speech as chancellor to a nearly full Labour conference hall. To be the fiscal embodiment of “Hope Again”. To give us all a reason to live just a little longer.

Only he just couldn’t do it. He was never going to be able to do it. When John sees a “Hope Again” banner, what he reads is “Despair Again”. Come the end of his half hour on stage, he had managed to convert most of the audience to his way of thinking. At lunchtime, the queues for the assisted dying helpline tailed back into the city centre.

Not that Healey didn’t give it his best shot. He dropped the word hope into almost every sentence – or his minders had dropped it in for him – and every time, the lights seemed to get a bit dimmer. It was a battle of hope against hope. People had come willing him to succeed. To pull off one of the most astonishing personality transplants of the year.

Within minutes, though, a pall of depression hung over the hall. We were all just waiting for it to end. Hardly anyone could be bothered to even clap. The only standing ovation came for the reintroduction of the £15m Union Learning Fund. To give this some perspective, £15m is just a bit more than what the London townhouse of the Tory shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, is worth. Not that it’s a bad idea. It’s just not going to reboot the economy.

And it’s hard to blame Healey. Maybe another more dynamic and charismatic chancellor could have shifted the mood in the hall with feelgood vibes. But as well as being a bit miserable, Healey is also a realist. He knows things are tough and likely to get tougher. No amount of energy price caps and £2 bus fares are going to make a major dent in a cost of living which is only heading in one direction. Nor is it his fault. He is not responsible for austerity, Brexit, the war in Iran and the cost of borrowing. But he is the current fall guy. The chancellor tasked with fixing the unfixable.

Sign up to First Edition

after newsletter promotion

So what we got instead was a touch of nostalgia. A deep dive into the stories Labour has written about its achievements. Times when hope was very much alive. Just not now, no matter how often Healey prefixed his sentences with the H-word. Inevitably, though, the truth came out. How he wished he was chancellor back in the late 90s when the economy was on track and there was money to spare. Instead, we were where we were. You can tell people that the UK is the fastest-growing economy in the G7, but it counts for little if everyone still feels broke and broken.

There was talk of growth. Of reindustrialisation. But mostly of the need for fiscal discipline. Which is code for saying that the budget in four weeks’ time is unlikely to be a bundle of fun for anyone. Look forward to some tax rises and welfare cuts. There was also a commitment to spend £6m on shipyards to build the UK’s nuclear submarines. Money that had already been promised. Always the best money for a government to spend. Old money repurposed as new.

Come the end, no one could have been in any doubt about the scale of the challenge ahead. Despite trying to be someone else, Healey had not been able to be anything but himself. And why not? It’s not as if there are any easy answers. Nor do the Tories and Reform have any solutions. They are just chancers pedalling pipe dreams. But most of the Liverpool audience hadn’t come for this. They had been told to come for hope and they wanted half an hour off to enjoy themselves. Instead they had been confronted with cold reality.

Merseyside blaze that killed mother and three children caused by lithium-ion battery

A fire that left a mother and her three children dead was caused by a lithium-ion battery, firefighters in Merseyside have said.

An electrical event caused the battery, of a type commonly used in vapes, ebikes and e-scooters, to go into “thermal runaway”, Merseyside fire and rescue service said.

Crews arrived at the blaze, which ripped through the house in Bootle, at about 3.45am on Tuesday 22 September.

Four people were discovered in an upstairs bedroom showing no signs of life, a fire service spokesperson said. North West ambulance’s hazardous area response team later confirmed that all four had died.

They were named by police as Elisha Brabin, 36, Leo Brabin, 16, Ellis Brabin, eight, and seven-year-old Prudence Brabin.

At the fire’s height, six crews were on the scene and eight firefighters entered the house.

The fire service’s head of prevention, Kevin Johnson, said: “This is a devastating incident and our thoughts are very much with the family and friends of the mother and children who lost their lives and those who were injured.

“This tragedy highlights the very real risks posed by lithium-ion batteries, which we confirmed as the source of the fire.”

The service did not confirm what the lithium-ion battery at the home was being used for.

Johnson said: “We’re urging people to follow the manufacturer’s instructions, only using batteries and chargers which have been supplied with the vehicle or approved by the manufacturer, as anything else can pose a huge fire risk.

“It’s also important to know and recognise the signs that your lithium-ion battery may be failing – if it is swelling, making unusual sounds, has a strong smell, is failing to charge or is smoking, please stop using immediately.”

In a tribute issued on Wednesday, relatives of the victims said: “Elisha was our beloved daughter, wife, mother, sister, aunty, niece and cousin. She was a devoted and loving mother who lived for her children. They were her whole world, and she meant everything to us.

“Our beautiful babies, Leo, Ellis and Prudence, were loved beyond measure and brought so much joy, happiness and love to our family. They filled our lives with laughter and precious memories that we will cherish for ever.

“The tragic loss of Elisha and our three precious children has left us heartbroken. They have all been taken from us far too soon. The loss we are experiencing is unimaginable, and the impact on our family will be felt for ever.”

The Guardian Mon, 28 Sep 2026 17:00:14 GMT

Campaign broadcast across France encourages people to come forward even if they have little to no memory of attack

Gisèle Pelicot is the figurehead of a new campaign run by her daughter to encourage people who suspect they have been drugged and sexually assaulted to come forward, even if they have little to no memory of the attack.

Caroline Darian, 47, who believes she was also drugged and assaulted by her father, Dominique Pelicot – her mother’s ex-husband – launched a primetime public information push on Monday across France’s television network, on social media, in the press and on posters.

Her 73-year-old mother became an international symbol of courage and resistance when she insisted shame must change sides during the trial of her former husband and dozens of men who raped her while she was unconscious.

Video clips featuring Gisèle Pelicot state that in 75% of cases of sexual abuse while drugged, the perpetrator is a relative or friend. She urges those who believe they may be victims to contact the Centre of Excellence on Substance-Facilitated Assaults (CRAFS).

The centre is attached to the Paris university hospital service (AP-HP) and staffed by experts who can suggest to those who believe they may have been a victim of drugging and abuse what evidence there might be and how it can be obtained.

Darian, the founder of the association Mendorspas (Don’t Put Me to Sleep), said: “When you launch a campaign of this scale, having my mother’s backing sends a really powerful message. It’s also a message of hope for victims, showing that it is possible to get back on your feet.”

The trial of Dominique Pelicot two years ago shocked the world. For almost a decade he had drugged his wife, raped her and invited strangers into their home in the village of Mazan, 20 miles from Avignon, to rape her while she was in a state of near coma.

Pelicot’s horrific ordeal might have gone unremarked had she not decided to waive her anonymity and insist the case be held in public. Dominique Pelicot and 50 other men were convicted.

The trial sparked the reporting of other cases of what UK police call drug-facilitated sexual abuse, or DFSA. Earlier this month, a man in his 60s pleaded guilty to drugging and raping his wife over two decades and inviting strangers to abuse her, in the latest in a string of similar crimes.

After the publication of her book A Hymn to Life: Shame Has to Change Sides earlier this year, Pelicot said: “Shame sticks to you, it sticks to your skin. And that shame is a double sentence, it’s a suffering you inflict on yourself.”

Darian told Le Parisien: “It’s not because someone doesn’t remember that there aren’t traces or tests possible. Our aim is that these women can take back their own stories, so they no longer feel ashamed or afraid of not being heard by the police, not believed by the legal system and not supported by their family or those close to them.”

She added: “Launching a campaign on this scale is quite unprecedented for an issue that was not recognised at all as a public health concern as recently as five years ago. When I started campaigning, nobody had heard of it [chemical submission] apart from a small circle of doctors. The Mazan trial was a major turning point with a global reach.

“We’re getting somewhere but the fight is far from over. The message we want to send is that if you have a doubt, you need to look into it. Just because you cannot remember something, doesn’t mean there are no traces of it.”

Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio. org/rcip/internl. html

How the Manchester City scandal could play out

Thirty six years ago, the team I support, Swindon Town, were severely punished for financial irregularities that pale into comparison with those of Manchester City (Manchester City found guilty of breaking Premier League’s financial fair play rules, 25 September). We were initially sentenced to be relegated two divisions but, after appeal, refused entry to Division One. It was an incredibly painful experience for us as fans and I feel for those City fans who have enjoyed the last years so fully, but now see it tainted through no fault of theirs.

At the time, a number of journalists made the case that, as off-field crimes had resulted in on-field success, the punishment was fitting. What is different this time is the scale of the offences and the amount of on-field success. Once the appeal process has concluded, and if Manchester City still face punishment, a proportionate scaling up of consequences from those that we experienced in 1990 could mean that club facing relegation and removal of titles.

The question is whether the footballing authorities are willing to deal with one of their marquee brands with the same dispassionate ruthlessness that they used to deal with us 36 years ago. Tim BeaumontLiverpool

It’s unusual for me to find fault with anything that the wonderful Barney Ronay writes, but I must dispute his piece about Manchester City (The age of asterisk: Manchester City’s glittering era of success is tainted now, 25 September) on two counts.

As a supporter of 50 years’ standing, I would not be unhappy to see my beloved club relegated or hit with any other fully justified punishment. But if money alone ensured success, a number of English clubs would have won far more trophies in the past 10 or 20 years.

Money did not enable City players to train harder or run faster, let alone put together all the manifold and complex qualities that go into making the remarkable football team that they have been at various times.

As the magnificent Rodri has said, City’s victories were paid for with effort, with partnership and with being shoulder to shoulder each and every day. Furthermore, the claim that City wouldn’t have won this or that trophy without this or that player is impossible to prove. Richard BryantLondon

As a lifelong Liverpool supporter I might be expected to indulge in a little schadenfreude at the kicking that Manchester City is receiving, but it is obvious that over the last 15 years or so, the club has brought much more than footballing glory to Manchester. Tens of millions of pounds have been spent on the successful regeneration of a huge area of urban decay and the club’s City in the Community scheme has benefited large numbers of children through its training sessions in schools and imaginatively planned multifunctional play areas in parks. Marilyn RowleyDidsbury, Manchester

Barney Ronay might be right to feel some sympathy for Manchester City followers. But this should surely be restricted to children and to longstanding supporters who endured years of miserable underachievement. What if the Seven Up! series started today?

The Guardian Mon, 28 Sep 2026 16:53:34 GMT

Gordon McDougall recalls finding the original children to feature in the documentary strand that started in 1964

In your editorial on the Up series (20 September), your point is well made that exposing seven‑year-olds on television today would expose them to dangers not encountered in the 60s. However, Seven Up! was made in the early part of 1964, not 1963 as you stated, and it was the brainchild of Tim Hewat, the producer of World in Action.

As he was leaving the series, the oversight was given to the Canadian director Paul Almond and, for our first jobs after passing through training, Michael Apted and I were given the task of finding the original 20 children (14 of whom were followed in subsequent films). The show was seen as a one‑off and it was only at the instigation of Denis Forman, then CEO of Granada TV, that the follow-up, 7 Plus Seven, was commissioned in 1969. I was too busy running the Stables Theatre Club to work on it, so Apted directed it alone.

There was no obligation on any of the participants to take part in any of the follow-up programmes and, as your editorial points out, some declined either partly or entirely. I have kept in touch with the 14 who made it through to 63 Up and, while some have complained of a socialist bias to the series, none have felt their lives impaired by taking part in it.

Indeed, as seen in Nick’s desire to be as famous as a scientist as he is from the series, or Tony being asked for a selfie instead of his taxi passenger, Buzz Aldrin, fame has had a pleasurable, even comic aspect. And the interaction between participants who would not otherwise have known each other has often been very positive.

Although Hewat’s intention was to show the inevitability of change beyond the age of seven and thus the inequality of society, our aim in the original search was to find interesting children. This was, of course, mediated by the decision to explore extremes – in income ranges and privilege as well as in urban/rural and north/south locations. But I feel it is certain that, were the series to be started today, the disparities between a similar selection of children would be even greater. Gordon McDougallClevedon, Somerset

Labour’s modest reheat of help to buy is worth a try

The Guardian Mon, 28 Sep 2026 16:51:26 GMT

Turning to George Osborne’s playbook may look awkward, but cutting deposits to 2.5% could jolt a housebuilding sector stuck in a funk

What you need to know about Your First Home scheme

There may be three reasons why the Labour government has hesitated until now to reheat the Tories’ decade-long help-to-buy scheme. First, the inflationary risks of throwing subsidies at the housing market at a moment when wider inflation, driven by energy prices and the Iran war, is on the march.

Second, the political awkwardness of turning to George Osborne’s playbook. Third, the spectre of Jeff Fairburn, the shameless former boss of Persimmon who bagged a £75m bonus in 2018 as help to buy turbo-charged the value of his share-based incentives. The government would look foolish if, in its desperation to meet its housebuilding targets (or just miss them by a smaller margin), it created more Fairburns.

So is Your First Home – Labour’s incarnation – justified? On balance, it’s probably worth a punt. Something has to happen to try to shift the housebuilding sector out of its current funk. The way things are going, and the way mortgage rates are heading, Labour won’t merely miss its target of 1.5m new homes in England in this parliament, it will be short by a few hundreds of thousands.

Like it or not, the government needs the private firms to boost construction. At the moment, the prevailing narrative is grumbles over labour costs, raw material costs, tax, regulation and more. Share buy-backs are being preferred over new projects.

A tweak on the “affordability” dial at least has the virtue of getting results. Or, at least, that was a top-line conclusion in the official independent report published by the housing department earlier this month on help to buy. The scheme represented “very high value for money”, it said, with a net present social value of £25.1bn, in 2025 money, over its 2013-2023 lifetime thanks to the increase in housing supply. As for the inflationary impact, the report put it at two percentage points – far lower than popularly believed.

From the government’s point of view, those trade-offs will look attractive when there is little else to excite in the economic outlook for 2027. Being seen to do something for aspiring first-time buyers unable to get on to the housing ladder is rarely a bad political look.

Just don’t expect miracles. The 10%-plus jump in housebuilders’ shares prices on Monday, from beaten-down levels, may give a misleading impression. Your First Home will reduce the first-time buyer’s deposit to as little as 2.5% of the price of the property, from 5% under help to buy, but it is being launched in a very different climate.

Back in 2013, interest rates were on the floor, and they would remain so for years. Now, the Bank rate stands at 3.75%, and the debate is about how many hikes Threadneedle Street has in store. A 20% equity loan from the government, with an interest-free period, makes a difference but obviously does not remove the impact of borrowing rates on the rest of the mortgage. And in this case the housebuilders will have to pay a fee to access the scheme – quite rightly, but they will presumably look to recoup some of that expense in the selling price.

Full details, including the household income cap, the property price caps by region and the interest-free period, will arrive in the budget next month. All matter, so it’s too soon to make firm judgments. But the general principle here is to try to stimulate more supply of new-builds by modestly improving affordability for first-time buyers. In current circumstances, it’s not unreasonable.

High screen time can hurt children’s learning and language skills, study suggests

The Guardian Mon, 28 Sep 2026 16:50:40 GMT

Effect of elevated screen exposure could be as significant as parental behaviour and premature birth, report says

The effect of high screen time on children is as significant as parental behaviour and premature birth, if not greater, a global study has found.

Researchers examined data on more than 2.8 million children across 64 countries and concluded that elevated screen exposure could affect children in areas including academic achievement and emotional problems. It is one of the largest ever studies on the subject.

The impacts are “similar in magnitude to or larger” than other factors linked to child development and mental health outcomes including family wealth, the behaviour of parents and whether or not children were born prematurely.

Higher screen use for gaming, social media and streaming can lead to lower academic achievement and language development issues, the study suggests.

Some experts said the report had limitations, arguing that the findings in “no way” support the belief that screens are the main cause of adolescent distress.

Researchers found in the review, published in the journal JAMA Pediatrics, that children who spend more time on screens have higher “socioemotional” and mental health problems. Academics conducted a so-called umbrella review, which summarises results from previous large reviews on the topic.

Researchers found that longer durations of digital and social media use were linked to “less favourable outcomes across multiple (although not all) measured domains of children’s developmental health”. The analysis covered a variety of devices, from smartphones to televisions, and a range of activities including scrolling social media, gaming and FaceTime calls.

“Together, the findings suggest that screen use may represent one potentially modifiable factor associated with children’s wellbeing across multiple domains,” the report said.

It found that greater screen exposure was associated with overall lower grades at school. When academics examined specific subjects, screen time did not appear to be linked to maths, reading or science attainment, but the researchers said these were “among the least studied”, so the finding may be due to a lack of evidence.

The researchers, led by academics at the University of Calgary in Canada, did find that higher screen time was also linked to poorer language development.

When they looked at mental health, they found that higher screen use was linked to emotional and “peer problems”; “internalising behaviour”, which includes symptoms of depression and anxiety; and externalising behaviour, including aggression and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder symptoms.

“Our review revealed that higher so-called doses of screen exposure are associated with lower overall academic achievement and poorer language development, as well as higher internalising and externalising behaviour, emotional problems and peer problems,” the authors wrote.

“Notably, these effect sizes are similar in magnitude to or larger than those reported for other well-established predictors of children’s outcomes, such as socioeconomic status, parenting behaviour and preterm birth.”

Tatiana Íñiguez Berrozpe, a senior lecturer in sociology at the University of Zaragoza in Spain, said the report showed an association between screen time and poor mental health and academic performance, but it was small.

“This is not an insignificant finding, but it in no way supports the mantra that screens are the main cause of adolescent emotional distress,” she said. “Screen use alone does not explain why a teenager is emotionally distressed or performs less well academically.”

Esther van Sluijs, a professor of behavioural epidemiology at Loughborough University, said the study was “high-quality” but could not differentiate between different types of screen use.

“It cannot draw robust conclusions about specific types of screen use, like social media use or gaming, as there was not enough data to study this. We should therefore be cautious in interpreting these results in the context of young people’s current screen use habits,” she said.

The Guardian Mon, 28 Sep 2026 16:36:03 GMT

Minnesota will receive fifth-round pick for quarterback

Jameis Winston to remain as Giants’ starting QB

The New York Giants have acquired quarterback JJ McCarthy from the Minnesota Vikings for a 2027 fifth-round draft pick.

The Vikings announced the trade on Monday pending McCarthy passing a physical.

The Giants made the aggressive move days after Jaxson Dart had surgery on his left knee that will sideline him for at least the rest of the regular season.

Jameis Winston started and led the Giants to victory over Tennessee on Sunday, but the team failed to score a touchdown and had just 238 yards of offense. Giants head coach John Harbaugh says that Winston will start again this Sunday against Arizona.

“Jameis is starting. You guys asked me that [Sunday] night. He’s our starting quarterback and that’s how we’re rolling,” Harbaugh said on Monday, after the McCarthy trade had been announced. “We’ll be ready to play this next game and going forward. Excited about Jameis ... I’m looking forward to seeing where we go and as we go we’ll get a chance to build around Jameis’s strengths.”

It’s unclear what New York’s QB situation will be moving forward after the addition of McCarthy. He was the 10th pick in the 2024 draft but lost the starting job in Minnesota to Kyler Murray and fell behind Carson Wentz on the depth chart. McCarthy’s career in Minnesota will go down as a failure. He was hampered by poor form, injuries and perceived immaturity during his time with the Vikings. He played just 10 games and so far has thrown more interceptions (12) than touchdowns (11) in the NFL.

Just 23, McCarthy still has plenty of time to develop. As a college quarterback, he won a national title at Michigan, where his coach was John Harbaugh’s brother, Jim.

“[Jim] always had good things to say about JJ,” John Harbaugh said on Monday. “I mean, I kind of watched it. I was following Michigan when Jim was coaching there. I don’t follow him as much anymore, but when Jim was there that was a team I watched closely. So I’ve watched JJ play a lot.”

McCarthy lost only three games as the starter through high school and college, including a 27-1 record at Michigan on the way to the championship, but he came to the Vikings with minimal experience as a pro-style passer after being in Jim Harbaugh’s run-heavy offense. The energy and toughness that helped McCarthy become a winner and a leader at the lower levels worked against him at times last season, with a tendency for recklessness and a pattern of inaccuracy that contributed to his disappointing debut.

Minnesota coach Kevin O’Connell’s credentials as a play designer, play caller and QB mentor gave the Vikings plenty of confidence that McCarthy could thrive with them, but a torn meniscus in his first preseason game required surgery and delayed his first professional game until September 2025.

The success Sam Darnold had under O’Connell in 2024 contributed to the decision to let him leave as a free agent and build around McCarthy and his salary cap-friendly rookie contract, but the combination of immaturity, inexperience and injuries was too much for the Vikings to overcome last year. McCarthy missed time because of a sprained ankle, a concussion and a broken hand.

Buccaneers quarterback Baker Mayfield is out at least three weeks with a dislocated thumb injury, Tampa Bay coach Todd Bowles said Monday.

Mayfield dislocated the thumb on his right throwing hand in a 23-16 loss to the Vikings on Sunday. He was hit by Minnesota linebacker Blake Cashman during a throw in the final minutes of the game.

Rookie Jalon Daniels will replace Mayfield. The Buccaneers host the Green Bay Packers this Sunday.

County pride and England chaos relegated Hundred to summer undercard

The Guardian Mon, 28 Sep 2026 16:25:31 GMT

Franchise tournament remains an enigma after an unexpectedly dramatic men’s international summer and a thrilling Championship title race

After pumping astronomical sums of money into English cricket, the headline act of the summer should probably have been the Hundred’s rebirth under private ownership. After all, the decks were relatively clear.

There was no Ashes series or Indian arm-wrestle in Test cricket to hog the limelight, rather a small-plates menu of touring teams. The Women’s T20 World Cup was on home soil, but for all that it outdid its 50-over equivalent in 2017 by way of engagement, the men’s football World Cup dominated. Plus, folks kind of knew Nat Sciver-Brunt’s England side was not quite ready to derail the Australian machine.

Yet six weeks after the Hundred finals at Lord’s, the mood at two of its host counties tells us something about where it sits in the sport’s consciousness. With the best will in the world, beyond a fun day out with the kids and a bumper pay packet for the players involved, it doesn’t appear to be that high.

At Warwickshire on Sunday, they were celebrating their ninth County Championship title, the outfield flooded with supporters and players in clover. No one seemed too fussed that Birmingham Phoenix, the entity that is 50.4% Warwickshire‑owned, had stunk out the men’s and women’s Hundred. There was no talk of atonement or it being a mixed season. By definition, it will go down as a famous summer.

Further north at Old Trafford things are very different. Manchester Super Giants won the men’s Hundred, which you would think means people at Lancashire, 30% shareholders and with crossover in staff, are pretty chuffed; that Daniel Gidney would be sprinkled with red rose petals as he leaves his role as chief executive.

Hardly. Finishing second bottom in Division Two with two wins all season, Lancashire have pulled the plug on their end-of-season awards do and supporters are in a state of apoplexy. Mark Chilton has been sacked as director of cricket performance and the incoming chief executive, Richard Kenyon, will soon lead a “clear and objective look at our performance operation” – AKA the dreaded review.

Clearly this is all a bit simplistic. The Hundred has got a fresh audience through the gates – albeit attendance dipped 5% in 2026 – and the lines between the host counties and teams are blurred. More broadly, even if Birmingham Phoenix ultras were not exactly marching to Edgbaston with pitchforks, the franchise world is hardly soft on failure.

Nevertheless, it says something about English sensibilities that the domestic cricket that truly stirred emotions – and in the case of Lancashire, recriminations – still came from its traditional year‑round structures. Money isn’t everything, it seems.

The main attention thief – why the Hundred remained on the undercard in 2026 – was still the England men’s team. Even in a supposedly low-key summer by way of opposition, with India’s visit for white-ball cricket the biggest money-spinner, their travails were impossible to ignore. And in particular a Test team that served as the latest reminder about best-laid plans.

It was supposed to be a quiet rebuild, with the status quo retained in terms of leadership and lessons learned from the winter’s Ashes debacle. Instead, the first half of the season was a psychodrama, featuring another late-night drinking incident, a strung-out Ben Stokes quitting as Test captain and Brendon McCullum being demoted to white‑ball head coach after the 2-1 Test defeat against New Zealand.

But looking ahead to the winter – white-ball tours of Pakistan and Australia, Test series in South Africa and Bangladesh, plus the 150th Anniversary Test in Melbourne – there is a sense of quiet optimism. Maybe, just maybe, England have emerged from the embers of Stokes’s Viking funeral in better shape.

England will begin the next phase of their World Cup preparations without Jos Buttler after the former captain was ruled out of the forthcoming tour of Pakistan.

Buttler injured his hamstring mid-innings against Sri Lanka at Headingley last week, retiring hurt but later returning to the crease in clear pain. He sat out the Metro Bank one-day international series decider at the Kia Oval on Sunday, which England won at a canter by 223 runs, and has now been told he will not be fit for the 50-over tri-series next month. There is no guarantee yet that the 36-year-old will be back for the subsequent trip to Australia in November.

“Jos won’t be in Pakistan,” the white-ball head coach, Brendon McCullum, saidd. “It’s disappointing not to have Jos but it will be good for us to see where we’re at. Between now and 14 months’ time lots of things will go wrong, there’ll be lots of selections you think will happen and someone will get injured or there’ll be a scheduling issue. You almost have to catastrophise these things a little to prepare yourself for that World Cup.”

In the short term, that means an extended chance for Jordan Cox as the wicketkeeper-batter. England are set to finalise their squad for Pakistan in the next 24 hours, with Sam Curran pushing for a return after groin trouble and further checks to be made on Adil Rashid’s bowling hand. Jacob Bethell is still recovering from a knee problem. Press Association

A year out from the World Cup in southern Africa, England’s white-ball set-up is on the rise. The Twenty20 team have won 23 of their past 26 games, while after years of neglect the 50-over side has won all six bilateral series this year. Harry Brook’s young thrustersteam continue to play catch-up – they are absurdly light on domestic 50-over experience – but you can see a team starting to coalesce.

If anything it probably shows how making McCullum head coach in all formats was a mistake in late 2024. Now specialising – and showing little bitterness at having had his wings clipped – McCullum has gone against his image and begun laying down a structured, rigorous setup. Fitness is his new pet project, while he is even pushing for more pre-World Cup warm-up games. Though Kevin Pietersen’s return as a mentor is a gamble on one level, it could prove inspired.

The Test team’s 3-0 sweep of Pakistan obviously had caveats, chiefly the tourists being ill‑equipped to deal with the Dukes ball wobbling off its seam and plumbing new depths of dysfunction when seven players were axed mid-tour. It was not without another sideshow for England either when, at 1-0 up, Brydon Carse wound up in handcuffs outside a Derby nightclub.

Joe Root’s return to captaincy also led to tactical gremlins re-emerging when the little‑known Razaullah went tonto at Edgbaston. Root’s returns with the bat dipped, but he provided a sense of calm and clarity after the whirlwind of Stokes, and oversaw a promising new-look pace attack. Ollie Robinson nipped out 29 wickets at nine runs apiece, while Jofra Archer and Josh Tongue bounced out perceptions of fragility by getting through 17 and 15 internationals respectively.

Another healthier aspect was competition for places, rather than pumping caps into a set lineup. Jordan Cox, Dan Lawrence and Emilio Gay did not bolt down spots – Ben Duckett made England’s only Test century all summer – but they made enough of an impression to force a tricky call when Jacob Bethell returns. The Lions setup also looks better for the appointment of Jonathan Trott as the head coach.

There is much work to do, but this looks a sound starting point when Stephen Fleming begins life as the new Test head coach. The sibling-like relationship with McCullum should get him up to speed quickly and allow a grownup division of resources. Fleming has already issued the order to give more credence to the World Test Championship, which can only be a good thing.

Not that it will usurp the Ashes as English cricket’s overriding obsession anytime soon, coming around again in 2027. In turn, expect the Hundred’s wait for top billing in an English summer to continue for some time yet.

‘Starship is in orbit’: cheers go up as huge SpaceX rocket circles Earth for first time

The Guardian Mon, 28 Sep 2026 16:23:49 GMT

Mission goes ahead despite some fears an initial engine failure after the Texas launch would scupper the attempt

SpaceX has sent its enormous Starship rocket into Earth’s orbit for the first time on a milestone flight intended to pave the way for future missions to the moon and Mars.

The rocket, the largest and most powerful ever built, blasted off from SpaceX’s Starbase launch facility in Texas at 7.48am local time (1.48pm BST), marking its 14th test flight and first attempt to circle the planet before falling back to Earth.

Despite an engine failure on ascent that threatened to prevent Starship from reaching orbit, mission controllers decided it was safe to press ahead with a burn that pushed the ship on to a planned trajectory to take it around the planet.

Cheers and applause broke out at SpaceX after initial suggestions that the orbit attempt might be abandoned were quashed and the decision to go ahead was announced. Moments after the orbit burn, Daniel Hewitt, an engineer who was narrating a live stream of the launch, declared: “Starship is in orbit.”

Elon Musk’s company has flown Starship in its full form since 2023 but previous test flights have only sought to put the rocket into suborbital trajectories, which are simpler and carry fewer risks for the public.

For suborbital flights, the trajectory is such that if the rocket explodes or malfunctions mid-flight, the remnants come down in the Indian Ocean far from populated areas. The risks are harder to control when rockets are on full orbital paths around the planet.

Starship soared to an altitude of about 171 miles (275km), with the original aim of completing six loops of Earth in nearly 10 hours before splashing down in the Pacific Ocean somewhere west of Chile. More than an hour into the mission however, SpaceX said Starship would come back early, aiming for a landing about three hours after launch in the north Pacific.

Martin Barstow, a professor of astrophysics and space science at the University of Leicester, said: “This is an important milestone for SpaceX, with Starship successfully reaching orbit, and at the first attempt.”

The achievement “marks the beginning of the transition from the testing and development phase to becoming a working vehicle able to deliver the large payloads needed to return to the moon,” he added. “Congratulations to the whole SpaceX team. Having this large launch capability will also be transformational for the whole space industry.”

On the launchpad, the rocket stands more than 120 metres tall, with the Starship upper stage sitting on the “Super Heavy” booster stage. To remain in orbit, the rocket is required to travel at about 28,000km/h (17,400mph).

A successful mission will be a relief for SpaceX and Nasa, who hope to use Starship to carry astronauts to the moon as part of a new era of lunar expeditions. It will also cheer investors after the company’s high-profile launch on the stock market in June. The company’s stock price rose sharply in the initial public offering before falling back. It has since recovered some of those losses.

During the mission, SpaceX staff watched the booster launch, ascend and separate from the Starship upper stage, then return to an offshore landing point in the Gulf of Mexico. The company did not intend to catch the booster in giant mechanical arms, as it did after a previous test flight in 2024.

Engineers modified the rocket’s hardware and software to overcome glitches that emerged during the last test flight. After stage separation, the booster should flip over and fire its engines to send it back to Earth, but on the last test flight the manoeuvre was ended early because three engines started to clog up with ice. The booster then attempted a landing burn with only eight of 13 planned engines reigniting, leading to a hard landing in the water.

On the latest test flight, Starship deployed 26 next-generation Starlink satellites. Three carried cameras to capture images of Starship’s heat shield that will feed into testing for future missions.

On coming back to Earth, Starship used its four aerodynamic flaps to control its speed and orientation and bellyflop horizontally towards its designated landing zone in the north Pacific. As it approached the water, the ship righted itself and slowed down before erupting in a ball of flames.

Musk has set himself the ambitious target of developing fully reusable rockets to speed up mission turnaround times and reduce the costs of future space travel. But several Starship test flights have ended in failure. In March last year, the rocket exploded soon after launch and scattered debris over the Bahamas. Two months later, Starship span out of control shortly after separating from its booster. A month after that, the rocket exploded during preparations for a test flight.
