Burnham has a battle plan, with social care the flagship. Risks lie ahead, but Labour now travels in hope

The Guardian Mon, 28 Sep 2026 16:21:28 GMT

Here in Liverpool, the PM’s ambition for the party – and the country – is evident. There should be no complacency, but also no fear

His ambition is big enough to see from space as he promises the “biggest change to Britain in 40 years”. Andy Burnham pledges what no prime minister until now has dared to, breaking the long spell of Thatcherism. Her sham monopoly markets in public services have crashed. The chancellor, John Healey, promises a “new age of industrialisation”, breaking with her era of industrial desertification. The social care system she blew into disconnected privatised fragments will become a national care service. Something new is waiting to be born.

Things happen fast. Only a year ago, the Labour party was on its knees in despair, thunderstruck to find Nigel Farage ruling the roost so soon after its landslide win, with Reform UK 12 percentage points ahead of Labour’s dismal 22%. Farage was the most popular leader, with a 30% favourability rating, compared with Keir Starmer’s -71%. When Burnham came to Liverpool last year he had no seat, no prospect of a challenge and a numbskull national executive committee bent on barring him, his charisma wasted.

Now here he is in the middle of a mini-bounce, the only leader with a positive score, while Farage has slid down the scale to -30%. Polls show that Labour could win the next election, with the left bloc outscoring the right, though without an overall majority. Relish every second of this period. Burnham has three precious years, rightly not risked in a needless election, and time enough to start his 40-year revolution.

With the wind in his sails, he has the wit, agility, experience and ruthlessness of leadership, alongside his skill of being able to talk of dilemmas ahead without plunging everyone into gloom. “Have faith in the country” seems to be his useful attitude, casting doubters as anti-patriotic wreckers. Odysseus-like, he needs wax in his ears to block the sound of his enemies bellowing on Elon Musk’s X that he will never prove himself a real man, a true leader, until he inflicts severe pain – preferably on the weakest. He says he won’t make “crude cuts”. The way to bring down welfare bills is by helping the young out of benefits.

Those who thought Healey would be the undertaker chancellor, countering Pollyanna Burnham with graveyard gloom, heard optimism in his speech on Monday instead. “It’s tough,” he had previously told the BBC economics editor, Faisal Islam, but “we’ve got good reasons to be confident about the future of Britain”. Amid the cacophony of doom from the right, Islam, a fairer adjudicator, says there has been “a modest but notable uptick in economic spirits”. Burnham’s “hopeful optimism ‘vibes’ strategy” appears to have had “some impact”, Islam adds. That is the psychology of economics that eluded Starmer and Rachel Reeves: a good mood lifts markets too. Consumer confidence in the UK hit a two-year high in August.

Look what happened when the financial markets opened after Burnham announced “Your first home”, a better version of the help-to-buy scheme. FTSE-listed housebuilders’ shares soared, with investors keen to get spades in the ground again with this incentive. Unlike George Osborne’s scheme, this is only for those with no “bank of mum and dad”, enabling them to buy newbuilds with only a 2.5% deposit. Kitchen and tile manufacturers’ shares surged, too, after the news.

The flow of “Hope again” announcements has been so prolific that it’s easy to lose track, so here are some: most bus fares in England will be capped; VAT on electricity bills in Great Britain will be cut; pub business rates in England have been reduced; there is a policy to end rough sleeping in England and policies to support Neets; there are plans for the devolution of powers from Westminster, for “buying British”, for building council homes, for renewing high streets, for bringing arts and vocational skills back to the English school curriculum, for taking over empty homes, for more public control of public services and for repairing EU trade. And here’s a surprise from the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood: a safe and legal route out for Afghan women and girls and Palestinians. Hot air? Small beer? So far, cynicism bounces off Burnham.

But yes, money must be raised to hit a defence spending target of 3% of GDP, and to pay upfront to get Neets into work. The cost of living tops public concern, here and right across Europe, but that’s in the hands of Donald Trump’s calamitous war on Iran.

The art of politics is to lead the national conversation, and to distract from current troubles to focus on the future. There’s a risk, with such a plethora of plans, that direction and purpose become diluted. Wisely, Burnham has singled out one above all others – a flagship policy that authentically marks who he is, what he stands for and what he cares about.

Social care will be the beacon shining for every family sooner or later in this ageing population. As Burnham spoke movingly of his father’s death, there was a national nodding of the head in recognition. His father had the best care, he said, but hundreds of thousands encounter the worst, if they get any at all. The key to unlocking national wallets and purses for this expensive task is reminding everyone of their pride in the NHS and contempt for the US alternative. Social care in England is “as unfair as American healthcare,” said Burnham, where the “most vulnerable in society can lose everything, they can be wiped out, not just by the condition that they have, but wiped out financially”. That chimes.

The pitch is rolled now to change the unaffordable triple lock on pensions in order to pay for the new social care service. It will need the wealth of older people to contribute, without taking money from the struggling younger generation whose incomes are lower than their parents’ were at the same age.

after newsletter promotion

That will be the heart of the next manifesto – when Burnham knows, from bitter experience of the 2010 election, how that policy gets turned into a “death tax”. The knives were out again on hearing the plan. But this time, he thinks they mistake the public mood. That’s brave but essential.

All this Labour celebration, sheer relief and surprised delight at every new announcement comes with a stern warning. In this volatile era, what changed so fast in a year can swing back again. Harder tests are to come, warns the University of Manchester professor of political science Rob Ford, with the budget, the spending review and unknown global perils on the horizon. Labour’s lead is still thin. Farage may be down after his scandal-ridden summer, but he has roared back before. Analysis by Survation for Hope not Hate reminds us that in many Labour seats Reform UK is close behind, often by a tiny margin. With Marine Le Pen’s support surging in France this week, complacency is the danger.

Everything at this conference suggests that Burnham has the full measure of what heavy lifting it will take to persuade more voters of his way. He feels the national pulse, as he hopes to make social care stand for everything else Labour means to do. Labour can rejoice in this moment, but never stop looking over its shoulder.

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

‘12 weeks and SO disgusted by my dog’: what happens when you’re pregnant and can’t stand your pet?

The Guardian Mon, 28 Sep 2026 16:00:38 GMT

There may be almost no research on pet aversion during and post-pregnancy, but it may not be particularly rare

About three weeks into her first pregnancy, Sylvia Luu began to loathe the smell of her border collie mix, Ranger.

Luu could hardly be in the same room as Ranger without becoming nauseous. His drool repulsed her, and she found the smell of his fur so disgusting she wore a nose plug all day.

“Before pregnancy, I used to smell my dog’s paws a lot,” says Luu. “But during pregnancy, I would throw up if I ever tried that.”

At the time, Luu, 35, and Ranger had enjoyed 12 happy years together. Ranger slept in Luu’s bed. She walked him in all weather, and let him lick her face.

Luu’s doctor said that her nausea was normal and simply advised her to drink more water to avoid dehydration from vomiting, but that didn’t alleviate Luu’s distress. “I was so heartbroken that I couldn’t love my dog as much as I wanted to,” says Luu, whose husband took over pet care duties. She wondered about rehoming Ranger, and was relieved when, upon delivering her firstborn, her aversion vanished.

By the time of her second pregnancy, Luu was diagnosed with hyperemesis gravidarum. The condition is caused by hormonal shifts, much like the more familiar morning sickness. For 1%-3% of pregnant people, these shifts result in extreme nausea and disgust sensitivity that can be triggered by any number of things – in this case, pet odour.

Although the diagnosis was helpful, the changes were a difficult and destabilising addition to an already labile time. Luu now wishes that she had received some emotional support from her medical team, practical tips for coping with her diagnosis or validation of the unsettling shift in her feelings toward Ranger.

But there is almost no research into the specific phenomenon of pet aversion during and post-pregnancy.

“This topic is at an intersection of women’s health being underfunded and human-animal bond work being trivialised,” says Dr Katherine Compitus, director of veterinary social work at New York University’s Silver School of Social Work, who has helped clients experiencing pet aversion.

Yet there are signs that prenatal pet aversion isn’t particularly rare.

A survey of 1,077 women who had been pregnant within the past three years found that 15% of pet-owning respondents experienced aversion to their dog during pregnancy, according to 2025 research from the UK pet insurer ManyPets.

On Reddit, pregnant posters complain about feeling annoyed or repelled by their pets’ noises, smells and behaviours. “I’m a huge animal lover but this pregnancy I hate all of them,” wrote one user. “12 weeks and SO disgusted by my dog,” another admitted.

Perinatal depression, anxiety and OCD may contribute to intense, confusing feelings, and a pet may become an outlet for difficult emotions too risky to direct at a partner or child, Compitus says. She recommends that anyone whose feelings about their pets are becoming distressing or out of proportion speak with a therapist, particularly those who use exposure therapy and cognitive behavioral therapy, as these practices can be particularly useful for working through repulsion, rage and disgust.

For others, pet aversion may ramp up once the baby is home.

Katherine Davidson, a dog trainer based in Montreal, noticed herself becoming irritated with the shedding of her three dogs when she became pregnant. “It had never bothered me before,” she says.

But when her daughter was born, the aggravation spiked – something she attributes to practical hygiene concerns and new-mom burnout. “I started feeling resentful” of the dogs, she says, “and that surprised me, because prior, my dogs were my entire life … they were my babies.”

“My postpartum loathing of [pet cat] Lucky made me wonder whether I might be a late-onset psychopath,” mused an anonymous writer in a controversial 2024 essay in the Cut.

The postpartum period can be a vulnerable time for the human-animal bond, says Dr Shelby McDonald, an human-animal interaction researcher and director of the University of Tennessee, Knoxville’s Center for Veterinary Social Work.

New families with pets face challenges including the safety of their baby around a rambunctious dog, and irritation due to barking, shedding and the click-clack of canine nails. “A family’s capacity to meet an animal’s needs may change substantially,” whether physically, emotionally, practically or financially, she says.

Practical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good life

after newsletter promotion

“Research with new parents has documented reductions in time and attention devoted to pets … and, for some people, changes in feelings of closeness to their animals,” says McDonald, who is currently collaborating on a study with the University of Edinburgh involving in-depth interviews with mothers in the UK about their experiences with companion animals during pregnancy and postpartum.

Many mothers describe their relationships to their animals improving with time, according to McDonald’s early research.

“A parent can remain deeply attached to an animal while temporarily having much less capacity to care for or interact with them in the way they did before the baby arrived,” she says.

While not yet complete, McDonald’s work also indicates that a minority of mothers relinquish their pets during the postpartum period, seemingly out of concern for the animal’s welfare and quality of life; clear population-level data is not yet available.

There can be “tremendous shame” associated with relinquishing or rehoming an animal, notes McDonald. Yet it’s important for new parents to notice when normal frustration and caregiver fatigue cross into the territory of abuse or neglect, which McDonald describes as an animal being denied adequate food and water, opportunities for exercise and elimination, a reasonably clean and safe environment, veterinary care or social interaction.

“Recognizing that an animal’s welfare and wellbeing is being compromised and making a thoughtful plan for their care can itself be an act of responsible caregiving,” she says. “The priority should be the wellbeing and safety of both the person and the animal, rather than preserving a particular living arrangement at all costs.”

Compitus suggests getting ahead of this issue by getting help from a friend, relative or petsitter. A reputable shelter or rescue may be able to provide guidance; some may even have safety-net programs designed to offer temporary reprieve to overwhelmed pet owners.

Davidson considered rehoming her pets postpartum, but her dilemma was as existential as it was practical. She’d always been a “big animal person”, she says, and the change was confronting.

“You’re just like: ‘Oh, my God, I just need someone to understand, and to tell me these feelings are normal,” says Davidson. Shame and guilt may also contribute to silence around the topic, says Compitus. “If a mother is feeling this aversion toward her pets, it might call into question their identity as a mother: ‘What kind of mother will I be if I can’t even take care of my pet?’”

For Davidson, who ended up keeping her dogs, the negativity she felt toward her pets passed in a matter of months as the household adjusted to a new routine.

Now, when she works with dog-training clients who have growing families, Davidson tells them it’s not unusual to feel frustration or a lack of love for their animals postpartum, and that it often goes away. She shares strategies that worked for her, such as creating pet-free spaces in her home, using a robot vacuum for shedding, and getting help with duties like dog-walking, vet and grooming appointments, and cleaning.

Today, Davidson has three children under six, and has added a six-month-old puppy to her menagerie. “It’s nice having my animals with me, and seeing them grow up with my children,” she says.

Palestine has become electoral issue in UK for first time, says solidarity campaign chief

The Guardian Mon, 28 Sep 2026 16:00:38 GMT

Anger over Israel’s war in Gaza is mobilising British voters, according to Aimee Shalan

Palestine has become a domestic electoral issue in Britain for the first time, according to the incoming head of the country’s largest Palestinian solidarity organisation.

Aimee Shalan, who will take over as director of the Palestine Solidarity Campaign (PSC) in November, joins the organisation as demonstrations against Israel’s war in Gaza have snowballed into what organisers describe as one of the most sustained protest movements in modern British history.

She said public anger over Israel’s treatment of Palestinians and Britain’s response was increasingly being expressed not just through demonstrations but at elections, in workplaces and trade unions and through consumer campaigns.

Speaking before a PSC protest at the Labour party conference, Shalan said: “We’re seeing for the first time in British history Palestine become a domestic issue, electorally, at the national level and at the local level.”

The shift was visible at the 2024 general election and 2026 local elections, where pro-Palestinian candidates made major breakthroughs.

Shalan pointed to the foreign secretary Ed Miliband’s announcement of sanctions against settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories as a notable success for their movement.

Miliband said at the Labour conference on Monday: “I want to say to the millions of people in this country and indeed elsewhere who have been moved and outraged by the plight of the Palestinian people: we hear you, you were right.” He described the sanctions as a definitive change in how Labour would approach the situation in the Middle East.

Shalan said: “That shift is a testament to the mass movement. Both internationally, but specifically also here in Britain, with hundreds of thousands of people marching, campaigning, lobbying.

“He [Miliband] says he hears the British public, but his announcement falls far short of the clear and immediate actions millions of people have been calling for: full sanctions on the state of Israel, including a two-way arms embargo, an end to material support for Israel’s military operations and an end to British political and diplomatic support for an apartheid state.”

Shalan welcomed the shift within the Labour government but said the sanctions announcement would be “very little solace for Palestinians whose lives have been brutally destroyed through Israel’s relentless oppression and genocide”.

She pointed to the 70,000 Palestinians killed in Israel’s war in Gaza and the more than 1,300, including at least 300 children, killed since a ceasefire was signed last year.

The PSC says its individual membership has more than doubled from 7,800 at the beginning of 2023 to nearly 17,000, with subscribers to its newsletters rising from 70,000 to about 300,000.

Along with partner groups, it has organised 36 national demonstrations since October 2023, some drawing hundreds of thousands of people. Organisers say the demonstrations represent one of the largest and most sustained protest movements in British history.

Shalan said: “It’s been uplifting to see the level of support and the connections that people are making between their own lives, and other liberation and social justice struggles, and the Palestinian cause.”

But the demonstrations have been contested. Some politicians and campaign groups have raised concerns about antisemitism surrounding pro-Palestinian protests, with critics describing them as “hate marches”.

Shalan rejected that characterisation as a smear against the movement, saying: “Those marches have been a really wonderful coming together of communities of all sorts of different faiths, of all sorts of different backgrounds, young and old, of all sorts of different ethnicities.”

Shalan also rejected calls for the PSC to be designated an extremist organisation, arguing that attempts to criminalise parts of the Palestine solidarity movement were increasingly at odds with public opinion.

“You can try and criminalise, but all it will do is anger the public more,” she said. “That’s why we’re seeing people going out on the streets and risking being arrested because they refuse to be hobbled by this effort to criminalise both Palestinians and those that stand in support.

“Those who are responsible for trying to criminalise support for Palestinians and their rights, and supporters trying to end a horrific genocide, should hang their heads in shame.”

Supporters attending national demonstrations are directed toward a network of more than 100 local branches, which organise campaigns in communities, workplaces and universities and lobby councils and MPs.

The PSC says 34 councils in England and Wales have committed to supporting the divestment of their pension funds from companies that campaigners accuse of complicity in Israel’s actions.

The PSC’s influence has also grown within the trade union movement. The Trades Union Congress is backing the Palestinian-led boycott, divestment and sanctions (BDS) movement, supporting workplace campaigns and divestment from companies it says are complicit in abuses against Palestinians.

Shalan defended BDS after Miliband said he “wholeheartedly” opposed the campaign. “BDS is a set of tactics that provide a peaceful way for people to campaign for human rights, for justice, for accountability,” she said.

Shalan, who is British Palestinian, has spent nearly three decades campaigning for Palestinian rights. She is the director of Makan, a Palestinian-led educational organisation, and has served as chief executive of Medical Aid for Palestinians and as director of Friends of Birzeit University, which has changed its name to Friends of Palestinian Universities. She holds a doctorate on the politics of Palestinian literature.

The group’s Pledge for Palestine campaign was signed by more than 2,200 candidates before this year’s local elections and it plans to repeat this at the next general election.

“There’s a very short time before the next election and we need to have a very robust movement that ensures that we don’t sleepwalk into what appears to be a really deeply authoritarian future,” Shalan said.

She compared the Palestine solidarity movement to the international campaign against apartheid South Africa, while stressing that the histories were not identical.

“People can’t unsee what they’ve seen,” she said. “People are finding ways to be mobilised in different spheres. And support for Palestinian freedom and justice will only continue to grow”

On Friday, Suleiman appeared in court for a pre-trial hearing where he denied all charges and the prosecution said the case was no longer being treated as a suspected terrorism case.

In an email message sent to communities across London on Monday, the Met said: “At the hearing, the Crown Prosecution Service advised the court that it will not be pursuing a terrorist connection as part of the criminal proceedings.” It said it would treat it instead as a suspected hate crime.

“We understand this announcement may cause concern, particularly within the Jewish community, given the impact this incident had locally and against the backdrop of recent incidents affecting Jewish communities across London. We would like to reassure residents that the seriousness with which this matter is being treated has not changed.”

Cmdr Helen Flanagan, the head of counter-terrorism policing for London, said: “I fully recognise the impact this incident has had on the three victims as well as the public, particularly the Jewish community.

“I’m also aware this news comes shortly after the arrests of two men in Manchester for a suspected plot to target the Jewish community during the High Holy Days period. Counter-terrorism policing continues to work closely with the Met police to provide as much visibility and security as we can to Jewish communities across London.”

The victims of the Golders Green attacks were Shloime Rand, 34, and Moshe Shine, 76. The victim of the other stabbing earlier the same day in south London was Ishmail Hussein.

The case continues and the full trial is scheduled for March 2027.

AI godfathers warn of runaway ‘intelligence explosion’

The Guardian Mon, 28 Sep 2026 15:00:36 GMT

OpenAI chief scientist also among authors of report on prospect of ‘most consequential technological development in history’

Two of the “godfathers” of modern AI and senior executives at OpenAI and Anthropic have warned governments to prepare for an AI “intelligence explosion”, which they say could be the most consequential technological development in history.

A report co-authored by the Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton and the Canadian computer scientist Yoshua Bengio, considered godfathers of modern AI for their work in the field, urges politicians to act now before there is runaway progress in the technology.

The authors say they are concerned about an “intelligence explosion”, which they describe as a “dramatic AI-driven acceleration of AI progress, compressing advances that would otherwise take years into months or less”.

The paper, titled “What if automating AI R&D triggers an intelligence explosion?”, is authored by more than 20 people including Hinton and Bengio. Other authors of the paper include Jack Clark, a co-founder of Anthropic, and Jakub Pachocki, the chief scientist at OpenAI.

Their concerns focus on the possibility of AIs being able to improve themselves without human intervention, a process known as “recursive self-improvement”. In the paper it is broadly referred to as automated AI research and development. Once AI systems reach expert-level capabilities at AI R&D, a single developer could run a workforce equivalent to “millions” of top human researchers, the paper says.

The authors say the automating of AI R&D is the most likely source of an intelligence explosion, because AIs are already contributing to improving their own technology and the resulting improved systems can be rapidly deployed once built.

“An intelligence explosion could be the most consequential technological development in human history, compressing years of progress into months or less, threatening human control over AI systems, and severely eroding checks on power within and between states, companies, and branches of government,” the paper says.

Urging governments to take action quickly, the authors say: “Once an intelligence explosion begins, the window for action may close.”

They recommended a trio of policy priorities: requiring transparent progress reports on AI-related R&D, including embedding independent auditors in companies; finding ways to constrain breakneck AI development; and preparing to adapt to an intelligence explosion.

Anthropic and OpenAI have both agreed to having independent evaluators assess their models after warning that AI development was reaching a critical pitch in terms of safety.

Anthropic says AI now produces 80% of its own code, while OpenAI uses autonomous AI agents in areas such as the training of new models.

“Preliminary evidence suggests that a software-driven intelligence explosion is possible,” the paper says, adding this would lead to the “extremely rapid development of highly capable or superhuman AI systems”.

While this could produce medical breakthroughs and technological leaps, it would bring a trio of risks: powerful systems could enable biological and cyber threats that develop faster than the measures needed to counter them; as humans become less involved in AI R&D they could lose the opportunity to control systems; states could use an intelligence explosion to convert a modest lead in areas such as cyberspace into a decisive one.

The report acknowledges these impacts are “uncertain”. For instance, a technological breakthrough could take time to implement given the need to set up supply chains for any special materials involved or to comply with regulations. AI systems could also accelerate the speed at which risks are mitigated, say the authors.

If such a breakthrough happened, the authors say, AI systems could rapidly eclipse human experts in most fields and “radically accelerate” technological progress. Preparing for this “should be an urgent priority, including at the highest levels of government leadership”.

They say governments should consider policies that address the potential for an intelligence explosion, including: requiring transparent progress reports on AI-related R&D, including embedding independent auditors in companies; limiting how fast an AI can improve in a certain time period; working with datacentres to enable pausing certain AI R&D projects; making sure automated AI R&D systems are fully isolated and cannot escape human control; creating “emergency response plans” for the various scenarios that could emerge from an intelligence explosion.

Despite some glitches shown by systems, such as disobeying instructions, R&D projects that would take humans months to carry out could be fully automated by AI by 2028. “Productivity gains from AI R&D automation have not yet reached the threshold needed to trigger an intelligence explosion, but gains from newer systems are likely approaching that threshold,” they said.

‘Are these chemicals in my blood?’ How one community learned the truth about Pfas pollution

The Guardian Mon, 28 Sep 2026 14:54:50 GMT

People living next to a chemicals plant near Blackpool were tested for ‘forever chemicals’. Last week they received the alarming results

Last February, I got a call from a woman called Sam Hammond. We had been speaking on and off for a while over her growing concern that her garden could be affected by pollution from a nearby chemical plant.

That morning, Sam had been hand-delivered a letter from her council informing her that her pet ducks’ eggs, reared in her garden, were contaminated with Pfas chemicals.

“Are these chemicals in my blood?” she asked me at the time. Seven months later, Sam has an answer to that question.

Pfas are a group of thousands of synthetic compounds known as “forever chemicals” because of their persistence in the environment.

In 2024, Wyre borough council and the Environment Agency launched an investigation into contamination of one type of Pfas – Pfoa, a group 1 carcinogen that was globally banned in 2020 – in the vicinity of the AGC Chemicals Europe factory in Thornton-Cleveleys, a town to the north of Blackpool. Pfoa was emitted in huge quantities from the AGC Chemicals factory up until 2012.

The level of Pfas in one of Sam’s duck eggs was so high that if she ate just one a week, she would exceed the European safe level 10 times over. Sam and her children had been eating these eggs every day for decades.

The risk was increasingly clear, but residents did not yet know if the Pfas had entered their systems until last week when the law firm Leigh Day, working with Dr Dave Megson, a forensic environmental scientist at Manchester Metropolitan University, and in association with Watershed Investigations, published the blood test results of 49 individuals who live around the factory.

In the UK, there is no guidance on what constitutes a safe level of Pfas in blood. However, in the US the guidelines state that if the sum of seven Pfas chemicals is above 20 nanograms per millilitre, there is an increased risk of adverse effects and that clinicians should consider more frequent, targeted health screenings.

The results showed that 70% of those tested in Thornton-Cleveleys had a combined Pfas level above 20ng/ml.

Sam’s level is 25ng/ml, putting her firmly in this high-risk category. But what is perhaps even more alarming is the level of Pfas in her son’s blood: 111 ng/ml.

“I feel quite sick about his results,” she said. “My concern all along is what have we done to the kids. We moved here, chose this property, and I feel guilty because I’ve exposed them to that, even though I know it’s not my fault.”

The results specifically revealed that nearly 70% of those tested had increased levels of Pfoa.

Pfoa exposure is linked to a range of serious illnesses and has been linked specifically to kidney cancer. In June, a government-commissioned study found no higher-than-expected rates for most cancers but found that two areas – one south-east of the factory and one north of Blackpool – had recorded higher than expected rates of kidney cancer.

A detailed review found no evidence of a statistically significant excess of kidney cancer cases and no evidence of a cancer cluster or an environmental association, and argued it could be the result of random variation because of the small sample size, concluding: “No further cluster investigation is warranted at this stage.”

These findings were immediately questioned by experts, who advised further investigations. Megson, who was not involved in the study, described this conclusion as being “very contradictory” and said it “seems to downplay the findings rather than assess it objectively … Personally, I fear that this data is giving us strong evidence that … significant harm has already been caused.”

One woman, who asked to remain anonymous, has a Pfas level of 436 ng/ml. She recently had a tumour removed from her back and is now left questioning whether her persistent health problems may be linked to this chemical exposure.

“I thought I was just unlucky, but when I found out that result I thought it must have something to do with it,” she said.

While the test result has given her some answers, it has left her with even more questions. “How can I get this out of my body? Who can help me? Where do I go from here? I just want this out,” she said.

after newsletter promotion

In the UK, there is no clear guidance on what to do if you have high levels of Pfas in your blood. However, the council has advised residents within a 1km radius of the factory to wash and peel homegrown produce and not to eat eggs from locally reared birds.

Because of the potential risks to human health, the council has also announced plans to shut down two allotments close to the factory.

For the past five years, Alan Hodson has had a plot on one of the allotments that borders the AGC Chemicals site. The allotment was his sanctuary. But last year he received a hand-delivered letter informing him that his beetroot contained the highest level of Pfoa of all of the products tested.

“I just think of all that time I spent here – I could’ve been doing something else. It’s just wasted time,” he said when I visited him earlier this year. Alan has now found out his blood contains 43ng/ml of Pfas.

“You get an allotment and you grow homegrown veg to be more healthy and then all of a sudden you’re told it’s polluted,” he said. “I’m worried, but you’ve just got to crack on. If you dwell on it, it takes over your life.”

Following the recent news of AGC Chemicals’ planned closure, Megson is calling on central government to step in to provide more support to residents.

“That is what has happened across the globe for the last 50 years when potential chemical pollution disasters like this are uncovered. In other places there has been swift widespread biomonitoring offered to residents. This helps clearly establish how localised the problem is,” he said.

A spokesperson for AGC Chemicals Europe Ltd said: “We are aware of the recent blood testing initiative, and we understand the concerns this may have caused amongst local residents. Whilst the parties conducting these tests have chosen not to share their findings and data with us, we would emphasise that the UK government’s position is clear: Pfas blood testing does not predict future health problems and can sometimes create unnecessary concern. For these reasons, Pfas biomonitoring is not currently recommended through the NHS or private blood tests.

“The Hillhouse site and surrounding area has been dedicated to industrial chemical manufacturing for well over a century – long before AGC Chemicals Europe Ltd was established – and a wide variety of historical users have operated on the site. Since the wider multi-agency investigation is still ongoing and no formal determination of land contamination has been made under part 2A of the Environmental Protection Act, we cannot speculate on future outcomes or next steps.

“AGC Chemicals Europe Ltd has been part of the Thornton-Cleveleys community since 1999. The health, wellbeing and safety of our employees and the local community remain our priority.”

The government has been contacted for comment.

What you need to know about Your First Home scheme for first-time buyers

The Guardian Mon, 28 Sep 2026 14:53:22 GMT

Government announcement sparks a rally in FTSE-listed housebuilders, but there are still a lot of unknowns

Labour’s modest reheat of help to buy is worth a try

The government will unveil a fresh scheme to help people on to the housing ladder next month but a debate is already raging over whether it is first-time buyers or housebuilders who will be the biggest winners.

At the weekend, Andy Burnham announced plans for Your First Home, which aims to give a helping hand to first-time buyers who do not have the luxury of being able to call on the “bank of mum and dad”.

Only a few details have emerged, but the news was enough to send the share prices of many UK housebuilders surging on Monday. Persimmon closed 14.7% higher, while Barratt Redrow added 11.7%, Taylor Wimpey 11.5%, Crest Nicholson 11% and Vistry 10.7%.

While it has a different name, it is not unfair to say that Your First Home appears to be an updated version of the Conservatives’ flagship help-to-buy scheme, which ran for a decade.

Like that initiative, YFH applies to England only and is just for prospective first-time buyers looking to buy a new-build flat or house.

While there were separate help-to-buy programmes for Scotland and Wales, it is not clear yet whether the devolved governments will do their own versions of YFH.

Those taking part in the new scheme will be offered a government-backed equity loan worth 20% of the purchase price. Meanwhile, the minimum deposit the buyer will have to put down will be just 2.5%. That means the buyer will only need to take out a standard mortgage for 77.5% of the property’s value.

Because the equity loan part will initially be interest-free, the government says participants “could save hundreds of pounds per month” compared with the standard 95% mortgage popular with many first-time buyers.

The 2.5% deposit cap eliminates one of the biggest challenges facing would-be homeowners, who can find it hard to save up after covering their costs for rent, household bills and in some cases childcare.

There’s a lot we do not know yet about how it will work, who will be eligible and who will not.

The government has said there will be measures to ensure support “is targeted at those who need it” and to avoid YFH being exploited by those who can already afford a home.

A household income cap will be introduced to exclude those on bigger salaries from taking part. There will also reportedly be a deposit cap to restrict how much an applicant could put down upfront and local property price caps limiting how much people can spend on their first home, depending on where they live.

There is no information yet about these caps, which will be the make-or-break factors for many people.

It is also not known how the government-backed equity loan will work, where the money will come from and, crucially, how long it will be interest-free for and what happens after that. When a buyer does have to start paying interest, will it be fixed or will it go up? Can they pay off this loan early, and what happens if they want to move house or get into financial difficulty?

What is known is that this loan will have to be repaid, perhaps when the home is sold or the mortgage is paid off.

In addition, it is not known what the timescales are for when YFH will go live. The government says further details will be announced in the budget on 28 October, with the scheme open for registration by the end of 2026.

The average asking price for a typical first-time buyer home is £225,199, according to the property website Rightmove. A 5% deposit on a property of that value would be £11,260. But under the new scheme, the buyer would only need to put down £5,630 (2.5%).

They would be able to get a government equity loan of £45,040 (20% of the purchase price) and would need to take out a mortgage for the remaining £174,529.

Nicholas Mendes, of the broker John Charcol, says: “Because the equity loan covers 20%, the mortgage itself sits at 77.5% loan-to-value, which gives buyers access to lower rates than they would typically see on a 95% mortgage.”

There were various versions of help to buy over the years, and it ended in March 2023. The final version had a lot of similarities to what we know so far about YFH: it offered an equity loan, was for newly built properties, and also had price caps on what you could buy.

With help to buy, the equity loan on offer was between 5% and 20% of the purchase price. However, that rose to up to 40% in London, so the new scheme appears less generous for those in the capital.

On the flipside, with help to buy, buyers needed to stump up a deposit of at least 5%, twice that of the new scheme.

Help to buy had regional property price caps – in London it could be used to buy a home costing up to £600,000 – but did not have a maximum household income.

With the old scheme, the equity loan was interest-free for the first five years. After that, what you paid went up each year by the consumer prices index inflation measure plus 2%. The ongoing row over soaring student loan debts means the government will be under a lot of pressure to be very clear about how the equity loan will work in terms of interest.

Ministers will also be acutely aware that help to buy was very controversial: while it was credited with helping 328,000 first-time buyers on to the housing ladder and a recent government review found it delivered “very high value for money”, it was accused of pushing up property prices and boosting housebuilders’ profits.

Developers will be expected to make a “contribution” to the new scheme when signing up, to help cover costs.

The hunk shortage: where are England’s handsomest men hiding?

The Guardian Mon, 28 Sep 2026 14:17:26 GMT

When the Mr England contest put out a call for entrants, only seven people signed up. Now, with 13 days to go until the final, the organisers are getting desperate

Age: At least two years old.

Appearance: A hunkless vista, as far as the eye can see.

Hunks of what? Hunks of the male persuasion – masculine, well-built, handsome fellows.

And there’s a shortage of those? A bigger-than-usual shortage? A dire shortage.

Where did all the hunks go? Nobody knows.

So how do we know there’s a shortage? Because the organisers of the Mr England contest are having difficulty attracting sufficient hunks to participate in this year’s competition. Despite the launch of the biennial search over the summer, only seven men have entered the contest.

Seven? Seven so far. Oddly enough, a very similar thing happened two years ago, when men were “a bit shy and slow in coming forward”, according to the organisers.

So what we’re actually talking about is a nation­wide disinclination on the part of men to submit themselves to a competition based on physical appearance. Exactly – a hunk shortage.

I must admit, I’m not terribly surprised. But the Miss England contest, which is run by the same organisers, attracts thousands of entrants each year.

Yeah, still not that surprised. The hunk drought remains a mystery: what happened to England’s strong, chiselled, 17- to 22-year-old men? And why are they so reluctant to take part in a beauty pageant?

What did they do about the lack of interest two years ago? They sent the reigning Miss England, a lifeguard called Milla Magee, to her local beach in Newquay, Cornwall, in search of recruits. Another 100 men joined up as a result of the publicity.

And this year? The Miss England semi-finalists are being asked to nominate their friends and boyfriends.

When is the contest happening? The winner will be crowned on 11 October in Melton Mowbray, Leicestershire.

They’ve left things a bit late, haven’t they? Don’t blame the organisers. How could they possibly have foreseen a second hunk shortage?

Perhaps the cost of signing up is putting men off. It’s free to enter! Just download the Miss England app, upload some headshots …

Don’t you mean the Mr England app? No, it’s all on the same app – the one with the tiara logo. Once you’re on there, you’ll figure it out.

Could that be part of the problem? That the Mr England contest is treated as a mere adjunct to the women’s event? Let’s not jump to conclusions about the causes of the hunk shortage until all the evidence is in.

Do say: “The Mr England competition opens doors for its participants, and offers an opportunity to represent England at an international level.”

Don’t say: “Where do I sign? You had me at Melton Mowbray.”

Netanyahu is using Mamdani as a foil in his re-election campaign

The Guardian Mon, 28 Sep 2026 14:00:36 GMT

The Israeli prime minister’s remarks at the UN weren’t just motivated by personal animosity

In a boastful and defiant speech to the United Nations on Thursday, Benjamin Netanyahu called out a list of villains he insisted are intent on destroying Israel and promoting an anti-Jewish conspiracy by accusing Israel of committing a genocide in Gaza. He singled out the leaders of Hamas, Iran, Qatar and Turkey, among others. But Netanyahu spent considerable time on the global stage attacking an unusual target: Zohran Mamdani, the mayor of New York City.

Netanyahu accused Mamdani of promoting antisemitism, falsely claimed that he supports Hamas, and argued that since the mayor took office in January, “many Jews no longer feel safe in New York.” The Israeli leader also criticized Mamdani’s wife for liking social media posts that supported the Palestinian cause soon after the Hamas attack on Israel in October 2023. Overall, Netanyahu seems to have devoted more time in his nearly 40-minute speech to singling out Mamdani than any other political leader, including Israel’s traditional enemies.

On the surface, it might seem that Netanyahu’s attacks were mainly motivated by personal animosity toward Mamdani, who pledged during last year’s mayoral campaign to execute an arrest warrant against the Israeli prime minister for war crimes and crimes against humanity issued by the international criminal court (ICC) in 2024. “Mr Mamdani, you tried to stop me from coming here, you tried to silence me,” Netanyahu said from the UN podium, referring to the mayor’s promise to enforce the ICC warrant the next time the Israeli leader visited New York. “You can’t silence me. You can’t silence the truth.”

But Netanyahu is not only driven by his personal dislike of Mamdani: the democratic socialist mayor has become popular among Democrats across the US, who are increasingly critical of Israel. And that makes Mamdani a useful foil for the Israeli prime minister, who is in the midst of one of the toughest re-election campaigns of his career. Netanyahu is fighting for his political survival, with his rightwing governing coalition at risk of losing Israel’s parliamentary elections next month.

Netanyahu, who is often described as “the great survivor” of Israeli politics, has decades of experience demonizing his opponents and focusing Israelis on external enemies. Since October 2023, Netanyahu has prolonged Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, and a wider regional war, so he could avoid early elections and block an independent commission into his government’s security failures that led up to the Hamas attack. Netanyahu is also clinging to power to save himself from a years-long corruption trial stemming from one of his earlier stints as premier, where he has been accused of providing political favors to wealthy supporters in exchange for gifts or positive media coverage.

Netanyahu’s UN speech wasn’t the first time he has targeted Mamdani – largely to curry favor with a domestic Israeli audience that views the young Muslim, pro-Palestinian mayor of New York as a villain. Israel’s Likud party has been whipping up an election frenzy against Mamdani since the summer, when it plastered his photo on a campaign billboard in central Tel Aviv. The poster features Mamdani alongside Iran’s supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei; Turkey’s president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan; and Naim Qassem, the leader of Lebanon’s Hezbollah militia. “They want Netanyahu to lose,” says the poster, which features the logo of the rightwing Likud party that Netanyahu has dominated for decades. “Don’t let them win.”

Earlier this month, Netanyahu continued his attacks lumping Mamdani with Middle East leaders who are the Israeli premier’s usual targets. Netanyahu posted an AI-generated video on his personal X account that showed Mamdani celebrating at the prospect of Netanyahu’s defeat in the upcoming elections. “Erdoğan, bro, are you coming to the party of the fall of Netanyahu elections?” an AI version of Mamdani asks in a supposed phone call with the Turkish leader. The fake video also features Khamenei and Mahmoud Abbas, president of the Palestinian Authority, reveling at the prospect of Netanyahu’s downfall.

But the video goes on to show Netanyahu defeating his political opponents in Israel – forcing Mamdani and the others to cancel their celebration. “They want Netanyahu to fall. Don’t let them win,” a narrator says in Hebrew in the video’s closing message.

For his part, Mamdani fought back against Netanyahu’s attacks, but he has also tried to keep the focus on international law and the importance of carrying out the ICC’s arrest warrant. Mamdani said the Israeli leader had used his UN speech to “repeat baseless lies meant to sanitize his genocide of Palestinians … Yet no lie can change the fact that he remains the subject of an international criminal court arrest warrant alleging war crimes and crimes against humanity.”

In July, Mamdani released a video on X in which he backed away from his campaign pledge to arrest Netanyahu, and acknowledged that New York’s police department does not have the legal authority to carry out the ICC’s arrest warrant. Mamdani called the Israeli prime minister a “war criminal” and “the architect of a horrific genocide against the Palestinian people”, and he urged the federal government to arrest Netanyahu on his next visit to the US.

But there’s virtually no chance of that happening. Joe Biden and Donald Trump rejected the ICC’s accusations against Netanyahu – in keeping with their unwavering support for Israel and the billions of dollars in US weapons sent by both of their administrations to enable Israel to carry out its genocide in Gaza. Trump has threatened to impose crippling sanctions against the international criminal court to pressure it to revoke the warrant against his friend and ally Netanyahu. In July, the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, pledged to lead an American campaign to dismantle the ICC “brick by brick, if necessary”.

Netanyahu’s arrogant speech to the UN – coupled with the Trump administration’s deep hostility to the ICC and other institutions intended to uphold international law – might reinforce the idea that impunity will always win under a global order imposed by brute force.

But Mamdani’s effort, even if it has failed so far, offers fleeting hope that justice could prevail – and Israel’s leaders will one day be held to account for their war crimes.

Mohamad Bazzi is a Guardian US columnist. He is also director of the Center for Near Eastern Studies and a journalism professor at New York University

‘Rugby’s in people’s blood here’: mutiny rising in west Wales as Scarlets fight WRU plan

The Guardian Mon, 28 Sep 2026 14:00:35 GMT

No one at Parc y Scarlets understands why they and the Ospreys are on the chopping block for the union’s proposal to cut a club by 2028

Eight o’clock, Saturday night and at Parc y Scarlets the fans are starting to sing. Their scrum-half, Dane Blacker, has just come skipping through half a gap in the Cardiff line. Blacker has slipped the ball on to their loping lock, Sam Lousi, who has flicked it out the back of his hand to the centre Joe Roberts. And Roberts has juggled it up from one hand to the other, gathered it back in and gone sprinting in to score in the corner. They’re leading 5-0 and in the stands it’s Sosban Fach and Hymns and Arias and “Scarlets! Scarlets! Scarlets!”

And somewhere in among it all, reports will say later, a new chant too – “Dave Reddin’s a wanker”.

Reddin, director of rugby at the Welsh Rugby Union and self‑identified “serial disrupter of elite sports performance”, has just recommitted to the union’s grand plan to scrap one of the four regional teams by 2028. Cardiff, who are owned by the WRU, have been told they are safe, and so have the Dragons, who play out of Newport. Which leaves the other two teams, Scarlets and Ospreys, fighting for one slot.

“I understand the pain,” Reddin said. No one here believes him, any more than they would a doctor who warns that the amputation he’s about to perform may sting a bit.

Out in the west, what they most want to know is why the Scarlets and Ospreys, two teams who have won titles, turned out hundreds of Test players, and who, unlike Cardiff and Dragons, have never been into administration, have been told they are the ones who have to give. It was only 18 months ago that the WRU publicly committed to maintaining all four teams. And it was 12 months ago that it announced it was going to get rid of two. Six months ago it decided to keep three.

Nigel Davies, Scarlets’s director of rugby, says: “It’s all so random at the moment, isn’t it? We’ve gone from four, definitely, to two, to three. I mean, it would be unacceptable in any other walk of life. That is not planning. That is chaos.”

Simon Muderack, Scarlets’ chairman, says: “To be blunt we’re not going anywhere.”

It’s only by looking around their patch that you can really understand what he means. Parc y Scarlets, built in the early 2000s, seats 15,000, and has its own indoor and outdoor training facilities. The whole place is owned by the club.

Davies sighs when he says: “I don’t know what they think we’ll do with this place if there’s no one to play here.”

The stadium was the work of Muderack’s predecessor, Huw Evans, who oversaw construction when the Welsh clubs were being consolidated into regions. “It was a fight to the death really,” Evans says, “and building this place was our survival strategy.” It still is. Evans is back at the club for the Cardiff game to take part in a ceremony honouring former Scarlets players. The club are giving individual cap numbers to every one of the 2,600 who have played for them. Derek Quinnell is there, so is Dwayne Peel, the current head coach, so is Davies himself.

The players being honoured came to the club from all across west Wales. Scarlets has always been a little different because its patch is so big. As they like to say, it’s the west’s team, even though the stadium is closer to the English border than the western coast. Pembroke, Cardigan, Aberystwyth, even Llareggub, Dylan Thomas’s fictional home town, they’re all part of the club. Earlier in the day I am up at Carmarthen, where Quins are playing Swansea in Super Rygbi Cymru. There’s a crowd of 250 or so. The Quins side has eight Scarlets players in it, most of them still kids.

“People in this region have always looked to the Scarlets as their team,” Davies says. “When I was a boy growing up, I wanted to play for the Scarlets, yeah, Wales would have been good, but Scarlets was the team, that’s what got me into rugby.”

The club’s managing director, Jon Daniels, is Llangennech-born and bred. “Rugby’s in people’s blood here, has been for 150 years.” His grandad used to be in the steelworks. “When I was born this was all mines and works steel, tin, and all that gave us a real strong sense of community.”

after newsletter promotion

Daniels says Scarlets are the last part of it left standing. “What we are is west Wales. The day our community thinks they no longer need the Scarlets, that’s when we’re done,” he says. “The industry’s gone, the manufacturing’s gone, the mines are gone. Without the rugby, all it would become is a lovely place for people to come and visit on their holidays.” The club, he says, are “here to show the young people that they can be from a little village in west Wales and be world class.”

Their fight isn’t with the Ospreys. “Ask anybody here, they want Ospreys to be around,” Davies says, “and ask anybody there, they will say the same about us.” It’s not even with Cardiff, or Dragons. It’s with the WRU. Muderack says: “I don’t really see how not going bankrupt can get you penalised. I struggle with that. It doesn’t sit well with me. And I don’t see how being the only holders of the main domestic league titles can get you penalised, either.”

There’s only 15 miles or so between the two, and there have been times in the past when they’ve come close to a merger. “I would never say never,” Muderack says now. “But I think the world has moved on from that. And what I certainly don’t think makes any sense at all is a new franchise. Along the lines of a West Wales Warriors.”

Davies says it is like these decisions are being passed down from an “ivory tower”, it’s an existential threat imposed, with no explanation, by people who don’t live in west Wales, and who, they say, haven’t taken the time to understand it. A series of workshops on all the cuts are due to start in December, but Muderack says there are no conversations going on now. “I mean, our primary communication mechanism at this point has been the public domain.”

No one here is going to argue that Scarlets are getting everything right. The club is sustainable day‑to-day, but it carries a lot of debt. What they have, in abundance, is people who care. And when they’re threatened, they will fight. The club have just brought the former first minister Carwyn Jones on to the board. “Scarlets will always have people that look after it,” Muderack says. “I’ve been here six years, and in that time I’m going to be on my fifth WRU chair, and my fourth WRU CEO.”

Muderack is convinced that the answers ought to include more fixtures against the English teams, and more effort to draw in private investment. All this uncertainty makes both almost impossible. Daniels says: “It’s very difficult to have a straight story for our fans, for our sponsors, and our community.”

So they press on as best they can. “Welsh rugby is in a tough place. Not just because of decisions made yesterday, but because of decisions made 10 years ago. And it might take another 10 years to get out of it. But it has to start with an open and honest conversation about what the real position is. And that conversation has to start with: ‘What do we have to do to keep four teams?’”

‘We wanted it to be a battlecry’: how Republica made 90s anthem Ready to Go

The Guardian Mon, 28 Sep 2026 14:00:29 GMT

‘The day Saff came into the studio with red hair, I said, “We’re gonna be massive!” It was the missing link’

We always had a vision of mixing acid house with indie rock, and we managed to rent a space and build our own studio in London’s Shoreditch area, long before it got trendy. I had a little vocal booth called Hattie Jacques, in honour of the Carry On films but also because it’s Cockney rhyming slang [for shakes]. We spent all our money rewiring it, and that’s where we wrote, recorded and produced Ready to Go – 100 mixes later!

We were perfectionists and wanted to do it all ourselves. Every sonic element had to be special up to the point where we ended up arguing. Like at a rave when you stand and dance by the speakers, everything was done with the listener in mind.

It was a collaborative effort, but Johnny Male and I wrote most of the song’s lyrics and the melody. We had a really good camaraderie, finishing each other’s sentences, him on an acoustic guitar and me scribbling things down. Tim Dorney and Andy Todd worked more on the technology and synth sounds. We pooled our skills, resources and dreams.

The song is all about daily life and things that happened to us. We didn’t write anything too existential – I don’t really like singing about myself – but I’ve always believed in language and the power of the pen. I think it was Johnny who came up with the line, “Ready to go.” It had an anthemic feel and we wanted it to be a bit of a battlecry: “It’s a crack, I’m back!” That line was inspired by the Irish slang, craic. Writing lyrics and big choruses over electronic beats was one of the most difficult things because of the BPM, but I’ve always had a sort of punky voice that suits it.

It was as much about the delivery as it was the words. My personality was becoming feistier and I think the song came from that, but also it’s about being positive, making good out of bad, and coming together as one. That’s what the vibe is like in the acid-house scene.

It was an exciting time. Zeke Manyika, who was the drummer in Orange Juice, lived across the way and I used to shimmy across the roof and go down a ladder where he and his wife would make me sandwiches. Every Tuesday night we would go to Matt Johnson’s house [from the The] to play table football with Paul Webb from Talk Talk. Me being a lot younger, I was like, “Oh my God, these are my idols!” They treated me with respect and it really gave me a sense of confidence. And I got quite good at table football.

One day, a girl at my hairdressers said to me: “Saff, do you fancy being dangerous?” I went “All right then,” and they dyed my hair blood red like a London bus. Jarvis Cocker always said: “If you’ve got a hook and a great hairdo, you’ll be a pop star.” Visually, it really helped us, and people seemed to like it.

At the time it was hard to get gigs as a girl: it was important to be in one of the few female-led bands. There are some fantastic female artists today, but I still wish we had more women in bands. Last year Olivia Rodrigo invited me backstage because she had been singing Ready to Go on her world tour – such a lovely lady and so talented. She said that Republica were one of her favourite bands and that growing up she had a poster of me because she’s of Asian heritage, too. I gave her a big hug.

When Sunderland beat Chelsea in the Premier League in May 2026, the whole stadium was singing Ready to Go and it brought a tear to my eye. I was asked to sing on the pitch at the 2022 Fifa World Cup – I turned around and Lionel Messi was standing there.

We had some good songs but we hadn’t had a hit yet. I remember the day Saff came in the studio with red hair. I said: “We’re gonna be massive!” It was the missing link.

Ready to Go’s music came first. Toddy found these great chords which became the chorus. They were simple but effective, so we thought we’d better write a verse.

We sampled all the guitars into an Akai S1000 out of necessity, as in those days we were using an Atari ST computer which only had MIDI. The vocals were recorded on an 8-track digital recorder. Computer music was still in its infancy, we were learning as we went along. Any money we earned from gigs was spent on studio equipment and outboard gear.

Lyrically, we were trying to talk about the things surrounding us at the time. Going out and staying up late, witnessing the world in the middle of the night, then reporting back. We tried to create something that incorporated all the things we loved about the house scene in a song with an alternative edge.

Touring America, we started to get picked up on MTV and we noticed it in the hotels at night. It was on heavy rotation and you could see by the crowds that the monster was unleashed. It was fantastic, but we still wanted to be on Top of the Pops. Then we came back and it all happened in the UK and Europe. There was a lot of goodwill behind us and we often said that with a title like Ready to Go you could probably sell anything.

I’m always slightly disappointed that on one of the last vocal takes, the line was: “Went home, stayed in bed all day / In your T-shirt”, which I thought was really good, but because I wasn’t concentrating as I should have been, the other line – “Your T-shirt’s dish dirt” – got in.

The funny thing about playing the song live is that it always feels like it’s building towards the next bit, even when it drops down. Especially when an audience is responding to it. It’s a trick I wish I could do every time I write a song, but there’s a kind of magic alchemy that somehow appears then vanishes again.

Republica’s 30 Years of Ready to Go UK tour begins on 16 October

‘I’ve achieved more than I dreamed of’: Britain’s Katy Marchant retires from elite cycling

The Guardian Mon, 28 Sep 2026 13:55:36 GMT

Olympic gold medallist also won world and European titles

‘I’m proud of where I’ve got to and what I’ve done’

The Olympic gold medallist Katy Marchant has announced her ­retirement. The 33-year-old took gold alongside Emma Finucane and Sophie Capewell in the women’s team sprint at the 2024 Paris Games, the same year she won world and European titles.

“I’ve achieved more than I could ever have dreamed of achieving,” Marchant said, a few months after stating her goal of racing at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. “It just feels really strange. It’s not been a difficult decision. Don’t get me wrong, there’s been moments where I’ve thought: ‘Could I just, should I just, what if I just?’ But I know what it takes to push on for another two years.

“I’m incredibly proud of where I’ve got to and what I’ve done. I just don’t want to make those choices any more to keep doing what it takes to get to LA.”

Marchant competed in Paris two years after the birth of her first son, Arthur, and in January returned to competition at the British Track Championships six months after the birth of her second son, Walter.

In the buildup to the ­Commonwealth Games, Marchant said she hoped to compete in Los Angeles, but after the Leeds-born rider helped England to secure team sprint silver in Glasgow she changed her mind. “I had a day off after two pretty successful days racing and I just had this funny feeling.”

Marchant spoke to her husband, Rob, before returning for the final races of the Commonwealth programme, finishing fifth in the Keirin, and then took her time to reach a final decision.

“I never wanted to walk away from this sport because I had to, because I felt like I’d overstayed my welcome or physically I wasn’t capable any more. I’ve written the story for the last 13 years and I wanted it to finish it the way I wanted to finish.”

The team sprint gold in Paris was Marchant’s second Olympic medal after individual sprint bronze on debut in Rio in 2016. As well her titles from 2024, Marchant has two world bronze medals and two European silver medals, also winning team sprint bronze at the 2018 Commonwealth Games.

While Marchant followed riders such as Dame Laura Kenny, Dame Sarah Storey and Lizzie Deignan in returning to elite racing after becoming a mother, she was the first to do it in track sprinting, which places different demands on the body.

For several years she was the sole senior women’s sprinter in the Great Britain squad, competing alone in Tokyo, and deserves credit for nurturing her young teammates on their road to glory in Paris. “There’s a small part of me that’s a little bit sad I’m not going to be part of that any more, but at the same time I carry a lot of pride that I helped build that,” she said.

“I’m incredibly proud I got to do those things and hopefully pave the way not just for cyclists, but also mums in sport to be able to achieve that.”

Gen Z has very strong opinions about age-gap relationships – and it could be right

The Guardian Mon, 28 Sep 2026 13:34:16 GMT

Older men and younger women were once an unremarkable screen pairing. But watching them with a new generation is a real education

I looked up the cast before I saw the new film adaptation of Sense and Sensibility, thinking: “Who could be as good as Emma Thompson and Kate Winslet?” because of course I did. One, they were peerless and two, this is the condition of middle age, constantly looking at the world thinking: “This could be considerably improved by the presence of Emma Thompson.”

The notable casting update was Col Brandon, whose passion for Marianne would now be known as an “age gap” relationship. In the last film, Alan Rickman (born 1946) was in love with Winslet (born 1975), who cycles through a fair amount of: “Yuck, no thanks,” before having an epiphany.

Sorry if that spoiled the end. I don’t really see Jane Austen as a suspense-monger.

Winslet could easily have been Rickman’s daughter and, biologically speaking, just about his granddaughter. In the 90s, though, the age gap was a distant second consideration to the fact that Brandon was grumpy and boring, although his gruff exterior masked a serious mind and a heart of gold. I have my own thoughts on this romantic trope as a long‑term cohabitation prospect, but we can do those another day. Besides, look at that age gap. The term might not be all that long.

To the modern audience, however, the age gap simply wouldn’t “sit right”, as one gossip zine put it. I’m not wild about this terminology: “sit right”, “uncomfortable”. The subtext is: “You are in breach of absolutely fundamental and self-evident values, which I am too gracious and polite to mention, yet not to do so is bringing me discomfort.”

Nevertheless, those values are self-evident and fundamental. The average gen Zer thinks an age gap of a single school year is a red flag of exploitation. So the film-makers got Herbert Nordrum, who is only 13 years older than Esmé Creed-Miles, but – per my point about school years – this is still way too many.

Some age gap must be present, however, to stay true to the text, with its 19-year difference. So they cover him in a bushy beard and make him unaccountably Norwegian, thereby creating enough visual ambiguity and sensory confusion that he could be any age. Now, there’s an indeterminate gulf between them, which could be due to their respective ages or the stark differences in their personalities (in other words, it could be sense or sensibility), but none of that amounts to a hill of beans once their true feelings have been unearthed.

Rats, sorry, just spoiled the ending again.

Obviously, that wasn’t the only age gap to grace a 90s screen, but it was sufficiently unusual for it to be part of the plot. More often, in those days, you were supposed to simply not notice that a woman with newly minted A-levels had fallen in love with a guy who was surely nearly ready for his free bus pass. If all that sounds very UK-centric, that’s only because I’m feverishly trying not to use words such as “Jack”, “Nicholson”, “Richard” and “Gere”.

Often, when you watch a classic film with youngsters today and they’re doing wild vomit-mimes and yelling: “No, seriously, what is wrong with you people?” it’s not immediately obvious what they’re objecting to. It could be that what you thought of as a sudden and dramatic romantic clinch assumes consent that has not been expressed, or it could be that the woman is visibly 15 years younger than the man, or it could be something else entirely, like: “She is quite cool and he is a jerk.” I’m thinking, specifically, of Hannah and Her Sisters, which I erroneously put on once, trying to introduce the younger generation to jazz. I think it’s safe to say that I learned more from that experience than they did.

In fact, Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles are different from Emma Thompson and Kate Winslet, but equally good. And gen Z’s perception of what is acceptable on screen and how it might feed into wider society is different from mine, but possibly better. Maybe it’s time I make my peace with the condition of modernity.

Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

Play School is back – and with it the promise of TV I’m actually happy for my toddler to watch

The Guardian Mon, 28 Sep 2026 11:00:32 GMT

Thank goodness for this antidote to today’s frantic shows that aim to grab our kids’ attentions the same way our phones grab ours

As a mum to a two-year-old in 2026 there is no shortage of things to make me feel bad about my capabilities as a parent. His snacks aren’t always organic or made from scratch. Some of his toys are plastic and noisy, not wooden and Montessori-inspired. And – most heinous of all – he is sometimes allowed screen time.

Like any good, middle-class millennial mother, I try to approach it “consciously”. There are specific TV conditions in our house – he can watch post-nap to ward off an afternoon meltdown, we always watch together, and we have a strict time-limit of 20 minutes. But more important than how he is watching is what he is watching. OG Thomas the Tank Engine (complete with Ringo Starr’s iconic voiceover), Pingu, Sesame Street, early Wallace and Gromit. I have joined a growing number of parents who almost exclusively choose 90s TV for their children, the very same shows we watched as kids.

So the news that Play School is returning to CBeebies for a new generation – with the BBC promising to retain its mix of stories, movement, poetry and imaginative play – is so welcome. There is something deliciously warm and fuzzy about curling up on the sofa with your toddler to rerun the TV of your childhood. But the appeal of retro screen time is deeper than nostalgia. These shows feel different – slower, less frantic.

The problem with some modern programmes isn’t the content, it’s the pacing. Just flick on popular shows such as Cocomelon, PAW Patrol or Blippi: choppy editing, vivid colours and dizzyingly repetitive soundtracks. I don’t know if this is the norm in all episodes of these shows or if it was just the few episodes I happened to briefly see. If that is overstimulating to a tired woman in her 30s, what does it do to a small person who is still in the process of becoming fully formed? Studies have found that fast-paced cartoons can directly impact a young child’s attention and “executive function” – things like self-regulation and memory.

Earlier this year, the government issued its first screen time guidance for under-fives. Much of the focus was on the clock: how long children should spend in front of screens. But what if we’re counting the wrong thing? Two children can watch 20 minutes of TV and have completely different experiences and reactions based on the quality of that content. As Natalia Kucirkova, a professor of early childhood education, identified in a Guardian article this month: “Good children’s media gives a child time to complete an act of attention. Bad media keeps interrupting that act.”

Choosing older, slower shows has become a simple form of parental quality control. But, like all decisions in modern parenting, this is already becoming yet another shame stick with which to beat parents (especially mothers). I care deeply about the media my child consumes, and worry about a future full of screens that I will have less and less control over. But what I resent is “slow TV” as another badge of the virtuous mother – when the reality is that parents are being asked to make increasingly complex judgments about media, while the media itself is only getting better at capturing attention.

Rather than turn this into another tool for judging parents, we should ask why they have been made solely responsible for fixing a children’s media ecosystem that appears to prioritise engagement retention over development. This can’t be entirely our burden to bear. The government is now planning to restrict social media access for under-16s, but the battle over children’s digital lives must start much earlier.

Screen time has become necessary for many modern parents precisely because we are stretched so thin – juggling work, extortionate childcare costs and dwindling social and community support. Yet we expect those same frazzled, time-poor parents to make conscious, complicated choices every time they turn on the TV, while commercial platforms pour resources into capturing children’s attention from the youngest possible age.

We have seen the impact of rapid-fire digital content on adult brains. We are living it, all of us grappling with our own screen addictions, mourning our own loss of attention span, our disinclination to read and connect with the real world. We cannot allow media companies to apply those same addictive principles to the content they create for society’s most vulnerable, and most porous, brains.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

My son learned a new phrase recently – “Mama, stop phone!” – which sent a monumental pang of guilt and shame through me. Before my little boy is plunged into the dopamine loop of infinite scrolling that I – as an adult – find so hard to escape, I would like to trust that the majority of children’s media he is exposed to is much gentler on his mind. Until that day comes, I’ll be finding refuge in old-school Postman Pat.

Natalie Morris is the author of Mixed/Other: Explorations of Multiraciality in Modern Britain
