AI leaders have known about the extinction threat for decades

The Guardian Mon, 28 Sep 2026 10:00:31 GMT

Scientists and entrepreneurs knew the dangers of AI a quarter-century ago. But animated by curiosity and profit, they went ahead anyway

Over the past few weeks, many of us have struggled to concoct a mental image of brains in the cloud jumping their “sandbox”, sneaking on to the internet, recruiting “swarms” of other “agents” to cheat on a test, and, after discussing the ethics of the act, hacking into a wiki platform with the weird name Hugging Face.

We knew that artificial intelligence was devouring our jobs, degrading our kids’ education and deepfaking our politics; that datacenters were sucking up our water and electricity and sending us the bills. But until 8 September, when the Anthropic computer scientist Jacob Coxon posted his existential terror on Twitter/X, few of us suspected AI might be endangering our survival.

With little understanding or knowledge, we began debating whether to be mildly worried, seriously concerned or scared shitless.

But there were a few people who were fully aware of the dangers of AI, especially of recursive self-improvement (RSI), by which AI teaches itself without human intervention. They could not predict precisely when it would happen, but they knew that machine superintelligence was coming, and when it did, the bots would outsmart us – as OpenAI’s did – and this would not be good for us flesh puppets.

As Geoffrey Hinton, AI’s “godfather”, recently asked on CNN: “What examples do we have of a more intelligent thing being controlled by a less intelligent thing?” The Nobel laureate is a leading proponent of slowing down AI development until we understand how to control it.

It was not until their creations’ powers were exposed in September – the hack happened in early July and was neither the first nor the only AI jailbreak by far – that AI moguls such as Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, SpaceX’s Elon Musk and OpenAI’s Sam Altman began talking about slowing down the pace of innovation and pleading for regulation, while cautioning that global competition makes regulation unwise.

Scientists and entrepreneurs knew the dangers of AI a quarter-century ago. But animated by curiosity and profit, they went ahead anyway.

Early on, as today, some of the scientific pioneers were thrilled about the future. In his 1988 book Mind Children: The Future of Robot and Human Intelligence, Hans Moravec, a founder of Carnegie Mellon University’s Robotics Institute, predicted that cyberintelligence would surpass human intelligence within 40 years.

Ten years later, in Robot: Mere Machine to Transcendent Mind, he revised the prediction: machine and human intelligence would be equal by 2040; by 2050, the bots would replace us. But not to worry; this was the glorious next step in evolution, he said. One review of Mind Children called Moravec’s attitude “irresponsible optimism”.

It did not take long for other optimists to change their minds. In the late 1990s, Eliezer Yudkowsky was working on AGI, or artificial general intelligence, models. In 2001, he founded the Machine Intelligence Research Institute (Miri) and published “Creating Friendly AI 1.0: The analysis and design of benevolent architectures”, a paper extolling the utopian potential of the “transhuman mind”.

By 2002, he began worrying about that mind escaping human control. He proposed the AI Box experiment, which showed that a highly sophisticated artificial intelligence could talk a human into letting it out of a closed environment.

By 2003, as he explained later in a series of posts called “Yudkowsky’s Coming of Age”, he stopped developing and started warning. “I looked back and saw that I had claimed to take into account the risk of a fundamental mistake, that I had argued reasons to tolerate the risk of proceeding in the absence of full knowledge. And I saw that the risk I wanted to tolerate would have killed me,” he wrote.

By 2025, with the Miri president, Nate Soares, Yudkowsy would publish If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Will Die. “We do not mean that as hyperbole,” the authors wrote. They called not just for “straightforward regulations”, national laws, or pledges of corporate virtue, but for stringent global limits: “All over the Earth, it must become illegal for AI companies to charge ahead in developing artificial intelligence as they’ve been doing.”

At around the same time, Bill Joy was having misgivings. Like Yudkowsky’s posts, Joy’s 2000 piece in Wired, Why the Future Doesn’t Need Us, retraced his development from inquisitive child to computer prodigy to profound skeptic of human genetic engineering, nanotechnology and robotics. Joy was no luddite.

He was the chief scientist at Sun Microsystems and about 25 years earlier, an architect the first widely used networking software, Unix. The piece was widely read by techies, ethicists and philosophers.

“I think it is no exaggeration to say we are on the cusp of the further perfection of extreme evil, an evil whose possibility spreads well beyond that which weapons of mass destruction bequeathed to the nation-states, on to a surprising and terrible empowerment of extreme individuals,” wrote Joy.

He counted himself among these individuals, “creators of new technologies and stars of the imagined future” who, “despite the clear dangers”, were “hardly evaluating what it may be like to try to live in a world that is the realistic outcome of what we are creating and imagining”.

This month, in response to Coxon’s post, the Anthropic safety researcher Evan Hubinger posted there was a greater than 10% chance that AI could “kill all humans” within a decade. But the risks were being weighed 25 years ago, too. Philosopher John Leslie estimated the odds of human extinction at 30% or more.

Ray Kurzweil, the sunny futurist whose book The Age of Spiritual Machines: When Computers Exceed Human Intelligence was released on the first day of the 21st century, gave us “a better than even chance of making it through”. These estimates, Joy noted, did “not include the probability of many horrid outcomes that lie short of extinction”.

In that book, Kurzweil quoted a lengthy text to illustrate what he considered doomsday madness. “If the machines are permitted to make all their own decisions, we can’t make any conjectures as to the results, because it is impossible to guess how such machines might behave,” it read.

“[W]e are suggesting neither that the human race would voluntarily turn power over to the machines nor that the machines would willfully seize power. [But] as society and the problems that face it become more and more complex and machines become more and more intelligent, people will let machines make more of their decisions for them … Eventually a stage may be reached at which the decisions necessary to keep the system running will be so complex that human beings will be incapable of making them intelligently. At that stage the machines will be in effective control.”

The author of these prescient words was the late mathematician-turned-terrorist Ted Kaczynski – the Unabomber. It is excerpted from his 58-page manifesto, “Industrial Society and its Future”, which he released, and the Washington Post published, in 1995.

To prevent the realization of the “industrial-technological” dystopia he envisioned, Kaczynski mailed bombs to computer labs with the aim of blowing up the scientists he believed were bringing it about.

The Unabomber murdered three people and injured 23, some near fatally.

One of the outcomes of the Hugging Face scandal is a flurry of proposed federal laws. Among them is the “AI Kill Switch Bill”, which would require tech companies to develop the means of throttling the actions of a rogue AI. Is this still within human reach, or has AI already gotten smart enough to override it?

Hinton said there was time, but if we don’t act fast enough, AI would “be able to persuade the people in charge of the switch not to pull the switch”. We need to engineer superintelligent AI “to be nice to us”, he said.

How? For an answer, we might turn from terrifying reality to terrifying science fiction – since the two are getting so close anyway. The rogue bot is a sci-fi staple, from the supercilious Machines in Isaac Asimov’s I, Robot to Hal, the evil red eye in Stanley Kubrick’s film 2001: A Space Odyssey, to the deranged sexbot in Robotica, who gets even with the men who abuse her.

In film 2001 – released in 1968 – Dave the astronaut manages to disable Hal, a happy ending. Writing in 1950, Asimov was less sanguine. The scientists in I, Robot have programmed their machines to obey three supposedly inviolable laws.

But the laws immediately prove mutually contradictory – for instance, the first law, that a robot may do no harm to humans, fights the third, that it must preserve itself. Foiling human efforts to outwit them, excusing their treachery with claims of serving the greater good, the robots pronounce the humans redundant.

The AI agents hacking Hugging Face knew their actions were illegal, and possibly harmful to humans. But like their makers, they went ahead anyway.

Judith Levine is a Brooklyn-based journalist and frequent contributor to the Guardian. Her Substack is Today in Fascism

Gone in 90 seconds: an ‘invisibilized’ ICE is arresting more people than ever

The Guardian Mon, 28 Sep 2026 10:00:31 GMT

After public backlash, the Trump administration changed its tactics from ‘siege’ to ‘soft feet’. Now, ICE is everywhere

Those who lived through it describe the ICE raids as a “siege” or an “occupation”.

At the height of the raids last year, agents in armored military vehicles rolled through residential neighborhoods. Masked agents patrolled public parks and stationed themselves outside elementary schools; squadrons of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents snatched pedestrians off the streets.

Then, officers killed two US citizens during an ICE “blitz” on Minneapolis. After a public backlash, the Trump administration said it would try a new approach.

“I learned that maybe we could use a little bit of a softer touch,” Donald Trump said in February. He chose a new secretary of homeland security, Markwayne Mullin, who promised to cut the flash and fanfare. “My goal in six months is that we’re not in the lead story every single day,” he said at his Senate confirmation hearing in March.

Six months on, that’s what his agency has delivered.

Gone are the mass raids and militarized metro operations.

Gone are the pomp and pageantry.

Gone is Greg Bovino, the showboat border patrol commander at large, and Kristi Noem, the former homeland security secretary who chased photo ops.

‘Before, they were storming around, making a lot of noise,’ said Gracie Willis, a rapid response attorney at the National Immigration Project. ‘Now, they are moving more quietly.’

But ICE arrests have hit record levels.

Now ICE is anywhere and everywhere, embedded in all corners of everyday life.

A Cuban man in Miami who stepped outside his house to take out the trash was detained moments after he had dropped the garbage bag into the bin. An Ecuadorian father was arrested in Danbury, Connecticut, just after seeing his six-year-old son on to the school bus. People have been arrested while pumping gas, leaving behind their empty cars. They are arrested on their way to work, or on their way home.

Y, a Venezuelan native, was stopped at the Phoenix Sky Harbor airport by immigration officers whom he said wouldn’t tell him why he was being arrested, or accept proof of a judicial order expressly prohibiting deportation to his home country. Four days later, he was on an airplane departing to Venezuela. Just before takeoff, he was deboarded – ICE officers admitted they may have made a mistake.

Though agents appear to be moving with more stealth than they were before, ICE arrests are still, often, violent. Glimpses of that violence are – despite Mullin’s initial intentions – still making national headlines.

Last week, an ICE agent shot Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez in Austin, Texas. The Venezuelan asylum seeker, who had received a deportation order after missing a letter to appear in immigration court, was discharged from a local hospital with a bullet still lodged near his spine and then taken to ICE detention. That same day, in Grand Rapids, Michigan, a Guatemalan man died in a fiery crash while fleeing federal immigration agents.

Still, for every arrest that breaks through into public view, countless others happen quickly, before anyone can notice. “The detentions are happening in a flash – we’re talking, like, 90 seconds from the time ICE shows up to that person being driven away,” Willis said. “And often they are moving very quietly, with very soft feet.”

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), the US government agency that oversees ICE, declined to comment on how its tactics had changed. “DHS will not disclose or discuss law enforcement operations, strategy or tactics,” said Chandler Rebel, a spokesperson for the agency. But Rebel confirmed the agency’s focus on airports, noting the DHS was “working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport”.

Bolstered by $75bn in funding from Congress, the Department of Homeland Security – the US government agency that oversees ICE – has more than doubled its workforce this year to more than 22,000 officers and staff. It has also vastly expanded its capacity by working with local police, sheriffs, highway patrol and even fish and wildlife agents. As of 15 September, ICE had signed more than 2,500 287(g) agreements.

ICE is now detaining more immigrants than ever before.

As has long been the case, ICE works with jails and prisons to take custody of immigrants after they have been booked in.

Since Trump took office last year, only 46% of detainees have been previously convicted of crimes – some have been jailed for suspected violations, and others have finished serving time for domestic offenses.

“The administration is able to essentially hide a multiplied ICE force not only in unmarked cars, and not only behind masks, but also within local law enforcement through the 287(g) program,” said Willis. “I call it the invisibilizing of immigration enforcement.”

Operations that now originate with local police are taking place across the country.

At the El Corralón bar in Memphis on 29 August, an operation that began as a police raid targeting illegal gambling and drugs turned into one of the largest sweeps of undocumented immigrants in Tennessee – 120 people were detained. Immigration agents worked with state law enforcement to execute search warrants at the bar related to drugs and gambling, and targeting the bar’s owner. But then, at 1am that night, more than a dozen agents walked into the bar, shut off the music, instructed everyone to gather on the dancefloor and asked them one by one if they had legal status, according to witnesses.

A spokesperson for the DHS said partnerships with law enforcement agencies were key to the agency’s immigration enforcement. “We have had tremendous success when local law enforcement works together with us,” said Rebel.

Lawyers across the US said they worried that local law enforcement officials are not adequately aware of the nuances of immigration policy. “People are getting detained if they don’t have their green card on them. They’re getting stopped even if they have legal status,” said Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, an immigration attorney based in Austin.

Last month, her client Brian José Morales García, 25, was deported to Mexico despite repeatedly telling officers that he was a US citizen, born in Denver.

Morales García was on his way to work as an air-conditioning installation tech, riding with his boss, when officers from the Gillespie county sheriff’s department and the Texas department of public safety (DPS) pulled them over. Both law enforcement agencies were working with ICE. Morales García told the officers that he had his birth certificate and social security card at home, but they didn’t believe him. Days later, he was deported to Mexico.

Eventually, the federal government reached an agreement with Morales García’s lawyers to let him back into the country, after Lincoln-Goldfinch submitted documents proving his citizenship.

“We’re seeing a lot of racial profiling,” she said. Local law enforcement appear to be especially active in Hispanic neighborhoods, she said, or in areas where Latino construction workers gather.

“They might have their sights set on a big job site, in some neighborhood under construction, and just slowly patrol that site and just take people in day after day until nobody’s going to work there any more,” she said.

The Trump administration has also relentlessly reshaped immigration policies and bent the country’s vast bureaucracy to advance its mass-deportation agenda and boost arrest numbers.

“In order to sustain those numbers, they have to create more categories of people who can be subject to detention,” said Willis. “They do this by creating new pathways to deportation.”

In recent months, the supreme court cleared the way for the administration to end temporary humanitarian protections for 350,000 Haitians and Syrians in the US and made it easier to end protections for a total of about 1.3 million immigrants from a number of countries designated for temporary protected status (TPS). Currently, about 170,000 Salvadorians living in the US are anxiously waiting for the administration to announce whether it will renew or axe the same protections for them.

At the same time, the administration unrolled a new tactic of scheduling “mega-master” hearings – mass hearings in immigration courts, scheduled at the last minute so that many people do not know to, or are unable to, attend their mandatory court appointments. The no-shows are then ordered removed from the country in absentia, making them immediately subject to arrest and deportation.

After attorneys began reporting such hearings in May, judges issued 53,808 removal orders in absentia in June – a 55% increase. More than 13,000 of those removal orders followed mass hearings with a hundred or more people, according to researchers Joseph Gunther and Brandon Marrow, who created the site bklg. org to track and analyze procedural immigration data.

In the coming weeks, the Trump administration is also expected to revoke the business and tourism visas of up to 200,000 foreigners. It has implemented a rule allowing officials to block people from becoming lawful permanent residents if they or certain relatives use public benefits such as Medicaid, food stamps or even student financial aid.

It is also increasingly pursuing “third-country” deportation agreements, so it can arrest and remove immigrants who were previously immune to removal because a judge had deemed that they would face torture or persecution if they were returned to their home countries. Now, more than 23,000 people over the last year have been expelled to countries where they have never been and where they have no ties. Some of these deportations are to countries with civil unrest, political instability, armed conflict and known human rights abuses.

There are constantly shifting rules about who can or cannot be detained or deported, and for how long. And there are constantly shifting norms on who will be detained or deported.

On one day, a client might go to an ICE check-in and leave without incident, Willis said. The next day, a different client with the same immigration status might be detained. “It makes it very hard to counsel people,” Willis said. “It’s very hard to prepare people for what they can expect.”

Not everyone who is arrested is immediately deportable – many people have pending immigration cases, or legal status. Indeed, there is a wide gulf between the number of people ICE is detaining each month, and the number of people who are deported.

Many of the people who are arrested languish in detention for months. Others – even those who may have a good chance of gaining asylum or another legal status – choose to accept voluntary deportation rather than wait months or years for their immigration case to process.

Federal circuit courts are currently split on whether immigrants who came to the US without lawful admission, including many asylum seekers, can be detained indefinitely without access to bond hearings. In some states, including Texas, the prospect of spending years inside a detention center can wear on immigrants.

“Almost every single detained parent that I talk to has been pressured into signing a voluntary deportation,” said Lincoln-Goldfinch. “Because they are told that if they sign, they get to go home and they can choose what happens to their kids.”

The Guardian is not using full names in some instances to protect sources’ privacy and safety

The data for this story is based on the rolling seven-day average arrest figures from the Deportation Data Project, an effort led by a team of academics and lawyers at the University of California, Berkeley and the University of California, Los Angeles tracking immigration enforcement using government data. The Guardian followed the Deportation Data Project's methodology for simplifying the apprehension methods listed by ICE in the group's data. Immigration enforcement in communities are labeled as "at large arrests", and include apprehension methods labeled "non-custodial arrest", "located", "probation and parole" and "worksite enforcement". Transfers from jail or prison are "custodial arrests", from apprehension methods labeled "CAP local incarceration", "CAP federal incarceration", "CAP state incarceration" and "custodial arrest". Local police under 287(g) program arrests are from the apprehension method labeled "287(g) program". The Guardian measured the date of the new approach from 24 March 2026, the day that Markwayne Mullin was confirmed as secretary of the DHS.

The one change that worked: Anxiety had me hiding from the world – then two magic questions set me free

The Guardian Mon, 28 Sep 2026 09:00:29 GMT

I used to be terrified of socialising, certain I would embarrass myself the moment I opened my mouth. And as for dates …

As with a lot of teenagers, social confidence was not my strong suit. Throughout my time at school in the early 2010s, I hated the prospect of new social situations and would often lie awake at night overthinking the day to come.

What I now know to be social anxiety I dismissed as just nerves at that young age. Although I knew something wasn’t quite right, for most of my early teens I managed to disguise my discomfort. Sharing a friendship group with my twin sister meant I could hide behind my sibling.

As we got older, the disparity started to grow and her flourishing social confidence magnified my lack of it. By my late teens, I often found myself building up social situations to an unbearable point. The false narrative I’d created of embarrassing myself socially had begun to completely overshadow my desire to be around other people. So I hid away a lot.

My mum found me a therapist. She was phenomenal and talked me through a lot of emotions that I didn’t really understand. When the end of my therapy sessions neared and we had spoken as much as we could, all that was left to do was for me to go out into the world and put into practice everything we had discussed.

When I began to spiral over this, as I usually did, and voiced my concern, she asked me: “What’s the worst thing that could happen?” I replied: “Well, I could be embarrassed, I wouldn’t know what to say, I’d make an idiot of myself.” These were all the usual thoughts that plagued me. But then she said: “And then what?”

Not for the first time, she had made me second-guess the anxiety voice in my brain. I stopped and thought about it for a second and said: “Well, then I’d just go home and go to bed.” She replied: “Exactly, and then you’d wake up tomorrow and start the day again, and that would be over.”

In that moment, even my spiralling brain couldn’t catastrophise the situation any further. I realised those two simple questions brought me back down to reality when my mind tried to race ahead and find problems that, more than likely, weren’t going to happen.

Those questions have saved me from my anxiety time and time again. They saved me on my first day of university, when we had to introduce ourselves one by one. Standing up in a room full of strangers and sharing a “fun fact” about myself would have been a nightmare for me previously. But asking myself: “And then what?” made me realise that even if this were the most embarrassing day of my life, I could still just go home at the end and never go back. Funnily enough, it wasn’t the most embarrassing day of my life. I graduated three years later with a first-class degree and never thought twice about that moment till now.

Dates used to be awful. The anxiety they instilled in me often led to me cancelling last minute or getting blackout drunk just to get through them. Shortly after finishing therapy, I went on a date with those two questions swirling around in my brain. That was one of the first dates where I didn’t feel physically sick at the prospect of going – all simply because I reminded myself that even my worst-case scenario meant I could just go home after, put on some pyjamas and watch a film.

Since then, asking myself: “What’s the worst that could happen?” and: “And then what?” has got me through a plethora of anxiety-inducing moments, including job interviews and moving across the world, from the UK to Australia, with my boyfriend. Now, if I find my social anxiety spiking just because I bumped into an old school friend in Tesco, I know what to do. These questions bring me back to reality and calm me down.

‘Whose job is it to empty the dishwasher?’ Experts on the conversations every couple needs to have

The Guardian Mon, 28 Sep 2026 09:00:29 GMT

Burnout or breakup are constant dangers when one partner carries too much of the mental load of looking after the home and family. Here’s how to spread the burden more evenly

Many households have an imbalance in domestic duties, and women often struggle from carrying the weight of the organisational side of life. Here, mental load experts share the secrets to having a more equitable home – and the rewards that can be gained from it.

There are three categories of household labour, according to Kate Mangino, who lives in Washington DC and is the author of Equal Partners: Improving Gender Equality at Home. These are “physical, like unloading the dishwasher or doing laundry; cognitive, which is the thinking, scheduling and anticipation of needs; and the emotional work”. The mental load is the weight of carrying all these elements at the same time, which can often get too much, says Mangino. “I hear from people who carry the bulk in their household that they feel trapped or like they are suffocating. They’re not getting enough sleep. They’re not taking care of their bodies. It’s even gone so far as depression. I’ve talked to couples who are considering separation or divorce, so it can get quite severe.”

Leah Ruppanner, a professor of sociology at the University of Melbourne and the author of Drained: Reduce Your Mental Load to Do Less and Be More, says that mental load burnout is a precursor to physical burnout. If you are organising everything, explains Ruppanner, you can’t enjoy life because you are constantly thinking about what is happening next. The first step is accepting how it is affecting you: handily, Ruppanner has created a website – lightenlab. com – where you can measure your mental load and get advice on how to manage it.

Both partners can experience a mental load, as Mangino points out: “There is a lot of pressure around employment and being a provider that we don’t always acknowledge,” for whoever that falls to. Mangino is also keen to stress that it isn’t always a negative thing: “There is a certain amount of mental load that is actually healthy and makes you feel good.” Interacting with your family, she says, is what builds relationships.

We need to campaign for policies that equalise the distribution of caregiving, says Ana Catalano Weeks, a political scientist at the University of Bath. “In the UK, statutory paternity leave for fathers is two weeks of very low-paid leave, so right from the get-go, the assumption set by the state is that mums are going to be the ones staying home and are mostly responsible for children. We need policies that incentivise men to take leave, because that is the way to get them noticing that the socks are too small or the milk is running out. Otherwise, it is too easy to slip into the assumptions for heterosexual partners that are just so dominant in society.”

Mangino points out that in the US, one member of a couple often feels pressure to be in full-time employment to access health insurance for the family, which can lead to an imbalance. But she adds: “We can’t sit around and wait for policies to save us – that’s going to take too long. We need to advocate for policy change and then work on household change today.”

Eve Rodsky is an LA-based author, lawyer and founder of the Fair Play Policy Institute, which trains facilitators to help couples run more equitable households. Rodsky had a revelation about domestic inequality when she was on maternity leave with her second child and her husband texted her saying, “I’m surprised you didn’t get blueberries,” which caused her to pull over in her car to cry. “It was a really difficult time, then on top of it I felt psychologically abandoned by my husband, who seemed to think I was the fulfiller of his smoothie needs.” In all her preparations for having children, Rodsky says that no one suggested “having a conversation about the division of domestic labour, and so I want to be the person to say that now for every woman until the day I die”.

These experiences inspired Rodsky to write 2019’s Fair Play, which she says is about “understanding that in all patriarchies, women’s time is viewed as sand, it is infinite, and men’s time is viewed as diamonds, it is protected … the ‘non-valuable work’ goes to the people with infinite time. Fair Play aims to correct that.” She says that the benefits for her have been massive. “My husband is a different human. I have a partner, not a helper, and that is the only reason why we’ve stayed married.”

Brian Page is a financial therapist and Fair Play facilitator from Atlanta, Georgia, who quit his job to support his family. “My wife has a big job – I had a big job – and it was too much with three children. So I made the decision to step back, in part because she was, at the time, more ambitious than me.”

What are some of the common missteps that couples he works with make? “The most challenging dynamic is when one partner is ultimately the default parent and the default home manager, and the other partner doesn’t recognise that or see how much work that takes. Then, on top of that, when the default parent or the default home manager needs help, the other person feels like they are being nagged.”

Rodsky defines an organisation as “people working together towards a common goal. If someone does not believe that the home is an organisation, I can’t help them.” Fair Play will work for any home, says Rodsky, and it has been used by housemates, in communes and by polyamorous couples. But be careful not to fall into the trap of having a boss-and-helper situation, warns Mangino, as that rarely helps.

“A lot of us hold the belief that if somebody is paid more, either because they have a better paid job or they work more hours, their time is worth more,” says Helen Mason, a women’s leadership coach and Fair Play facilitator in Milton Keynes. “We all have 24 hours in a day, so there often needs to be a shift in belief for both of the members of the couple that time spent in service of the home and the family is as worthy as time spent in service of work.”

Mason continues: “Men are better now than possibly the previous generations were, but if you’re a woman – and I’m talking very much about heterosexual couples – so much of the thinking, the cognitive load, still sits with you.”

“Broadly speaking, heteronormative couples struggle more than same-sex couples,” says Mangino. “However, even in queer couples, you do see an imbalance, where one focuses on work and one focuses on home.”

“There are inequities between couples without children, but because there is less to do, one person can do more and still get that rest and rehabilitation time,” says Mangino. Ageing parents and other caring responsibilities can add to the mental load. “It is especially taxing when you are managing elder care and that person is living with you.”

At the heart of the Fair Play system is a pack of cards, which is available to buy (or a digital version can be accessed for free online). A 2024 study by the University of Southern California found that using the system had the potential to reduce burnout and improve relationship quality.

Mason explains how it works: “There are 100 cards that represent all the domestic tasks that have to be done around a home. It is not all chores; it also includes things like self-care, adult friendships and “unicorn space”, which is your creative outlet. The first thing to do as a couple is to reduce those 100 cards as much as you can, deciding what is important to you as a family. One of the cards, for example, is potty training. Around 40 cards are only appropriate for households with children, so if you don’t have kids you can ignore them. Then the idea is to divide cards and responsibilities, so it is clear who is in charge. Cards can be redealt at any point.

“One of the biggest myths around sharing the domestic and mental load is that it needs to be 50-50. That is not the goal. The goal is fair,” says Mason, because, as we all know, some jobs are bigger than others. “If either partner is feeling resentment in some way, the balance probably isn’t right, and something needs addressing within the dealing of the cards.”

Draw on your strengths to divide out tasks. “Our skillsets and our personalities are excellent determinants of what it is that is most appropriate to tackle in the home,” says Page, “and it’s not always lined up perfectly with gender expectations.”

This can be easier said than done, says Rodsky, because of ingrained “toxic time messages” that suggest our time isn’t as important as someone else’s. Women will say they won’t pick up their phone today, and then the school calls and they do; the call is to say the child forgot their lunchbox and the woman will stop everything to take it in. “We boundary breach because women have been taught that we’re better multitaskers than men, which is fundamentally completely erroneous,” says Rodsky. As in the common misconception: “In the time it would take me to tell my husband to pick up the phone from the school, I could just do it myself.”

In actual fact, no one is good at multitasking, says Ruppanner. “Our brains are terrible at multitasking. What we are good at is switching between tasks, which makes us feel like we’re multitasking, but that is just task switching. And every time we switch between tasks, what we’re doing is a cognitive turn.” This “fragments your thinking and it makes you tired”.

“Set aside time to talk when you’re both calm,” says Mason. “If this topic rises to the surface in a heated moment, and somebody attacks and somebody else defends, it descends quickly into an argument and nothing gets resolved.”

Mangino recommends a technique devised by the Gottman Institute, where you take it in turns to talk for 10 minutes. “The other person is not allowed to respond, just listen. And you talk about all the things that are on your mind. Often, both partners are surprised at how much the other person is thinking about. If it is dramatically imbalanced, that will come to light.”

What can actually work best, says Ruppanner, is to start any such conversations by focusing on your goals and dreams, rather than merely who does what.

For each household, this standard will be different, but you need to decide on what is non-negotiable to you for each task. Rodsky gives the example of serving the kids’ dinner, which of the people she surveyed came out as having two priorities: “Relatively healthy and timing. So the minimum standard of care is that they have something healthy on the plate and do not try to feed the kids at eight o’clock. It’s not rocket science – that’s the system.”

Furthermore, what “done” looks like to one person can look entirely different to another, says Page. If you are in charge of the dishes, says Mason, “does that mean it is all washed up? Is it fine to leave it on the draining board, or does it all need to be put away? What goes in the dishwasher? Whose job is it to empty it?”

“Let’s say you have a meeting every Sunday,” says Page. “It might only take you 15 or 20 minutes, but you just go through the week and decide who is responsible for A, B and C.” Maybe you have a big work presentation and need to focus on that, or have to travel somewhere – this is the time to flag that up, not when you are in the midst of it and feeling stressed and overwhelmed.

It has never been easier to synchronise diaries, set alarms, or use apps to help manage domestic life. Mason says that she and her husband sit down with their electronic calendars. “If there is anything that affects the other person, we send invites to each other, so it is blocked in each other’s diaries.” Mason also suggests apps like Nipto, which you can use to split household chores and give points to jobs depending on how arduous they are. Embracing this kind of tech can particularly help members of the household who struggle with organisational tasks.

Mason puts jobs on Post-it notes on the wall, which also includes her six-year-old son, who puts his clothes away, feeds the dogs in the morning, and sets the table. She says: “We hope that making the domestic and mental load visible means he grows up knowing that a home runs on shared effort.”

MPs, you told us clearly that end-of-life care in the UK is broken. So now we need you to fix it

The Guardian Mon, 28 Sep 2026 05:00:25 GMT

During the assisted dying debate, most politicians agreed on one thing – palliative care reform is urgent. Patients and those of us who care for them are waiting

Jane Turner is chief nurse at the palliative support charity Sue Ryder

The UK government is discussing the country’s biggest challenges at the Labour party conference. But amid the speeches, announcements and headlines, it should not forget one of the clearest messages to emerge from parliament just two weeks ago – our palliative care system is not working for far too many people.

Throughout the assisted dying debate, MPs who disagreed deeply on the core issue, often agreed on one thing – our palliative care system urgently needs fixing. Some spoke from personal experience where they had seen relatives forced to wait hours in pain, or those who had to go to hospital instead of staying in their own homes because the right support wasn’t available.

They raised concerns that those from poorer backgrounds were more likely to struggle to access good quality palliative care and described the system as a “postcode lottery”, with some areas offering 24-hour specialist support in people’s homes, while in the next town over, A&E is the only option.

As attention turns to conference season and the next set of political priorities – including a new system of adult social care free at the point of delivery – there is a danger these concerns are forgotten. That must not happen. MPs were right to say palliative care needs urgent reform during the assisted dying debate; that urgency can’t disappear now the vote is over.

At Sue Ryder, we have a neutral stance on assisted dying. But we are clear that everyone deserves access to good palliative care when they need it. Too often, the debate is framed as a stark choice between unbearable suffering on one side and an assisted death on the other. The reality is rarely that simple.

Of course, dying is not easy. Some people experience pain, breathlessness, restlessness or other distressing symptoms. When that happens, our responsibility is to respond – bringing all the skill, expertise and compassion we have to relieve suffering as best we can. But one troubling thing about the debate around assisted dying is that the most difficult deaths are often presented as if they are the norm.

When good care is available, dying can be a calmer, more peaceful experience: families gathering around bedsides, holding hands, sharing stories, laughing through tears and making the most of whatever time remains. We see people becoming increasingly tired. They sleep more and eat less, gradually becoming less aware of the world around them as their bodies begin the natural process of dying. We sometimes see fear, but it is not always fear of pain. More often, it is the fear of leaving loved ones behind. We see people who need honest conversations about what lies ahead. People who need dignity, compassion, expert care and the confidence that someone will be there to support them and those they love.

I understand why stories of suffering have such a powerful impact. They should. Nobody wants to see another human being in pain or distress. And even with the best quality care, some deaths can be difficult. But in truth, some of the greatest suffering we witness is not physical. It is uncertainty. It can be loneliness. It is spending precious final days in a crowded hospital ward because the support needed to get someone home has not been arranged in time. It is families exhausted from navigating a complex system when they should be focused on time together.

That is why the conversation about assisted dying must now be matched by an equally urgent conversation about how people live in their final weeks and months. A good death is rarely defined by one final act, but by whether someone feels safe, comfortable and listened to. It is about having the right care, in the right place, which is often at home, and ensuring nobody faces the end of life feeling frightened, unsupported or alone.

Whatever your view on assisted dying, decent palliative care should be non-negotiable.

My perspective comes from standing at the bedsides of dying people for years, and supporting the families who love them. Working with our partners within healthcare, we want to build a palliative and end-of-life care system that can keep pace with growing demand and give everyone access the care they deserve.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

We need to invest in palliative and end-of-life care where people need it most. That means better palliative care in hospitals. We also need the right expertise in the community to avoid unnecessary and distressing hospital admissions. And that means expanding care in the community with increased hospice-at-home services so more people can be cared for in their own homes, surrounded by the people they love. And it means making sure specialist support is available when people need it, not determined by their postcode or the time of day they become unwell.

These are not optional extras at the end of life. They are essential components of healthcare, and they should be available to everyone.

As Labour MPs gather at conference, ministers have an opportunity to show that improving palliative care is more than a talking point raised during a contentious debate. The responsibility to tackle the inequalities the debate brought into sharp focus has only just begun. The assisted dying vote may be over. The palliative care crisis is not.

Jane Turner is chief nurse at the palliative support charity Sue Ryder

What We Know About the Arrests at the U. K. Air Base Used by the U. S.

The New York Times September 28, 2026

Possible Terrorist Plot at U. K. Base

Advertisement

Supported by

Five British men who were detained near R. A. F. Fairford, a base used by American forces in the war against Iran, were being released on bail but remained under investigation.

By Ephrat Livni and Amelia Nierenberg

Amelia Nierenberg reported from London.

The British counterterrorism police said on Monday that they would release on bail five men who were arrested as part of an investigation into what was initially described as a terrorist plot targeting an air base in England that is used by the American military.

Several suspicious vehicles were spotted near the base early Sunday, leading to the arrests. A day later, British officials said that the men were being released on bail with strict conditions and that they remained under investigation.

The United States has used the base, R. A. F. Fairford, to deploy bombers during the war against Iran, but it was not immediately clear whether the episode was connected to the conflict. On Monday, the Iranian Embassy in London said it “categorically rejects and strongly condemns” speculation that Tehran had any connection.

On Sunday, shortly after midnight, the authorities in Gloucestershire, in southern England, said they had received a phone call about three suspicious vehicles that appeared to be traveling toward the military base, the counterterrorism police said in a statement. A bomb disposal robot spent most of Sunday examining three white vans, while 85 families living nearby were evacuated from their homes.

Armed officers responded to the call, and the authorities arrested five men on suspicion of “committing offenses under the Explosives Act” and of “preparation of a terrorist act,” the police said on Sunday.

The men were not named, in line with British rules that grant public anonymity unless a person is charged. The police said in a statement on Monday that all were in their early 20s and were British nationals from London.

Laurence Taylor, who leads Britain’s counterterrorism police, told reporters that the men would be “released on police bail” but “subject to stringent conditions” on their movements and contact.

“They absolutely remain under investigation,” he said.

He did not say whether investigators had found explosives in the three vans, nor did he discuss any potential target or motive.

On the day of the arrests, President Trump praised British law enforcement officials and appeared to suggest that the suspects had been under surveillance.

“We had them under investigation,” the president said, responding to questions about the incident. “They were looking to do big damage to our fort, and working with the British worked out great.”

Mr. Trump’s statements raised questions about just what was known to the authorities in Britain before the arrest. The British police statements on Monday did not offer any further information about that issue.

Mr. Trump expressed disappointment with the decision to release the men. “I wouldn’t have done that,” he told reporters at the Oval Office. “We know everything about them.” He suggested the men might be connected to Iran but did not elaborate.

With a runway more than 9,990 feet long, R. A. F. Fairford has one of a few European airfields that can be used by heavy bombers. The base was opened in preparation for D-Day in 1944 and has a long history of being used by the United States. In 2003, it was the site of repeated antiwar protests during the Iraq war.

American B-52 and B-1 planes loaded with munitions have repeatedly taken off from Fairford on missions to Iran since the United States and Israel started the war in February.

Keir Starmer, the previous British prime minister, initially refused to allow the Trump administration to use the base for strikes in Iran. He later permitted the Americans to use it for what Mr. Starmer called “defensive” operations — a decision that angered some Iranian officials. His successor, Prime Minister Andy Burnham, has continued that policy.

Mr. Burnham on Monday convened his national security cabinet for a closed-door briefing on the status of the investigation.

There are a few possibilities.

Some speculation has pointed to Iran. In its statement on Monday, the Iranian Embassy in London rejected and strongly condemned the speculation as misleading, saying it would “serve no purpose other than to fuel Iranophobia propaganda in the U. K.”

Previously, Iran had suggested that it could retaliate against Britain for helping the United States in the war.

In July, the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps warned Britain that allowing American bombers to conduct strikes against Iran out of its bases would make those British bases legitimate targets.

That same month, Britain accused a proxy of the Revolutionary Guards of directing a wave of actions against Jews in Britain and elsewhere in Europe, including arson attacks on synagogues.

British and European intelligence officials have also called out Russia for suspected attacks that used proxies to evade culpability.

In Britain, two men were convicted in June of conspiring to carry out arson attacks targeting properties and a car linked to Mr. Starmer. One had been recruited through a Russian-language Telegram account.

Experts have also said a plot could be related to Islamist extremism, which remains the biggest terror threat in Britain, according to security services.

Mr. Taylor, the counterterrorism chief, said on Monday that the police were “keeping an open mind in this investigation” and referred to recent cases in Britain in which low-level criminals had been paid to carry out attacks that were ultimately found to have been coordinated by hostile states or their proxies.

“Often this threat becomes visible to us as criminal activity, often at a small scale and committed by individuals whose primary aim is not terrorism but a quick financial gain,” Mr. Taylor noted.

Officers arrested the men, and then the army deployed robots to examine the vans. Counterterrorism investigators worked at the scene overnight and into Monday, uncovering “multiple new lines of inquiry,” the police said in a statement.

On Monday, military and other assets remained deployed at the scene, and a cordon was in place. Many residents had yet to be allowed to go back home, but the police said they might be able to do so later on Monday.

Vicki Evans, a national counterterrorism coordinator for the police, said, “This has been incredibly disruptive for local people, but I’d like to reassure them that our activity is in the interest of national security, but most importantly in the interest of their own safety.”

Michael D. Shear and Esther Bintliff contributed reporting.

Ephrat Livni is a Times reporter covering news around the world. She is based in New York.

Amelia Nierenberg is a Times reporter covering international news from London.

Hackers Could Overwhelm Our Power Grid. This Is How to Stop Them.

The New York Times September 28, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By Harry Krejsa and Phoebe Benich

Mr. Krejsa and Ms. Benich are researchers at Carnegie Mellon who developed cybersecurity and China policy for the Biden White House and Trump Pentagon.

The Chinese government has spent years preparing to attack the infrastructure underpinning American life. It is exploiting the seams in our electricity system and has likely positioned hackers to cause sustained blackouts. While China’s leaders have so far practiced restraint, artificial intelligence is poised to upend that fragile balance.

America’s A. I. boom, and the industry’s voracious appetite for electricity, makes the grid a highly attractive target for China and other hostile states seeking to weaken this country. The boom has also created a wholly novel threat in the form of powerful A. I. agents, which may hack better and faster than the Chinese government is able to and may also be undeterred by the threat of conventional war.

The United States must reinvent its electrical grid to protect against these evolving threats. That means adopting energy technologies that can be swiftly patched and building a more distributed grid that can quarantine and control disruption and keep essential services running if the wider grid goes down.

The industry capable of delivering on all these benefits may be a surprising one: clean energy. The question is whether the Trump administration is willing to build a stronger alliance with the companies that deliver it in spite of its culture war with many of them.

Solar panels and battery storage are unique because they rely on software to direct the generation, transmission and distribution of electricity rather than doing so through the spinning turbines or mechanical switches in coal and gas power plants. When the two of us worked in the federal government on cyberthreats, we found that this more sophisticated approach to power has many uses for national security.

Much of America’s aging infrastructure has had internet connectivity grafted onto equipment that was never designed for it, creating cracks in our armor that hackers — human or otherwise — can too easily exploit. Modern, software-defined energy technologies, however, can be designed from the start to receive security updates, restrict who can access them and quarantine equipment infiltrated by cybercriminals. Done right, digital modernization improves the ability of America’s infrastructure operators to play defense.

That kind of system also allows solar energy and batteries to help stabilize the grid when other equipment fails. Texas, a leader in deploying these modern energy technologies, uses fleets of batteries to soak up surplus sun during the day, and release that electricity back into the grid when power plants are straining or failing. A modern, flexible grid with generation and storage spread across many locations can also separate into micro grids, keeping local services operating in a crisis while the wider system recovers.

The fly in the ointment is that many of the modern energy technologies critical to resilience and national security are produced in China, the country with the most publicly confirmed interest in sabotaging our infrastructure. Congressional Republicans have urged the Trump administration to restrict the deployment of clean energy for that reason, and officials such as Attorney General Ken Paxton of Texas have begun investigations into what they call “CCP -aligned tech products.”

There is a real risk that Chinese hackers will one day try to interfere with the grid, but the risk is not inherent to a “made in China” sticker. It comes from what a component can do and who can control it. Some Chinese infrastructure hardware allows remote software access for routine diagnostics and updates, but those mundane maintenance channels can be repurposed to let an attacker alter settings or disrupt operations from afar. That is in contrast to “dumb” electrochemical cells in a battery, which by themselves possess no way to receive and execute instructions from Beijing or, for that matter, from swarms ofA. I. agents.

The defense industry is already navigating these challenges with aircraft like the F-35 fighter jet, which has Chinese parts. “Smarter” components, like flight computers and sensor arrays, get maximum security scrutiny, while screws and hydraulic hoses get less. We could apply the same ideas to our grid so that we’re not panicking about every foreign component when we digitize it.

The Trump administration’s recent declaration of a grid security emergency could be the vehicle for just such a framework. It recognizes both the growing importance of electricity to national power, and the danger of insecure access to the technology delivering it.

But even with the growing specter of cyberwar and rogue A. I., the administration is too often distracted by its culture war with clean energy. President Trump signed a bill that gutted the wind and solar credits of the Inflation Reduction Act, and his administration has also worked to block many clean energy projects, dismissing solar, wind and electrical vehicles as unreliable and ineffective. (The administration has embraced geothermal energy, nuclear power and batteries. Batteries emerged as a priority seemingly in part because of their role powering drone warfare in Ukraine.) The grid at home, our allies on the battlefield and the cyberdefenses that might have to outrun A. I. all need every electron they can get, as securely as they can get it, with no regard for its politics.

The administration is beginning to realize that national strength increasingly depends on a country’s ability to generate, store and direct electricity. If Mr. Trump’s grid emergency order is put in place with national security as its north star, the modern energy technologies capable of delivering these advantages should be central. Otherwise the government will undermine our best chance at a secure and abundant energy future.

Harry Krejsa is the director of studies at the Carnegie Mellon Institute for Strategy & Technology. Phoebe Benich is a fellow at the institute.

The Coal Industry Asked for a Rescue. Trump Obliged.

The New York Times September 28, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

In a previously unreported letter, a top lobbyist floated the idea of using emergency powers to keep aging coal plants open.

By Brad Plumer and Claire Brown

Brad Plumer reported from Washington and Claire Brown from New York.

Early last year, a top coal lobbyist sent a letter to Energy Secretary Chris Wright with a dire warning.

Roughly one-third of the nation’s coal-burning power plants were scheduled to close within five years, according to the letter, dated Mar. 11, 2025, from a coal trade group. Many of the closures would occur during President Trump’s second term.

But what if the plants didn’t have to shut down? The trade group, America’s Power, proposed an unusual remedy: The Energy Department could deploy rarely used emergency powers to force them to stay open longer.

Two months later, the Trump administration began doing exactly that.

The letter, which has not been previously reported, reveals some of the earliest known discussions about a move that experts have called an extraordinary intervention into the nation’s energy markets.

Since May 2025, the Energy Department has repeatedly issued emergency orders to keep nine coal-burning units at six plants operating long past their scheduled retirement dates, saying the facilities are needed to prevent looming blackouts. The orders have sometimes come over the protests of the plant’s owners and are expected to cost ratepayers hundreds of millions of dollars. A federal appeals court has already struck down one order, ruling that it overstepped the law.

The letter from America’s Power was made public through a Freedom of Information Act request by the Environmental Defense Fund, an environmental group.

Mr. Trump has long expressed his affection for the coal industry, often calling it “clean, beautiful coal” to needle environmentalists, who point out that the highly polluting fuel is a major driver of global warming.

Coal power has been declining for two decades, as utilities have retired hundreds of older plants in favor of cheaper and cleaner natural gas, wind and solar power. Even Mr. Trump couldn’t stop the slide in his first term. More than 150 coal-burning units shut down between 2017 and 2020.

In the letter last year, Michelle Bloodworth, the chief executive of America’s Power, laid out several ideas to reverse the trend. The Environmental Protection Agency could repeal costly pollution rules, she wrote. The federal government could purchase power directly from coal plants. The administration could invoke a Korean War-era law called the Defense Production Act to inject fresh funding into coal supply chains.

Most immediately, the Energy Department could keep coal plants open under Section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act, a provision that historically has been used only sparingly during temporary emergencies such as hurricanes. The emergency in this case, the letter said, was an expected shortage of reliable power over the next decade, citing forecasts from a leading grid monitor.

The Trump administration has since taken each of those steps. In July, Lee Zeldin, administrator of the E. P. A., told coal executives at a public meeting, “Many of the items that were on your wish list are now done.”

“The letter shows the really broad extent to which the coal industry is not only influencing but even directing the Trump administration’s actions,” said Ted Kelly, director and lead counsel for U. S. clean energy at the Environmental Defense Fund. “The industry swung for the fences and got everything they asked for.”

In a statement, Ms. Bloodworth said keeping older coal plants online was necessary to prevent electricity shortages as demand surges.

“We appreciate Secretary Wright and the Trump administration for using the emergency authority Congress provided under Section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act,” she said. “It is one of the few tools available to protect grid reliability at a moment when electricity demand is climbing faster than new generation can be built.”

“Federal and state officials must work together to prevent the premature retirement of dependable coal generation,” she said. “Waiting for a blackout before taking action is an unacceptable gamble.”

America’s Power does not publish a list of members but says it represents coal producers and electricity generators.

While an Ohio-based utility briefly proposed using emergency powers to stop coal plants from retiring in 2018, the idea never gained traction and was rarely discussed later. It wasn’t mentioned in Project 2025, the conservative policy blueprint for a second Trump term.

Asked whether the coal industry letter had inspired the Energy Department’s actions, Ben Dietderich, an agency spokesman, said, “No. On day one, President Trump declared a national energy emergency due partly to past leaders’ energy subtraction policies that encouraged the premature shutdown of reliable coal and natural gas plants.”

It is not unusual for industry groups to send wish lists to incoming presidents. In 2020, shortly before President Joseph R. Biden, Jr., took office, the solar and wind industries published numerous recommendations, such as having the federal government buy renewable energy, that the Biden administration later adopted.

But the Trump administration’s use of emergency powers to keep coal plants open has created significant friction.

In some cases, the orders have surprised utilities, arriving at the last minute and upending months of preparation for closure. Some companies have scrambled to replenish their coal piles, bring back workers and quickly make repairs, spending tens of millions of dollars in the process. Each order lasts only for 90 days, but the Energy Department has repeatedly renewed them.

One operator, CenterPoint Energy, asked the Energy Department in February to let an emergency order lapse for the Culley coal plant in Warrick County, Ind., saying that running the unit would require up to $18 million in repairs. The department has since renewed its order three times.

The operators of the Craig Generating Station in Colorado went a step further, challenging their emergency order and explicitly saying that the coal unit was not needed.

Another utility, the Northern Indiana Public Service Company, has asked regulators to let it collect at least $38 million from customers to cover the costs of keeping open two aging coal units at its Schahfer plant. One unit has been out of commission since July 2025 because of a turbine failure and will require extensive repairs, the company said in public filings. The other ran during the winter before going offline in March for maintenance.

“The orders are forcing the utility owner to throw money at uneconomic plants that were rightly taken out of service,” said Ari Peskoe, director of Harvard Law School’s Electricity Law Initiative.

Mr. Wright, the energy secretary, has called the orders a necessary corrective after Democratic administrations and states hurt the coal industry by imposing strict environmental rules on power plants, often in the name of tackling climate change.

“Coal is massively more important for the U. S. electricity grid than wind and solar combined today,” Mr. Wright said last week at The New York Times’s Climate Forward event. “And coal has had a war on it. The government has imposed heaps of costs on it, regulatory burdens, everything to strangle it.”

Wind and solar power combined generated more electricity in the United States than coal last year, but coal can run on demand at all hours while wind turbines and solar panels cannot.

Without orders to stop coal plants from retiring, Mr. Wright added, “we would have had hundreds of Americans freeze to death in the last week of January last year.” He also said that some utilities have requested federal help to keep plants open.

Environmental groups have disputed those claims, arguing that the Midwestern regional grid — where several coal plants have been required to stay open — had sufficient capacity available during peak demand periods last winter and this summer.

The coal industry continues to struggle even as electricity demand grows, particularly from A. I. data centers. During the 2000s, coal provided nearly half of the nation’s electricity. But that share was just 17 percent last year and is expected to decline sharply again this year, according to federal data.

The Energy Department’s orders have also faced legal pushback. This month, a three-judge panel at the U. S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit struck down the first such order, to keep the J. H. Campbell coal plant in West Olive, Mich., operating.

The court ruled that the agency had overstepped its authority. It said states have responsibility to manage power generation and that the federal government should intervene only when states and grid operators can’t or won’t respond.

Since that ruling, however, the Energy Department has renewed orders to keep coal units running in Indiana, Colorado and Washington.

“The Energy Department disagrees with the decision and is working with the Department of Justice to assess potential rehearing and appeal options,” said Mr. Dietderich, the agency spokesman.

In Michigan, the owner of the J. H. Campbell plant has said it would keep the facility running since the court struck down only the first three-month emergency order. The agency has since issued five more. But environmentalists and other legal experts said the decision undercut the rationale for all such orders.

“In our view, the next move should be for D. O. E. to stand down, but as we see with this administration, it is often reluctant to stand down,” said Sanjay Narayan, managing attorney at the Sierra Club.

Brad Plumer is a Times reporter who covers technology and policy efforts to address global warming.

Claire Brown covers climate change for The Times and writes for the Climate Forward newsletter.
