Embarrassing Breach at F. B. I. Fuels Fears of Harm to Its Employees

The New York Times September 28, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

In an internal memo, the F. B. I. said it believed the hackers may have stolen sensitive information on all of its employees.

By Dustin VolzAlan FeuerCharlie Savage and Adam Goldman

Dustin Volz and Charlie Savage reported from Washington, Alan Feuer from New York, and Adam Goldman from London.

The theft by a criminal hacking group of reams of sensitive personal data involving potentially tens of thousands of former and current F. B. I. employees is emerging as one of the worst breaches of sensitive government information, leaving the bureau rushing to protect its personnel as an uncertain deadline loomed.

Nearly a week after the group, known as ShinyHunters, revealed it had pilfered intimate details about bureau personnel from the agency’s jobs portal and threatened to leak them online, F. B. I. investigators are still piecing together how the breach took place and the total damage.

The hack appears to have swept up home addresses, Social Security numbers, secretive job assignments and much more, according to a New York Times analysis of some of the records. Some are already comparing it to China’s breach of more than 20 million records from the Office of Personnel Management over a decade ago, considered so catastrophic that officials and lawmakers vowed to never let something like it happen again.

Many F. B. I. employees first learned about the hack when news reports about it surfaced on Tuesday, according to current and former officials. The next day, F. B. I. staff received an email reminding them that October is cybersecurity awareness month, which struck some as tone deaf in light of the breach, one of those people said.

On Friday, bureau leaders, in an internal memo to its rank and file, declared the hack a cybersecurity incident and acknowledged its employees had personal information stolen.

“We are operating under the premise that the threat actor is also exfiltrating PII of all F. B. I. employees,” according to the memo, which was described by someone who had seen it, using the abbreviation for personally identifiable information.

The memo said the agency would offer virtual briefings in the weeks ahead and instructed employees to remain vigilant at home and at work, report any unsolicited contacts or threats, avoid answering calls from unknown numbers and set up voice mail accounts with A. I.-generated voices. “Bureau leadership remains committed to supporting the safety of you and your family,” it said.

Still, many past and present personnel remain in the dark about whether their data has been purloined. In recent days, some have anxiously asked Times reporters whether their names are contained in the hacked data, wondering whether they needed to take steps to protect themselves or their families.

In a statement on Monday, the agency said it was “working around the clock to investigate the cyber incident involving FBIJobs. gov and is in regular communication with anyone who may be impacted — including multiple bureau-wide communications within 24 hours of public reporting.”

It added, “The F. B. I. treats the security of its information and the safety of its work force as top priorities, and our investigation is ongoing.”

In announcing its hack, ShinyHunters, believed to be a loose collective of young hackers operating across the globe, said it had targeted the F. B. I. as retribution for a public advisory the bureau had issued in the spring, warning that the group was known to harass victims and family members with threatening or coercive maneuvers. In their note, the hackers demanded that the F. B. I. “correct or simply REMOVE” the advisory or risk further consequences.

In an email to The Times on Friday, ShinyHunters said that the bureau had until the end of Tuesday to fulfill its request, even as the hackers themselves appeared to acknowledge that the bureau was unlikely to acquiesce.

That note left open the possibility that the hackers would not dump the data online, even as the group reiterated its deadline. But on Monday, in a new statement, the group claimed it never intended to do so.

“Since the very beginning we had made our decision that we would never publish this data,” the group said. “We have never intended to nor have we ever planned to.” It added that the hack and threat to the F. B. I. was a “marketing campaign to protect our business” and said that “we are not taking any further actions” with the data, including revealing more about what is contained in the files.

“We seek no escalation as our goals have widely been accomplished,” it said.

It remains to be seen what ShinyHunters will do, and security researchers warned that even if they did not publish it online they could still sell it to other criminals or foreign governments.

It is also unclear just how much sensitive information the hackers stole. The group claimed publicly to have stolen records on everyone who has applied for a job at the F. B. I., and told The Times that the people with compromised information numbered in the tens of thousands.

Ciaran Martin, the former head of Britain’s cyberdefense agency, said the F. B. I. hack likely had “huge impact on the operational capability” of the bureau and could rank as one of the most consequential data breaches in history — graver even than the Office of Personnel Management burglary.

“Losing the data on 20 million federal employees to the Chinese was bad,” Mr. Martin said. “But you knew the Chinese weren’t going to sell or publish it.”

A sample of records that the hackers have shared with The Times and other news organizations includes newer hires as well as retired ones, with birth dates ranging from the early 1940s to the mid 2000s. The most recent date references in the spreadsheet were from late April, suggesting the stolen files are at most only months old.

Current and former U. S. officials said that at least portions of the sample, and potentially all of it, appeared to be authentic.

A Times review of the sample found that it contained a range of private personal data, including:

The names, home addresses, phone numbers, work emails, Social Security numbers and birth dates and hire dates of current and former F. B. I. personnel.

Names and numbers for spouses and other emergency contacts, including in some cases parents, siblings and even children.

Employee identification numbers that are used for the Transportation Security Administration’s PreCheck program, which could aid spies in tracking travel itineraries of agents, including those that work undercover.

Names of the units in which F. B. I. personnel are employed and their job titles, as well as the names of supervisors. While some list mundane departments, others reveal extraordinarily sensitive assignments including counterintelligence, narcotics and various desks focused on Russian, Chinese and Iranian national security threats. F. B. I. agents in those roles are generally expected to zealously protect their work in such fields to avoid putting a target on their back.

Additionally, ShinyHunters said that it had stolen medical data about employees, including psychiatric records and documents related to blood and urine tests. It also said that it had additional background check files on employees.

Former bureau officials and security experts said the hacked data prompted no end of worries. The data could also make it far easier for violent criminals to seek revenge against F. B. I. agents who sent them to prison. When they submit paperwork against criminal suspects, F. B. I. agents sign their names to the records but are typically trained to not let delicate personal information easily emerge online.

“It doesn’t take much imagination to picture scenarios where employees or their families could be threatened or harmed by this kind of information being released,” said Andrew Brandt, a threat intelligence researcher at the cybersecurity company Huntress. “The bigger worry is ShinyHunters selling the data to other criminal or nation-state groups who could put it to more damaging use, rather than dumping it themselves.”

Security experts said that given the breadth of the records, they would be of enormous value if they were acquired by foreign spies, who could then use the material to build elaborate dossiers on F. B. I. agents — including those who may be undercover or later assigned to such a post — and track them for years, if not decades. Aided by artificial intelligence, spies or hackers could also combine the information with other exposed data that is already in their hands or that is easily acquired on the dark web.

“Breaches do not exist in a vacuum,” Justin Sherman, a senior associate at the Center for Strategic & International Studies, wrote in a recent essay arguing that different exposed data sets can be combined and analyzed by hostile spy services.

The hack is just the latest in a string of embarrassing security failures for the F. B. I.

Two years ago, government investigators learned that Chinese spies had compromised vast segments of the nation’s telecommunications infrastructure in a hacking campaign known as Salt Typhoon. Among the most startling revelations was that the breach included sensitive wiretap networks at Verizon and AT&T that process court-authorized surveillance orders for the F. B. I. to monitor domestic criminal suspects.

China has denied involvement, but U. S. intelligence officials considered the compromise a counterintelligence failure of the highest magnitude, with national security implications that could last for years. It prompted such alarm within the F. B. I. that field offices were told to check if informants had been potentially compromised and, if necessary, take steps to ensure their safety.

The bureau still does not understand the full scale or scope of Salt Typhoon and its exposure from it, according to current and former U. S. officials. But the F. B. I. received another blow this spring when suspected Chinese hackers were found again inside a network it maintains for domestic surveillance orders.

In the case of ShinyHunters, it was not Chinese spies but a notorious gang of cybercriminals who hit the F. B. I. Already, bureau leadership had warned staff that hackers linked to ShinyHunters who infiltrated AT&T in 2024 may have stolen months of call and text logs belonging to some of its agents, which also fanned concerns about whether its informants had been exposed, as Bloomberg reported last year.

The members of ShinyHunters are seen as highly skilled — and audacious — English-speaking hackers who extort their victims for millions of dollars and brag about their exploits. In their recent correspondence with The Times, the hackers have favored British spellings of certain words.

A French citizen charged with participating in some ShinyHunters attacks was arrested in Morocco in 2022, extradited to the United States and sentenced to three years in prison. Other suspected members were arrested last year in France.

On Monday, a security journalist, Brian Krebs, reported that authorities in the Netherlands had arrested a 23-year-old convicted cybercriminal on suspicion of aiding in data thefts and extortions tied to ShinyHunters just days before the F. B. I. breach. ShinyHunters said in response on Monday that the Dutch suspect “has no association with us.”

The F. B. I.’s Dallas field office has been leading an investigation into ShinyHunters and working with international partners to hunt down other members, according to people familiar with the matter who were not authorized to speak publicly.

It is not clear exactly how ShinyHunters pulled off the F. B. I. hack. The group said it had used a zero-day, or previously undiscovered, coding flaw within the Oracle PeopleSoft software, an application that companies use for human resources and financial management.

But some security researchers said the story may be more complicated. On Friday, Google revealed in a blog post that its threat intelligence teams have recently seen ShinyHunters renewing a campaign of “mass exploitation” against victims using a bug with Oracle PeopleSoft that was publicly disclosed with a patch in June. The post does not mention the F. B. I. breach, but a person familiar with the matter said investigators believe the known bug was involved in the ShinyHunters theft of personnel files.

The flaw was considered important enough that the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency promptly added it to a catalog of high-risk known vulnerabilities that federal agencies are instructed to quickly address.

“This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise,” CISA said at the time.

In response to questions from The Times, ShinyHunters said in an email on Friday that the F. B. I. had not contacted the group and that it would hold firm to its Tuesday deadline.

The hackers said that the severity of the breach was “SIGNIFICANTLY” worse than publicly known but did not explain in what way. Cybersecurity researchers who have followed the collective have said it has a track record of sometimes embellishing its activities but so far, in this breach, its claims have been largely corroborated.

“We have no intention to reveal the true impact, we will leave that to the F. B. I.,” ShinyHunters said. “If they lie, we will not correct them.”

The group also said that it was aggrieved by the F. B. I.’s advisory and that the hack was “all about protecting our business.”

“This is happening so we are heard and acknowledged,” ShinyHunters said. “We may sound like children whose feelings are hurt, sure, but in our game, reputation is all that matters.”

Dustin Volz writes about cybersecurity and intelligence for The Times. He is based in Washington.

Alan Feuer is a reporter for The Times who covers the effects President Trump has had on the courts, the Justice Department and the broader rule of law.

Charlie Savage writes about national security and legal policy for The Times.

Adam Goldman is a London-based reporter for The Times who writes about global security.

Justice Alito Recuses Himself Days Before Major Climate-Change Case

The New York Times September 28, 2026

Supreme Court

Advertisement

Supported by

Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr. had faced pressure to recuse himself from the climate case because he owns stock in oil companies.

By Abbie VanSickle

Reporting from Washington

Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr. said on Monday that he will not take part in a major climate-change lawsuit scheduled to be heard next week by the Supreme Court.

The one-sentence announcement from the clerk of the Supreme Court provided no reason for the justice’s recusal. Yet Alito has faced pressure from environmental and court watchdog groups to step aside because he owns stock in two oil companies, and he flew on the private jet of an investor in a company involved in the dispute.

The case could determine whether oil companies face billions of dollars in potential liability for damages from climate change. It is the first matter scheduled to be argued before the court when the justices return to the bench on Monday following their annual summer break.

Justice Alito did not respond to a request for comment.

Supreme Court ethics rules, adopted by the justices in November 2023 after revelations about Justice Clarence Thomas and his undisclosed gifts and travel from Texas billionaire Harlan Crow, leaves decisions about when to recuse from cases entirely at the discretion of the justices themselves. They typically do so when their impartiality could be questioned, such as if a close friend or family member is involved in a dispute or if they have a financial tie to a party, but they are also not required to provide reasons when they choose to do so.

Justice Alito has not reported financial ties to Suncor Energy, the oil company at the heart of the dispute, nor to any other company directly involved in the case. But he has disclosed in his annual financial reports that he owns stock in ConocoPhillips and Phillips 66, both oil companies.

Critics have also pointed to his relationship with Paul Singer, founder of Elliott Investment Management, a hedge fund that is an investor in Suncor. In 2023, ProPublica reported that the justice had taken a luxury fishing trip with Mr. Singer and failed to disclose it. Justice Alito said at the time that he was not required to disclose the trip and had spoken to Mr. Singer only a handful of times.

A spokeswoman for Elliott Investment declined to comment on Monday.

Lisa Graves, co-founder of Court Accountability, a group focused on court reform, said she was glad that Justice Alito would not take part in the case, Suncor Energy v. County Commissioners of Boulder County, because she believed he had “an appearance of conflict that continues.”

“It’s troubling that he took so long to do so,” added Ms. Graves, who also heads True North Research, a watchdog group, which had called on Justice Alito to recuse himself from the case.

The case before the justices involves a lawsuit by Colorado officials, who had sued two oil companies — Exxon Mobil and Suncor Energy — arguing they should help to pay for the damages caused by climate change.

The suit is one of dozens of similar legal fights taking place across the country. The oil companies have pushed back, arguing that such state claims are barred by federal law. The justices’ decision could determine the fate of similar cases in addition to the Colorado suit.

This is the second time this year that Justice Alito has announced a last-minute recusal from a case involving fossil-fuel companies.

The justice announced in January that he would step aside from a dispute over whether oil companies could be held liable for environmental damage to Louisiana’s coastline. As in the upcoming Suncor case, Justice Alito announced his decision months after the court had agreed to hear the case and just days before the oral argument. In that instance, he cited his financial interest in ConocoPhillips, the parent corporation of Burlington Resources Oil and Gas Company.

In that case, although that company had withdrawn from the court filings in the Louisiana case, it remained a party to the case in a lower court, according to a letter from the court clerk.

In April, the remaining justices unanimously sided with the oil companies, finding that they should be allowed to fight the lawsuits in federal court rather than state court.

Jeremy Fogel, a retired federal judge and ethics expert who leads the Berkeley Judicial Institute, said that he agreed with Justice Alito’s decision to recuse because, while

Justice Alito doesn’t own stock in the companies directly involved, the court’s code of ethics applies to situations where a justice’s financial interests were likely to be affected by the outcome of a case.

The outcome of the Suncor case, he said, “seems more than likely to affect the interests of oil companies generally.”

Gabe Roth, who leads Fix the Court, a judicial reform group, called Justice Alito’s announcement on Monday “a prime example of why Supreme Court justices should be required to explain their recusals.”

He said in a statement that the last-minute recusal raises questions without providing answers.

“Is Justice Alito stepping aside because his clerks belatedly found some connection between this case and the companies whose shares he owns?” he said. “Or is this a rare instance where a justice believes that open questions about his impartiality demand his recusal? The court’s lack of transparency and nonexistent rules governing their papers mean we may never know for sure.”

Abbie VanSickle covers the United States Supreme Court for The Times. She is a lawyer and has an extensive background in investigative reporting.

Quiet Corner of U. K. That Hosts U. S. Bombers Wakes to Roadblocks and Evacuations

The New York Times September 28, 2026

Possible Terrorist Plot at U. K. Base

Advertisement

Supported by

Two villages and a town near R. A. F. Fairford were thrust into the spotlight after the authorities said they were investigating a possible terrorist plot targeting the base.

By Megan Specia

Reporting from Fairford, England

The front pages of newspapers across Britain were plastered on Monday with the same grainy photograph, one showing five men, their faces blurred, being detained by police in the village of Whelford, England, who were investigating a possible terrorist plot.

By Monday, armed officers were monitoring roadblocks on the country roads leading to the sprawling military base that has been used since spring for U. S. operations related to the war in Iran.

More than a day after the police arrested the men, Whelford remained cordoned off after dozens of people had been evacuated from their homes. The men were released on bail on Monday afternoon, an unexpected development that injected confusion and raised questions into what was going on. The police said they were still investigating.

The village is one of three localities that butt up against R. A. F. Fairford, a British base in a quiet corner of southern England. They have been thrust onto the international stage and swirl with questions about what the men were doing and at whose instruction.

The villages of Whelford and Kempsford and the town of Fairford sit in a triangle around the base. Fairford’s residents have had a front-row seat to the U. S. bombers that have been flying in and out with renewed frequency since the start of the war with Iran this year, swooping low over the town.

Helen Cheese-Probert, whose thatched-roof home is a short walk from the base in Kempsford, said she had awaken on Sunday morning by numerous calls from friends and family asking if she was all right.

“If you buy a house on a cricket pitch, you expect cricket balls,” said Ms. Cheese-Probert, 67, who was walking her beagle near the air base runway on Monday morning. “If you buy a house near an air base, you expect planes. But no one expected this.”

Ms. Cheese-Probert said she was used to seeing plane spotters crowding the roadways around the base but not armed police.

“When the war with Iran started, the number of plane spotters prohibited you from being able to walk along the pavement,” she said. In recent days, residents had begun noticing an uptick in security, she added.

Local Facebook pages and WhatsApp groups had been abuzz with concerns about men seen recently who residents thought looked suspicious.

In a closed Facebook group for Kempsford that a resident showed a reporter on the phone, one person posted on Sept. 16 that he had seen a man in a balaclava near the air base. At least three other residents offered similar accounts on that day. One noted seeing a masked man running through the village. It was unclear if they were speaking about the same person, and no one knew what the men were up to. Some of the security near the site on Monday were also wearing face masks.

Dom Morris, the Gloucestershire County councilor for Fairford, said he spent Sunday and Monday helping the dozens of people in Whelford who remained displaced.

About 85 households had to be evacuated quickly, and Mr. Morris said that the local authorities had worked to ensure that these people had places to stay and access to their medication and that there was aid for farmers who needed to reach animals left inside the security cordon.

On Monday evening, the residents were allowed to return to their home, but the cordon around the village remained, according to local police.

“To be really clear, Fairford, Whelford, Kempsford, we’re resilient,” he said, using a British swear word. “So there’s a bit of shock going on amongst villagers and people in the town. But there’s still people going about their lives, and that needs to continue.”

Mr. Morris said there had been some accounts from residents that a larger number of people had been seen near the base on Saturday night and early Sunday. Some residents feared that not all the people connected with the episode had been detained, he said.

Mr. Morris, who grew up in the area, said the base and the cooperation with the United States had long been a point of pride.

“Geopolitics aside, we get it, and it’s not unusual to have ebbs and flows,” Mr. Morris said. “But I think this is obviously quite different.”

The presence of American military aircraft at the Fairford base is not unusual; there is a long history of cooperation between the British and U. S. militaries at the base since it opened in preparation for D-Day in 1944. Because of the length of its runway, the base is one of only a few European airfields that can be used by heavy U. S. bombers.

In the pubs and cafes of other towns and villages near the base on Monday, road closures rather than broader security concerns seemed to dominate the conversation.

At St Mary’s, a picturesque medieval church perched at the center of Fairford, Liz Jefferies was clearing weeds from her husband’s grave under the early autumn sun.

Ms. Jefferies, 76, has lived in Fairford since 1971. In the months since the United States began using the base for its war against Iran, she said there had been a notable uptick in large bombers overhead.

“We don’t normally get much trouble around here, so it’s a bit of a surprise,” Ms. Jefferies said of the arrests. “It’s really not nice.”

Megan Specia reports on Britain, Ireland and the Ukraine war for The Times. She is based in London.

Cornell Sexual Assault Investigation to Be Reopened

The New York Times September 28, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

After outrage over allegations in a lawsuit, the Tompkins County district attorney will revisit the decision not to pursue criminal charges against seven fraternity members.

By Sharon Otterman and Hurubie Meko

A New York prosecutor said Monday that he would reopen an investigation into accusations of a 2024 sexual assault at Cornell University, two weeks after a woman filed a lawsuit accusing the school and law enforcement officials of not doing enough to investigate her case.

In her lawsuit, the woman alleged that she was plied with alcohol and drugs and then raped by multiple men at the Chi Phi fraternity house on Oct. 19, 2024, when she was a 20-year-old undergraduate. She said she reported the incident to the Cornell University Police Department several weeks later, but that no criminal charges were filed by prosecutors.

Matthew Van Houten, the Tompkins County district attorney, said in a statement on Monday that he was now reconsidering that decision. He said that while the original statement the woman gave to police did not seem to warrant criminal charges, he would now let a grand jury decide.

The district attorney for Tompkins County in New York said he is reopening an investigation into a report of a sexual assault at Cornell University.

“Jane Doe’s sworn statement in November of 2024 did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped,” he said in the statement.

Mr. Van Houten said he would now reopen the investigation “recognizing that the process of healing from trauma is personal and different for every human.” A senior female prosecutor has been assigned, and any additional allegations from the lawsuit will be considered. ABC News first reported Mr. Van Houten’s comments on the investigation.

“Seeking justice sometimes requires us to reconsider or reopen cases when we are provided with additional evidence,” Mr. Van Houten added.

Thomas Giuffra, who represents the plaintiff in the lawsuit, said on Monday that his client’s report to the police at the time was not materially different to what is in the lawsuit.

“Once she was emotionally ready, she went to the university police and bravely shared what had occurred to her,” he said.

She never heard from the police again, her lawyer said. Mr. Giuffra said that until his client filed her lawsuit earlier this month, she had not been contacted by investigators from the Tompkins County District Attorney’s Office or any investigators trained in interviewing survivors of rape.

The lawsuit, which has received national attention, has cast a spotlight on a persistent issue of accusations of sexual assault among students on Cornell’s campus, and sparked anger in Ithaca, New York, and beyond over how Cornell handled the woman’s initial allegations.

Mr. Van Houten said he and his staff had received many calls and emails questioning why he had not prosecuted the case, including some that were insulting and threatening. An editorial in the Cornell student newspaper printed the names of the accused men and demanded that the university reveal why at least some of them were allowed back on campus after the university’s own investigation.

The lawsuit alleged that the seven accused fraternity members were given the opportunity to “mitigate their conduct by submitting essays to Cornell.” Critics have seized on that line as evidence they were treated with leniency.

But Cornell said the essays were only part of the consequences the students faced. After the woman’s 2024 allegation, the Cornell police provided information to the district attorney and the university investigated the incident through its administrative disciplinary system. The men involved were “issued a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions,” Cornell said in a statement on Monday.

The university released an earlier statement to the campus on Nov. 26, 2024, about “ongoing investigations into the serious and deeply disturbing allegations of drug abuse and sexual violence at the Chi Phi fraternity house.”

It also convened a task force on sexual assault, which made recommendations. A 2025 survey conducted by the university found that 35 percent of undergraduate women reported experiencing “nonconsensual sexual contact” during their time at Cornell, an increase from the 23 percent in the 2023 survey.

Chi Phi, the fraternity chapter where the woman said the assault occurred, was closed in 2024 and remains barred from campus, Cornell said Monday. “Any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false,” its statement said.

The woman participated in the administrative disciplinary process, and later withdrew from Cornell, Mr. Giuffra said.

The lawsuit contains harrowing details of the alleged assaults, as well as a screen shot of a lewd Snapchat conversation in which one fraternity member appears to invite many others to join in. Mr. Giuffra said that chat, which went on for several pages, had been provided to the university as evidence. The lawsuit states that during the assaults, the woman was under the influence of both alcohol and ketamine, a drug she alleges she was pressured into snorting and had not tried before.

Named as defendants in the lawsuit are Cornell; the Chi Phi fraternity; the woman’s own sorority, Delta Delta Delta; an off-campus bar that allegedly served her alcohol; and the seven fraternity members who are alleged to have been involved in the assault.

Chi Phi did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Tri Delta said it couldn’t comment on pending litigation but added that as an organization “we are committed to supporting women and victims of sexual violence.”

Jeremy Saland, the lawyer for one of the named defendants, said Monday that his client did nothing but respond to and make an “immature comment on Snapchat.” He called the lawsuit “intentionally dishonest.”

On Monday, Mr. Giuffra said the district attorney’s statements about reinvestigating his client’s case were “a long overdue step.”

As of Monday, Mr. Giuffra had been contacted by the prosecutor’s office, but his client has yet to be interviewed, he said. Some of the district attorney’s statements appear to be an effort to excuse failures in the initial investigation into his client’s case, Mr. Giuffra said.

Jane Manning, a former prosecutor and director of Women’s Equal Justice, a nonprofit which serves survivors of sexual assault, said it appeared that prosecutors had decided there was no case based only on the initial police paperwork, a practice she said was common but is “unacceptable.”

It’s “basic due diligence” for a prosecutor to interview a complainant before deciding whether to prosecute, she said.

Another likely complication was that New York law defines rape narrowly, Ms. Manning said, excluding a person who is subjected to unwanted sex while voluntarily intoxicated unless they are fully unconscious at the time of the assault. The law is one both prosecutors, including Manhattan’s district attorney, Alvin L. Bragg, and advocates have called to be amended.

The woman in this case was conscious during much of the assault, finally blacking out at around 5:45 a. m., her lawsuit states.

In his statement on Monday, Mr. Van Houten said his office in part determined to not pursue charges because Jane Doe’s initial, six-page long statement to police appeared to describe an encounter that was “voluntary, conscious, and consensual,” he wrote.

Sharon Otterman is a Times reporter covering higher education, public health and other issues facing New York City.

Hurubie Meko is a Times reporter covering criminal justice in New York, with a focus on the Manhattan district attorney's office and state courts.

In Ohio, a Humbling Question for Senator Jon Husted: Are You the Incumbent?

The New York Times September 28, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Even some devoted conservatives know more about Sherrod Brown, the Democratic challenger, than the Republican incumbent, who needs the MAGA base to turn out.

By Emily Davies

Reported from grocery stores, gas stations, diners and a county fair in Troy, Delaware, Findlay and Columbus, Ohio.

Republican senators vying for re-election this year have had to contend with a cratering economy and an unpopular president. Senator Jon Husted of Ohio appears to have an additional challenge: Even some of the state’s most devoted conservatives don’t know who he is.

Mr. Husted’s Democratic opponent is Sherrod Brown, a fixture in Ohio politics since the 1970s, who lost his Senate seat two years ago. Mr. Brown’s renown has become something of a liability for the sitting senator, who needs the state’s MAGA-friendly Republican base to care enough about the seat to vote in a year when President Trump is not on the ballot.

But being perceived as the challenger may also benefit Mr. Husted at a moment when voters are struggling economically and don’t think Congress has done enough to help. With polls showing Mr. Brown and Mr. Husted in a tightening race, the Republican’s campaign has leaned into the misconception, spending millions of dollars on ads that refer to his opponent as “Senator Sherrod Brown.”

“I don’t know a whole lot about Husted,” said Debbie Grenko, 67, a Republican, as she stroked her pony, Spirit, at the Delaware County Fair in central Ohio last week. “It’s Sherrod Brown in there, right?”

One Republican strategist in Ohio, granted anonymity to speak candidly about the race, said the campaign was intentionally casting Mr. Brown as the incumbent, a rare opportunity amid dismal Republican approval ratings for the party to harness anger at the status quo.

“Name ID is not everything,” said Drew Thompson, Mr. Husted’s campaign manager. Ohioans, he said, “are familiar” with Mr. Brown’s record “and they rejected it two years ago.”

The approach has reached some voters, including Ted Hull, who on Wednesday night was watching a “wiener dog race” at the Delaware County Fair. He said he planned to vote for Mr. Husted. Mr. Hull, 72, said that Mr. Brown, whom he thought was still in office, seemed to have “become lazy” on the job.

“There should be term limits,” Mr. Hull said.

Mr. Brown served for nearly two decades in the Senate and 14 years in the House of Representatives. Mr. Husted was appointed to the Senate two years ago, when JD Vance vacated the seat to become vice president. A former lieutenant governor and speaker of the Ohio House of Representatives, Mr. Husted is far from the firebrand that many have come to associate with the modern Republican Party. He is mild-mannered and more comfortable talking about economic policy than rousing a crowd.

Quality polling on Ohio is limited, but one poll released last week found that nearly a quarter of voters believed Mr. Brown was the incumbent.

The high-stakes race has become one of the most expensive in the country, with nearly $400 million of spending on advertisements, according to AdImpact, for a seat that both parties believe could determine control of the Senate. So far, Republicans have outspent Democrats by more than $75 million. The cryptocurrency industry’s main super PAC, Fairshake, launched a $30 million advertising campaign against Mr. Brown last week.

Mr. Trump plans to campaign in Ohio on Saturday, the Republican National Committee announced. It will be the first of “more than two” trips the president hopes to make before Election Day, according to one person familiar with his plans who was granted anonymity to discuss campaign strategy.

In Washington, Senate Republicans are also hoping to help Mr. Husted this week by voting on a bill to address the growing data center backlash by encouraging — but not requiring — state utility regulators to insulate consumers from rising energy costs associated with the facilities. Mr. Husted put the bill forward himself, after Democrats blitzed the airwaves with ads seeking to define Mr. Husted as the “face of data centers” in Ohio.

As lieutenant governor, before public backlash had emerged about rising energy costs and unsightly development associated with data centers, Mr. Husted supported tax incentives for such projects. In August, the National Republican Senatorial Committee circulated a memo warning that data center politics was endangering him.

All of these dynamics have left both sides bracing for a nail-biter in a red state that Mr. Trump won two years ago by double digits, according to a half-dozen Democratic and Republican operatives interviewed by The New York Times.

“The environment is bad, but there is a sense in D. C. that this race is over, and it’s not,” said Jai Chabria, another Republican strategist in Ohio and one of Mr. Vance’s top political advisers. “Senator Husted is in a much better position than is conventional wisdom.”

The landscape is tough across the country for Republican incumbents, with prices persistently high and Mr. Trump’s approval rating hovering near an all-time low for modern presidencies. In Ohio, fluorescent signs remind voters that gas frequently costs more than $4.40 per gallon. At the height of harvest season, diesel was even more.

For their part, Mr. Brown and Democrat-backed PACs have sought to take advantage of Mr. Husted’s relative unknown, with ad after ad trying to define him before voters hear from the senator himself. Aside from data centers, the ads also highlighted Mr. Husted’s votes to cut federal health care benefits.

“Sherrod has done a really good job reminding Ohio voters that he was one of the original economic populists in Ohio,” said Aaron Pickrell, a Democratic strategist who ran former President Barack Obama’s campaign in Ohio in 2012, the last year the state was truly a presidential battleground. “This race is extraordinarily close.”

Some of the attacks against Mr. Husted appear to be working. Ben Meddles, 55, a firefighter in central Ohio, said he regretted voting for Mr. Trump, and that in turn was affecting his choice for Senate.

“You go in to vote and you feel good,” said Mr. Meddles, watching his daughter’s dachshund Frankie compete in the “wiener” dog race. “And then sometimes, six months to a year later, you’re sorry for the way you voted.”

He said he was frustrated with the president for starting a war with Iran, imposing tariffs on Canada and spending so much time trying to take control of Greenland, which Mr. Meddles dismissed as “showboating.” It all felt like a distraction, he said, from the president’s failure to deliver his signature campaign promise: economic relief at home. That promise, Mr. Meddles said, was why he had cast three ballots for Mr. Trump over the last decade.

Mr. Meddles, who said he makes about $80,000 annually, wanted to make sure he chose a candidate who had shown that they would focus on improving the economic outlook. Mr. Husted “hasn’t stood out in the crowd doing anything good,” he said.

Mr. Husted will need to balance keeping enough distance from the president to retain voters frustrated by his second term while also embracing Mr. Trump enough to energize the conservative base, several Republican strategists said in interviews this week.

In the last few months, Mr. Husted has spoken at the Republican Party’s midterm convention in Dallas and appeared with Mr. Vance at a steel manufacturing plant in Ohio. Last week, Mr. Husted voted to block a resolution that would have required Mr. Trump to seek congressional approval to continue the war with Iran.

But he has also stressed that he wants to see a swift end to that war. On Friday, at a manufacturing company outside of Cleveland, Mr. Husted declined to answer questions from a reporter about whether he supported the White House’s handling of the war, which has driven up gas and diesel prices.

At the fair, Ms. Grenko had spent nearly $7 per gallon on diesel to fill up the five trucks she needed to cart her ponies to the event.

That cost had been so crippling, she said, that she swapped her favorite mac-and-cheese brand, Kraft, for the Great Value version sold at Walmart. She also started to buy off-brand coffee creamer and toilet paper, and to eat more rice each week to fill up.

In some ways, Ms. Grenko embodied both the opportunities and the challenges facing Mr. Husted. A loyal Trump Republican who gets her news exclusively from Fox, Ms. Grenko said she didn’t mind making those sacrifices if Mr. Trump was doing what he thought was best for the country.

But her willingness to give up comforts for Mr. Trump does not mean she will vote for Mr. Husted, given how little she knows about him.

“I want him to step out, step up and say, ‘OK, this is what I think,’” she said, an American flag blowing in the wind behind her.

“Like Trump,” she continued. “Trump’s not afraid to say what he stands for.”

Emily Davies is a political correspondent for The New York Times.

Release of 5 Men in U. K. Prompts New Questions Over Possible Terror Plot

The New York Times September 28, 2026

Possible Terrorist Plot at U. K. Base

Advertisement

Supported by

The British counterterrorism police said the five British nationals arrested near R. A. F. Fairford on Sunday were being released on bail but remained under investigation.

By Michael D. Shear

Reporting from Liverpool, England

The counterterrorism police in Britain on Monday said that five men arrested Sunday near an air base were being released on bail, an unexpected development in what officials originally said was a major incident involving a possible terrorist act.

The five men were taken into custody early Sunday morning near the perimeter of the sprawling R. A. F. Fairford base in southern England. Nearby homes were evacuated as bomb detection robots searched three white vans. Officials initially said the men were suspected of violating the Explosives Act and of preparing to commit a terrorist act.

Laurence Taylor, who leads Britain’s counterterrorism police, said in a brief statement to reporters Monday afternoon that the men would remain under investigation and would be subject to “stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others.”

But their release raised new questions about what happened near the base, how the men managed to drive three vans so close to an area where American bombers are stationed and whether the British Army’s bomb disposal unit had failed to find any evidence after examining the vehicles for more than 24 hours.

Britain’s national security laws give the authorities widespread latitude to detain terror suspects, so the decision to grant the five men bail suggests the police may not have found enough to link them to a specific act. The British counterterrorism police have not named the men, in line with policing rules that grant anonymity unless a person is charged.

The release of the men, who the police said were all British nationals in their early 20s, came less than 24 hours after President Trump told reporters on Sunday that the suspects had intended to do “big damage” to the British air base. Mr. Trump praised the country’s police, describing their efforts as “fantastic” and “amazing,” and said of the men, “We had them under view for a long time and we got them.”

The police in Britain did not confirm Mr. Trump’s suggestion that the authorities in both countries had the suspects “under view.” Mr. Taylor said he was aware of speculation about what might have been known in advance but told reporters, “I will not always be able to share this type of information.”

On Monday, Mr. Trump said the men might be connected to Iran but refused to elaborate, adding: “I know the answer. I can be very specific, but I’d rather not say it.” He also expressed surprise at the decision to release the men.

“I wouldn’t have done that,” he told reporters. “We know everything about them. We would not have released them.”

Earlier on Monday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham had urged people not to speculate. “The investigation remains ongoing,” Mr. Burnham said. He asked British residents to let the police “establish the full facts.” He later convened members of his national security cabinet for a closed-door briefing on the status of the investigation.

Public details about the incident remain murky at best.

Investigators arrested the five men in the early hours of Sunday morning, and a bomb disposal robot spent most of Sunday cautiously examining three white vans while 85 families living nearby were evacuated from their homes.

On Monday, armed police officers staffed roadblocks on the country roads leading to the air base. And more than a day after the police first made the arrests, the tiny village of Whelford, one of three on the outskirts of the base, remained entirely cordoned off.

A farmer told the BBC that she had called the police early on Sunday morning after seeing a large group of hooded and masked men in the fields near the base. The farmer, whom the BBC did not identify, said she was shocked that it was left to her as a member of the public to see and report the men.

Her timeline appeared to conflict with the one given out by the police. She told the BBC that she called the local emergency number at 1:36 a. m. on Sunday. The police have said that they received the first call at 12:45 a. m. and that the men were arrested shortly after.

Wes Streeting, the British defense secretary, praised the farmer in an interview with BBC Radio on Monday morning, while suggesting that she had only a limited picture of what had unfolded.

“I want to pay tribute to that member of the public for her vigilance,” he said. “She’s done exactly what we would hope a member of the public would do in the situation she found herself in.”

But he added, “She will of course only have had a partial view, and I don’t want to go beyond and stray into kind of operational and security detail at this stage.”

The prime minister’s plea to avoid speculation has done little to dampen conjecture that the suspected plot at R. A. F. Fairford might be linked to the war in Iran. American bombers have conducted long-range strikes on the country from the base since the United States and Israel attacked in February.

“If it is Iran-related, it could be hard-liners trying to undermine Iranian government efforts to negotiate a settlement of the war with the U. S., or proxies such as Hezbollah, unhappy that Iran is not paying sufficient attention to their interests,” said Antonio Giustozzi, a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, a security think tank in London.

Another possibility is that Tehran may have “decided negotiations with Trump are going nowhere, despite recent Iranian concessions, and that the pressure has to go up,” Mr. Giustozzi said.

Mr. Taylor, the counterterrorism police chief, acknowledged the widespread speculation about whether the men were connected to a hostile foreign country such as Iran or Russia.

He declined to confirm that but said that the police were “considering this from every possible angle, including that this may be actively committed by proxies or individuals, either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state.”

He added: “I have spoken before about the increasing breadth and complexity of the threats we are facing. Often this threat becomes visible to us as criminal activity, often at a small scale and committed by individuals whose primary aim is not terrorism but a quick financial gain.”

Iran’s Embassy in London said in a statement Monday that it “categorically rejects and strongly condemns” what it called “unfounded and malicious speculations” that Iran was involved in the air base incident.

Former Prime Minister Keir Starmer initially refused to allow British bases to be used by the United States to strike Iran, provoking Mr. Trump’s ire. But after Iran conducted drone strikes on British allies across the Middle East, Mr. Starmer changed course and said he would allow what he called “defensive” American strikes on Iran from Fairford. That prompted a furious debate in Britain, including repeated protests near the base by activists who oppose the U. S.-Israeli war.

Mr. Burnham, who replaced Mr. Starmer in July, quietly continued that policy.

On July 23, a few days after Mr. Burnham became prime minister, the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps of Iran warned Britain that the government’s decision to allow strikes from one of its bases would make it “a legitimate target for our forces.”

Residents of three villages near the base — Whelford, Kempsford and the town of Fairford — have had a front-row seat to the American bombers that have been flying in and out of the base with renewed frequency since the start of the war with Iran earlier this year, swooping low over the town.

On Monday afternoon, a 1,300-foot cordon around the trucks remained in place and many local residents had not yet been allowed to go back. Mr. Taylor said efforts were underway to let the families return as soon as possible.

If Iran was linked to the incident near the British base, it would likely add to the public’s deep skepticism about the war. In public surveys, large majorities of the British public have said they do not support Mr. Trump’s decision to attack Iran.

In one survey from March, about three-quarters of the respondents expressed concern over the war’s impact on Britain’s security. In the same survey, more than 80 percent expressed concern about the conflict’s consequences for the British economy.

Megan Specia contributed reporting from Fairford, England, and Adam Goldman contributed reporting from London.

Michael D. Shear is the chief U. K. correspondent for The New York Times, covering British politics and culture and diplomacy around the world.

Judge Blocks U. S. From Tying Emergency Grants to Election Changes

The New York Times September 28, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

The Trump administration had threatened to withhold some Homeland Security money unless states explored paper balloting and citizenship verification.

By Scott Dance

The Trump administration cannot withhold emergency preparedness grants from states that do not change how they conduct elections, a federal judge ruled Monday.

The Federal Emergency Management Agency warned state and local governments in June it would withhold up to 20 percent of some terrorism-preparedness grants unless officials demonstrated that they were exploring a transition to paper ballots or verifying voters’ citizenship. The grants, totaling $1 billion each year, help harden urban areas against terrorist attacks, develop antiterrorism plans and conduct terrorism drills.

The changes to elections that FEMA sought were in line with President Trump’s false and largely debunked claims of widespread voter fraud.

A group of local governments in Tennessee, Texas and Ohio sued FEMA and the Department of Homeland Security, its parent agency, over the move last month, arguing the federal government did not have the power to force changes to how they conduct elections. They also said the rules would disenfranchise eligible voters.

Judge Amir H. Ali of the U. S. District Court for the District of Columbia, an appointee of President Joseph R. Biden Jr., agreed that the conditions exceeded the administration’s power over elections and ordered them stricken from the grant programs’ application process.

FEMA and Homeland Security officials did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the ruling.

The ruling follows several actions by the Supreme Court addressing Mr. Trump’s push to exert more control over elections ahead of the midterms. This month, the court blocked changes to mail-in voting but approved increased screenings for ineligible voters.

Scott Dance is a Times reporter who covers how climate change and extreme weather are transforming society.

Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

Fresh pies. Book groups. Puzzle challenges. Developers of master-planned communities see fear of social isolation and desire for friends as a business opportunity. Welcome to Amity Lane.

A cross street in Indigo, a master-planned community outside Houston that tries to foster connection. Credit... Antranik Tavitian for The New York Times

Supported by

By Conor Dougherty

Kiara Aponte and Samir Husain loved everything about the Tudor-style house they bought in a leafy Houston suburb. It had a brick fireplace in the sunny living room and a yard with climbing roses. Upstairs sat a pair of Jack and Jill bedrooms where Ms. Aponte imagined future children quarreling over the connecting bathroom.

But beyond their property line, something was missing. There were sidewalks, but nobody walked on them. They identified their neighbors not by name but by the car in the driveway. No one ever popped over to borrow eggs.

“There weren’t a whole lot of interactions, period,” Ms. Aponte said.

“Just like a smile, wave and move on type of situation,” Mr. Husain added.

In 2024, two years after paying $280,000 and moving in, they left in search of better neighbors.

The couple told the story of how they fell out of love with their house during a lunch at Della Coffee & Wine, the social hub of a new master-planned development called Indigo. Indigo sits about 30 miles from downtown Houston and about a 15-minute drive from their old house, next to a cow pasture and a prison. Despite being in the suburbs, the development has a village feel. Ms. Aponte and Mr. Husain live along a car-free parkway with a view of sidewalk plantings and strolling neighbors instead of a wall of cars.

Housing developments reflect the times in which they are built. Developers erect gates when people are worried about crime, market big kitchens when land is cheap and turn dining rooms into offices when the world is mired in a pandemic. Today, with social isolation a major preoccupation, consultants are using phrases like “emotional reliability” and “community as an amenity” to describe buyers’ desires for places that foster connection and neighbors who like hanging out.

In California, the community of Silverwood asks its residents to sign a kindness pledge. A development in Utah called Firefly markets its slow streets and bountiful parks as an alternative to screen time. Developers are trading empty clubhouses for working farms and marketing halls designed around neighborly collisions.

As you pull up to Indigo from the highway, signs that advertise homes selling in the low $300,000s are broken up by messages like “Know Your Neighbors.” About 275 homes of a planned 692 have been built along streets with names like Kindred Way.

Ms. Aponte and Mr. Husain moved to Amity Lane and now live in a freshly completed duplex with a strip of grass for a backyard. A sapling sprouts from a circle of dirt. By the numbers, it is a step down from the Tudor. The space is smaller, and they share a wall. They also lost money on the old house, while forfeiting an ultralow interest rate for a high one. Mr. Husain said it was worth it.

“I don’t even ever think about the fact that I’m paying way more in mortgage,” he said. “Because everything has been pleasant and happy.”

Selling the American dream increasingly means selling less. As home prices and borrowing costs have exploded, developers are squeezing more buildings onto the same acreage while downgrading the traditional starter home — a smallish, detached house — to 1,000-square-foot cottages and attached duplexes or triplexes.

It is one thing to drive to the fringes of a city to get a house with a yard, another to have to commute an hour to downtown and have to share a wall. To counter the diminished expectations, exurban communities are playing up urban features like walkability and adding amenities like brew pubs with adjoined parks so parents can gather without arranging for a sitter.

The underlying message is that while you might not get a lot of house, you’ll get a suburban approximation of the no-longer-affordable hipster urban neighborhood. In doing so, developers are inverting the ideas of privacy and abundant space that had once been the suburban ideals and repackaging them as antidotes to suburban ills like loneliness and isolation.

“You spend most of your time in the car, your kids don’t see other kids because it’s unsafe to walk — it’s brutal,” said Teri Slavik-Tsuyuki, a consultant who helps developers design new communities, describing her view of traditional suburban living. “That is what we’ve created, and developers have started to realize that it’s their problem to solve.”

The instruments of this transition are master-planned communities, roughly defined as town- or neighborhood-size projects in which a single entity controls the infrastructure and community vision. The homeowners’ associations that run these projects have long operated as mini-governments that handle services like landscaping and trash collection. Increasingly, they also emphasize “lifestyle” programming run by full-time coordinators who plan events and help neighbors make friends.

“It used to be that local institutions were largely responsible for the creation of community, and then for a variety of reasons — suburbanization, technology — we broke apart all those connections,” said Todd Hornback, chief executive of Cohere, a Phoenix company that manages homeowners’ associations, including the one at Indigo. “Community is no longer created organically in new places. It has to be designed and practiced.”

Cohere organizes Fourth of July parades and buys snacks for its residents’ game nights. One of its properties has a nearby neighbor deliver a freshly baked pie to new occupants. Instead of career property managers, Mr. Hornback said, the company tried to recruit HOA managers from nonprofits like the Boys & Girls Club and had recently started hiring pastors.

Mr. Hornback pitches this as good business: Word of mouth from early residents builds demand that allows developers to raise prices as they build homes for later phases. When Cohere asks residents what they like about a particular community, Mr. Hornback said, they rarely speak about their home and instead list things like “a small-town feel.” In business terms, he calls this “R. O. I.” — return on investment — “of belonging.”

An hour away from Indigo, a developer named Tom Woliver is building a community called Two Step Farm. It feels a bit like a theme park of small-town Texas, with a herd of goats and a dance hall built from reclaimed wood. When I visited the project, Mr. Woliver and his wife, Christina Acuña, regaled me with facts about dance-hall history and their trips to antique fairs to find décor. To drive the point home, Ms. Acuña showed me a video in which she fired a gun at an aluminum road sign for a town named Shiner (population: 2,069) so that it looked properly worn. It now hangs in the dance hall, next to a Lone Star beer sign that’s also riddled with holes.

“You have to go all-in on story,” Mr. Woliver said.

Indigo’s developers, Scott Snodgrass and Clayton Garrett, are first-time builders who came to real estate through agriculture. Mr. Snodgrass ran a coffee bean wholesaler while Mr. Garrett was a lawyer who quit full-time practice to be the general manager of a commercial bakery.

Before Indigo, they teamed up to start a company called Agmenity, which builds working farms into new developments, part of a growing “agrihood” craze that appeals to people who want to pick their own tomatoes and radishes. After six years of working inside new communities, they decided to try building one themselves.

Indigo’s layout borrows from the new urbanist movement that preaches walkable neighborhoods with a variety of housing types clustered together. When fully built out, the project will have everything from a 66-unit apartment complex with 500-square-foot rentals to 6,000-square-foot houses with price tags above $2 million. Building types aren’t grouped together — the plans call for 1,000-square-foot cottages to sit across the street from the biggest homes — and the whole thing is oriented around a Main-Street-style commercial center lined with brick buildings that will have ground-floor storefronts and apartments on top.

Mr. Snodgrass and Mr. Garrett said they had also tried to strip their homeowners’ association of many of the rules that made suburbia feel so bland. While many developments prohibit people from having businesses in their homes, for instance, Indigo encourages them.

In comparison with nearby developments and their large lots and cul-de-sacs, Indigo seems teleported from a random downtown. That discordance appeals to buyers like Helen Clancy, who moved to Indigo last November. Ms. Clancy, 49, was living in a rental apartment in Montrose, a rapidly gentrifying Houston neighborhood where she had been priced out from buying. Indigo felt like a good approximation of that same urban feel, so she bought a 1,600-square-foot home for $360,000.

Ms. Clancy is a former journalist with a Ph. D. in social work who now does communications for a charitable foundation. She wrote her Ph. D. thesis about community bonding after extreme weather events, and the shelves in her living room are topped with candles and lined with books about social isolation, like Robert Putnam’s “Bowling Alone.” She is a member of Indigo’s foodie club, book club and cleanup club. She also goes to lavender circle L. G. B. T. Q. club, even though she is not gay, just because she wants to hang out.

During our interview, Ms. Clancy excitedly recounted, with jazz hands, that she had recently told a neighbor that if she ever wanted to come over to hang out she should just pop over — and the neighbor actually did!

“Somebody rang my doorbell for an unexpected visit,” she said, “and we talked about books.”

Indigo, while walkable, has none of the history or tradition of most neighborhoods developed before cars. And so Mr. Snodgrass and Mr. Garrett hired a consultant to create a “belonging framework” (town meetings have to include child care, resident clubs cannot limit membership). An outdoor games company designed an activity called “IndiGolf,” which encourages residents to pair up and walk around solving a series of puzzles and challenges. (Example: Use nonverbal communication to find a marked rock in the Zen garden.)

Speaking with residents in living rooms and the coffee shop, I noticed that several of them wore a bulky bracelet with a translucent box containing a small circuit board. The doohickey was not a hot new piece of jewelry, but rather a device collecting biometric data like daily step and sleep data. It is part of a Texas A&M study, funded by the federal government, of the impact of social belonging on physical health. Every few weeks a research team comes out to collect data, including a blood sample, and compares residents in Indigo with those from a less walkable development nearby.

When I asked Ms. Clancy if this gave her any pause — I mean, giving blood and all — she said that, in fact, the experiment comforted her. “If they were doing this as a gimmick, they wouldn’t go through all this trouble to work with researchers,” she said.

The initial marketing for master-planned communities can be self-fulfilling. “By advertising that they’re into sociability and having some cues, the social crowd will move there,” said Ann Forsyth, a professor of urban planning at Harvard and co-director of the school’s New Towns Initiative.

Indigo, because it leans so heavily into the friendliness vibe, seems to have attracted people like Ms. Clancy. Many are in life transitions — divorced, widowed, just starting families — where making friends can be hard.

The social activity has helped create good will that has eased some of the development’s practical problems, of which there are many. Ms. Clancy moved in several months late because the developers could not secure power, a delay that caused a handful of buyers to back out.

Mr. Snodgrass and Mr. Garrett were surprisingly unguarded about Indigo’s many setbacks. Sitting at Della Coffee & Wine one afternoon, Mr. Snodgrass cataloged a list of sidewalks that had to be torn out and redone. Cost overruns have forced them to take on more debt and caused some of their contractors to quit.

Living near people is hard, in Indigo and everywhere else. Indeed, one of the biggest problems with suburban life, Mr. Snodgrass said, is that people have forgotten how to resolve their problems on their own and instead outsource their issues to a homeowners’ association.

Recently, for instance, one of Indigo’s blocks was roiled by a series of intertwined complaints: A dog was pooping on a neighbor’s lawn, a resident was leaving trash cans in the driveway on non-collection days and a sonic fence was installed in someone’s front yard to ward off coyotes. Each of these arrived as an atomized complaint to the HOA.

Instead of issuing violations, Mr. Snodgrass said, the HOA responded by asking the neighbors if they had talked to each other. The answer, as usual, was no. So they are setting up a neighbor-to-neighbor meeting. Mr. Snodgrass expects the meeting to be every bit as awkward as it sounds. But so what: Isn’t arguing a vital part of a real neighborhood?

“We can have all these fun events and clubs, and that’s great,” Mr. Snodgrass said, “but we will know things are working when people can resolve these problems without support from an HOA. It’s messy, but we’re here for it.”

In April, Ms. Aponte and Mr. Husain had their first child, a boy named Amar, the first new baby at Indigo. Ms. Aponte said that when they came home from the hospital with their son, neighbors across Indigo offered to start a meal train. It was the sort of gesture that they craved in their old neighborhood but never had.

Still, they politely declined the meals. Mr. Husain had persuaded his parents to sell their home and buy the unit next door to them at Indigo. Then his sister bought one next to that. So they have all the help they need.

On a rainy afternoon in July, Ms. Clancy, having just agreed to water another neighbor’s plants, left her house and strolled down one of the walking paths to Della Coffee. She was there to have a glass of wine with Nancy Wenzel, 72, a retired teacher who had moved in after her husband died. Soon they were joined by a couple, Casey and Will, who arrived with their two young daughters.

For the next hour the group talked about their book club and how everyone was watching the new “Little House on the Prairie.” Amazon drones have started delivering to the area — can you believe that? One of Casey and Will’s daughters noted that she had a cat named Weasley and two bug bites that were red. Then she got embarrassed and buried her head into one of her fathers’ chests.

They pulled a couple of bistro tables together, and then a third when another couple arrived. By the time they left half the cafe was consumed by a loose rectangle of conjoined tables.

Conor Dougherty covers housing and development, focusing on the rising costs of homeownership. He is based in Los Angeles.

Fire, Smoke and Desperation After a Strike in the Heart of Kyiv

The New York Times September 28, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

A Russian jet-powered drone hit Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences, the source of almost all of the country’s major scientific discoveries.

Credit... Gleb Garanich/Reuters

Supported by

By Kim BarkerMaria Varenikova and Oleksandra Mykolyshyn

Reporting from Kyiv, Ukraine

In the middle of a workday, in the middle of the Ukrainian capital, a Russian jet-powered drone struck the National Academy of Sciences on Monday, setting the top two floors on fire and forcing people to crawl out of windows to await rescue.

As firefighters worked to put out the blaze, employees of an institution that has accounted for almost all major scientific discoveries in Ukraine had to climb down ladders to reach safety.

Russia has been pounding Kyiv around the clock for weeks with new jet-powered drones, which have proved difficult to knock down with Ukraine’s current air defenses. Daily life in the capital is now punctuated by the rat-a-tat of air-defense guns, followed by a drone hitting something — a data center, a random street, a gas station, a warehouse, a high-rise building.

This drone hit just before 1:30 p. m. Kyiv time, when people at the academy were on lunch break but most were eating in their offices. The injured were treated on the sidewalk outside the building — a yellow, pink and white architectural landmark originally designed in the 1850s to be a countess’s boarding school for girls.

“My office is gone now,” said Vira Yevhrafova, 65, deputy chief scientist at the academy. “It was on the second floor — everything has collapsed, everything.”

The attack on Monday killed at least one person and injured six. One man was missing. It is a typical toll for these drone strikes, now so regular they barely make the international news unless the images are particularly dramatic. The daughter of the woman who died showed up at the building and burst into tears. She was sad and angry but had nothing else to say.

Ukrainians lamented the sight of brilliant scientific minds fleeing their burning offices. “What an idiotic war,” Andriy Kovalenko, a lieutenant in Ukraine’s military and a former government official, posted on social media along with a photo of two people crawling out of windows.

The attack on the sciences academy was just the start of a busy day for rescue workers and military drone interception teams. Less than two hours later, another drone hit a clinic about a mile south. An hour after that, a drone was intercepted right as it hit a nearby building.

After yet another fatal strike in Kyiv, with yet another body covered by a sheet and then carted away, Ukrainians again took stock of Russia’s effort to bomb them into submission.

“I think what they want now is to frighten us and bring our lives to a halt,” said Vira Balanovska, 43, who walked with her 9-year-old daughter past the burning academy. “It’s not just about attacking warehouses so that we won’t have food. They also want to intimidate us — to make it so that we can’t work, study, do scientific research or really do anything at all.”

Evelina Riabenko contributed reporting.

Kim Barker is a Times reporter writing in-depth stories about the war in Ukraine.

Maria Varenikova covers Ukraine and its war with Russia.
