After a Life in Isolation, a Tennessee Woman Waits for Her Execution

The New York Times September 28, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Christa Pike could be the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. Her supporters say she has changed in isolation; her victim’s family wants her to die.

By Emily Cochrane

Emily Cochrane reviewed hundreds of pages of legal documents and spoke with lawyers, experts, supporters of Christa Pike and Colleen Slemmer’s mother. Christa Pike’s lawyers agreed to share questions with Ms. Pike and record her answers without outside editing or approval.

For the better part of three decades, Christa Pike has waited alone on Tennessee’s death row.

She tortured and murdered a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, with her boyfriend and a friend. They slashed at Colleen with a box cutter, carved a pentagram into her chest and removed a piece of her skull. Only Ms. Pike received the death penalty. She was 18 at the time of the killing.

If her execution goes as planned on Wednesday, she will be the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.

“I run through this execution every day in my heart,” Ms. Pike said in an unedited audio recording, shared by her lawyers in response to questions from The New York Times. “Whatever happens on Sept. 30, this will not be my hell anymore.”

Americans have increasingly opposed the death penalty and have shown particular reluctance toward sentencing women and teenagers. Women account for about 2 percent of new death sentences issued since the modern era of capital punishment began in 1973; Missouri was the last state to execute a woman, in 2023.

Ms. Pike, now 50, does not deny her guilt. Still, some experts question whether she would be sentenced this way today. Her abusive childhood never came up at trial, something defenders now ask judges and juries to consider in sentencing. In isolation, she was diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder, which her lawyers say contributed to her mental state during the murder.

Her age is another factor; she was just above the legal threshold to be considered for the death penalty.

“Christa Pike would likely not be sentenced to death if she were tried today,” said Robin Maher, the executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center. “A lot has changed.”

But the death sentence for Ms. Pike was never a question for Colleen’s mother, May Martinez. She clings to her daughter’s memory, condemning a lack of support and scrambling to piece together the funds to travel to the execution in Nashville.

“Nobody,” she said, “remembers Colleen.”

On the night of her murder, Colleen tried to call her mother.

Colleen, 19, lived hundreds of miles from the family home in Florida, having enrolled in a Job Corps educational program in Knoxville, Tenn., that would allow her to pursue an interest in computers. The call quickly ended because of a shaky phone signal.

When Ms. Martinez called back, her daughter “was already gone,” she said.

The grisly details of what happened that night in January 1995 gripped eastern Tennessee.

Three students from the program — including Ms. Pike and her boyfriend at the time, Tadaryl Shipp — had lured Colleen into the woods on the University of Tennessee campus. They tortured her, slamming her head with chunks of asphalt. Mr. Shipp later described carving a pentagram in Colleen’s body, inflaming fears of Satan worship.

Ms. Pike confessed two days later, after the body was found. She had taken a piece of the skull, showing it to at least one person.

During her trial, prosecutors displayed the broken skull and the missing piece.

“That was the hardest thing in the world — to watch your daughter’s skull be passed around,” Ms. Martinez said. Over a decade would pass before a court ordered the return of the skull to her family.

“I’m not the same person I used to be,” Ms. Martinez said.

She remembers her daughter as a vibrant, generous presence, who volunteered at the Special Olympics and loved bowling and computer games. Her world collapsed after Colleen died.

She has held onto every memento of her daughter’s life, from the books Colleen read to a teddy bear she fashioned out of Colleen’s old T-shirt. Every year, she hangs the Christmas tree ornaments her daughter made, with purple lights for Colleen’s favorite color.

Her fury at Ms. Pike — and the lengthy appeals process — has burned since the trial. In 1996, she told The Knoxville News-Sentinel that “they should kill her right away.”

Ms. Pike was the only student to receive the death penalty. Mr. Shipp, then 17 and shielded by Tennessee law from capital punishment, was sentenced to life in prison.

Ms. Martinez does not remember receiving a direct apology in court.

“I’m very remorseful now; I wasn’t in the beginning when I first caught this charge,” Ms. Pike said. “I didn’t care what I had done.”

She added, “I didn’t care about anyone but myself and my co-defendants and maybe our families.”

When Ms. Pike was moved to prison in Nashville, her world shrank. She was confined to her cell for 23 hours a day. Only one other woman, Gaile Owens, was ever on death row in Tennessee at the same time. Before her sentence was commuted in 2010, Ms. Owens spent three years in a cell near Ms. Pike, but the two did not have physical contact.

Ms. Pike compared her experience to being locked in a bathroom with a meal tray, a television and a radio. “The biggest punishment was taking me away from people and human contact,” she said.

In 2001, Ms. Pike and two other women were evacuated to another part of the prison because of a fire. The two women, who had a history of confrontation, began to argue, and Ms. Pike used a shoelace to choke one of them until she was unconscious.

Ms. Pike was found guilty of attempted first-degree premeditated murder.

Shortly after the attack, doctors diagnosed Ms. Pike with bipolar disorder. Her lawyers attribute the violence to her mental health and her past. According to court records and psychological assessments, Ms. Pike was physically and mentally abused by immediate family as a child. As early as kindergarten, she endured repeated rape and assault, first by men she knew and then by a stranger.

Her lawyers said that since being medicated and attending therapy, Ms. Pike has not been disciplined for violence. Practicing Buddhist meditation in recent years, Ms. Pike said, has also been a way to “train my chaotic mind.”

In statements and interviews, women imprisoned alongside Ms. Pike said she was welcoming from afar, despite the restriction on her physical interactions. She dispatched hygiene items from the prison commissary, cooked food over a lamp and called out greetings on her shackled walks to shower. (In 2024, a settlement with Tennessee allowed her to physically interact with other women in the prison.)

“I’ve always seen her show kindness,” said Ashlee Sellars, 48. “I’ve seen her be protective.”

Marcy Graves Wilson, 60, recalled her fear in 2017 when she learned that her daughter, Teddy, would be housed nearby. But Ms. Pike sent the new girl shower shoes when she didn’t have any, a gesture that deepened into a heartfelt relationship until Teddy died from an overdose.

“Knowing Christa has changed my feelings about the death penalty,” Ms. Wilson added. “I feel like she has so much that she could offer.”

Supporting other incarcerated women, Ms. Pike said, is an attempt to atone for the harm she caused.

“Over years of sitting in here with deep contemplation and reflection, I know and understand the life that I have taken and how much it matters, how much it means, how many effects she could have had on the world, just like the effects I could have on the world,” Ms. Pike said.

Ms. Pike’s lawyers have spent recent weeks trying to stop the execution. Gov. Bill Lee, a Republican, said early Monday afternoon that he would not intervene to allow her to serve the remainder of her life in prison.

Her lawyers had argued that she could support other women in prison and that her crime could not be separated from a traumatic childhood. In a statement, they said they were “deeply saddened and heartbroken” by Mr. Lee’s decision.

They also had questioned whether medical staff can administer the lethal drugs without causing excessive pain. And they have appealed to the U. S. Supreme Court to pause the execution, questioning whether “the mental suffering and psychological terror she will experience” under the protocol qualifies as cruel and unusual punishment under the Eighth Amendment.

“I don’t think that someone should kill me to teach me that killing someone is wrong,” Ms. Pike said. “I’m not going to be the one here left to suffer anymore after they do this.”

Two weeks before her execution, Ms. Pike was isolated again, part of Tennessee’s new pre-execution protocol. She had been moved, and her things were in garbage bags. She had given up unpacking.

In Florida, Ms. Martinez and her husband have struggled with a surge of grief, scrounging for money to fund the drive to Nashville. Ms. Martinez has been enraged by the attention on Ms. Pike. To her, even in isolation, Ms. Pike has had access to comfort and support denied to her daughter.

“Nobody could ever, ever convince me she’s changed,” Ms. Martinez said.

Ten days before Ms. Pike’s scheduled execution, they celebrated what would have been Colleen’s 51st birthday.

Kitty Bennett contributed research.

Emily Cochrane is a national reporter for The Times covering the American South, based in Nashville.

Trump Administration Asks Justices to Allow It to Deny Hormones to Trans Inmates

The New York Times September 28, 2026

Supreme Court

Advertisement

Supported by

The Bureau of Prisons policy, which has been blocked by lower courts, would give transgender prisoners access to psychotherapy and antidepressants instead of certain gender-transition medical treatments.

By Ann E. Marimow

Ann E. Marimow covers the Supreme Court.

The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court on Monday to clear the way for federal prison officials to stop providing certain gender-transition medical treatments to transgender inmates.

Soon after returning to office, President Trump signed an executive order directing that imprisoned trans women be housed in men’s facilities. It also barred transgender inmates from receiving gender transition medical treatments for gender dysphoria — significant distress linked to a mismatch between a person’s birth sex and gender identity.

Lower courts, however, have blocked the policy and ruled that transgender inmates must continue to receive hormone therapy while a lawsuit over the executive order moves forward. The lawsuit was filed by three trans inmates on behalf of about 2,000 transgender individuals.

D. John Sauer, the solicitor general, on Monday asked the justices to intervene on an emergency basis, arguing that the government and the public were being harmed because the lower courts have blocked a policy that prison administrators have ”determined is necessary to maintain institutional security.”

The Supreme Court requested a response from lawyers for the trans prisoners by Oct. 8.

The prison policy is one of a series of actions by the administration limiting transgender rights. The president also directed government agencies to withdraw federal funding from schools that allow transgender athletes in girls’ and women’s sports. And the administration has asked the Supreme Court to allow the U. S. military to fully enforce its ban on transgender service members. That case remains pending.

The Supreme Court has in recent years dealt with several cases involving transgender individuals. In June, the court upheld two state laws barring the participation of transgender female athletes from girls’ and women’s sports teams. Last year, the court upheld a state law prohibiting some medical treatments for transgender youths, rejecting arguments that it violated the Constitution.

At the Bureau of Prisons, officials have taken the position that the benefits of hormone therapy are unclear for adults with gender dysphoria. The policy allows trans prisoners to receive psychotherapy and antidepressants but not hormone therapy or items like undergarments that match their identities.

Lawyers for transgender prisoners have said gender-transition treatment, which can include cross-sex hormones, social transition and in some cases surgery, is the only approach known to effectively treat gender dysphoria. The treatment has come under scrutiny for adolescents but has been accepted as effective for adults for several decades, and is supported by the major medical and mental health organizations in the United States.

In their suit, the trans inmates argue the administration’s policy violated their constitutional rights, including the Eighth Amendment’s protection against cruel and unusual punishment. They said the administration’s policy amounts to a denial of medically necessary care that has been prescribed by medical providers.

Judge Royce C. Lamberth of the District Court in Washington has issued several rulings halting the policy nationwide while litigation has continued. He said the Bureau of Prisons did not adequately “consider its own experience providing gender-affirming care under its prior policy.”

A divided panel of the U. S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit denied the government’s request to block the judge’s order, writing that prison officials had not adequately explained their security concerns about providing gender-transition care.

Amy Harmon contributed reporting.

Ann E. Marimow covers the Supreme Court for The Times from Washington.

Trump Sharply Scales Back Fuel Economy Rules for New Cars

The New York Times September 28, 2026

U. S. Economy

Advertisement

Supported by

The move marked the final step in the administration’s efforts to dismantle policies aimed at speeding the shift to electric vehicles.

By Brad Plumer and Maxine Joselow

Reporting from Washington

The Trump administration on Monday finalized its plan to significantly weaken fuel efficiency standards for automobiles, scaling back Biden-era rules meant to reduce gasoline consumption and speed the shift to electric vehicles.

Under the new rules from the Transportation Department, automakers will be required to achieve an average fuel efficiency of 34.9 miles per gallon for new cars and light trucks in model year 2031. That’s far below the standard of 50.4 miles per gallon set by the Biden administration.

President Trump portrayed the change as a way to lower car prices for consumers, as affordability has become a major issue in the coming midterm elections. He posted on social media over the weekend that the new rules marked a “BIG DAY FOR AMERICAN AUTO WORKERS AND CAR BUYERS.”

But critics said that less efficient vehicles could cost consumers more at the pump in the long run. U. S. gasoline prices have spiked because of the conflict in the Middle East, with the national average price for unleaded gas near $4.50 per gallon, up more than 40 percent since this time last year.

The new standards should be easy for automakers to meet, analysts said, and the agency’s own analysis suggests that new cars sold in model year 2024 already came close to meeting the new rules. Last year, Republicans in Congress also eliminated fines for any automakers that don’t meet the standards, saving them millions of dollars and making the new rules largely toothless.

Mr. Trump has sought to dismantle federal policies that had pushed automakers to manufacture more efficient gas vehicles and transition to battery-powered models. He has described those policies as an “E. V. mandate” and has argued that stringent regulations push up the price of new vehicles.

“Thanks to President Trump’s leadership, we have finally ended the illegal mandate that forced automakers to produce more expensive electric vehicles that American families didn’t want,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a statement.

The move marked the final step in a remarkable retreat from U. S. attempts to counter China’s dominance of electric vehicles.

In February, the Environmental Protection Agency ended all federal limits on planet-warming pollution from cars. Last year, Congress repealed tax credits of up to $7,500 for buyers of new electric cars and also blocked California from setting its own stricter limits on automobile pollution.

Opponents have called the moves shortsighted.

“For fifty years, fuel-economy standards have saved Americans money and cut pollution at the same time, creating cleaner air, lowering prices at the pump, and reducing our reliance on fossil fuels,” said Gina McCarthy, the climate adviser under President Joseph R. Biden Jr. “Rather than keeping the U. S. at the forefront of innovation and improving affordability, this administration has chosen to do the opposite.”

Many automakers had chafed under the Biden-era rules, saying that they would have been extremely challenging to meet and required a rapid shift toward electric vehicles. A leading industry group on Monday said it was still reviewing the final rule but offered tentative praise.

“The standards finalized under the previous administration effectively required a switchover to electric vehicles that was out of step with market realities and customer demand,” said John Bozzella, the chief executive of the Alliance for Automotive Innovation, a lobbying group for major carmakers. “Today’s final rule is an appropriate course correction.”

The announcement could further encourage U. S. carmakers to manufacture more big, gasoline-burning pickup trucks and sport utility vehicles, which are more profitable than traditional cars.

But that could threaten automakers’ competitiveness in the long run.

Electric sales are growing rapidly in the rest of the world, spurred by concerns about spiking oil and gasoline prices. U. S. carmakers that delay E. V. development could be at a significant disadvantage to foreign rivals in the coming years, analysts said. Last year, less than 10 percent of new cars sold in the United States were electric.

Source: IEA. Note: Electric category includes plug-in hybrids. Sales for 2026 are estimated.

“Many parts of the world are obviously adopting E. V. s much faster than the United States has, so where do U. S. automakers stand?” said Jessica Caldwell, the head of insights for the automotive website Edmunds. com. “They can’t exactly just turn their backs on the technology.”

The Transportation Department said that the looser standards would reduce the average cost of a new vehicle by $1,300 and save Americans $138 billion over the next five years.

Some economists have disputed those figures. A recent paper published in the journal Science argued that the administration’s calculations contained major inconsistencies, such as in its assumptions about how consumers value the benefits of saving fuel.

“If you do the analysis right, we found that revoking these standards does not save consumers money,” said Christopher Knittel, a professor of energy economics at M. I. T.

Congress created the mileage standards in 1975 in response to an oil embargo by Middle Eastern countries. Since then, automakers have steadily improved the distance that cars can travel on a tank of gas while expanding their electric and hybrid offerings.

Transportation is the country’s largest source of the greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide that are warming the planet. The Biden administration had ratcheted up the mileage standards as part of its sweeping strategy for tackling climate change.

But Mr. Trump, who has rejected efforts to address climate change, attacked E. V. s as part of his campaign to retake the White House.

His administration has also scrapped a companion rule that would have strictly limited carbon dioxide emissions from new cars and trucks. Those rules had been intended by the Biden administration to align with the fuel-economy standards.

Jack Ewing contributed reporting from New York.

Brad Plumer is a Times reporter who covers technology and policy efforts to address global warming.

Maxine Joselow covers climate change and the environment for The Times. Contact her securely on Signal: @MaxineJ.55

Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

The reception to Paul Verhoeven’s lurid 1995 melodrama starring Elizabeth Berkley, Kyle MacLachlan and Gina Gershon was humiliating, but it’s since become a thought-provoking camp favorite.

Illustration by Leesa Allmond; Videos via MGMCredit...

Supported by

By Maya Salam

Maya Salam believes the line between good entertainment and bad entertainment can be surprisingly flexible, and has enthusiastically debated this logic for years.

What’s a “good-bad” movie? It’s the kind of flick that might have you cackling, hollering or groaning, one that is not necessarily great cinema but is great fun. It’s highly watchable even though — or maybe because — it’s memorably ridiculous. And it always has at least one element that pushes it into absurd territory.

It didn’t take long for Elizabeth Berkley’s career to crater after “Showgirls” hit theaters in September 1995. Her agency immediately dropped her and potential opportunities shriveled.

Paul Verhoeven, the Dutch director known for pushing themes to cartoonish lengths in service of satire, felt remorse for the fallout. “If somebody has to be blamed, it should be me,” he said in 2015. “I asked Elizabeth to do all that.”

“All that” indeed. In this NC-17 film, Berkley stars as Nomi Malone, a young woman who yearns to dance under the glittering Las Vegas lights. But Nomi is not your typical starry-eyed dreamer.

She flings and flails her limbs in every direction. She thrashes like a fish out of water while giving a nude lap dance to Kyle MacLachlan’s character, an opportunistic bigwig. She licks a stripper pole.

The explicit, herky-jerky performance was particularly jarring right after Berkley’s fame-making run on the wholesome teen sitcom “Saved by the Bell.”

“It was really painful at the time,” Berkley said in 2021 of the backlash. “I was a very young woman.”

Over the last 30 years, though, “Showgirls” has done the almost impossible by becoming one of MGM’s best sellers, undergoing a critical re-evaluation and maintaining a legion of devotees.

“Tonight is like this magical full-circle moment,” Berkley said to a crowd of thousands at a 20th-anniversary screening in 2015. “I really do want you to know this movie is something I love, but I love it because you love it, too.”

What Makes It Good

Aside from the haywire overacting, “Showgirls” feels familiar at first: a tale about a fresh-faced ingénue who wants to make it big and the men who control all avenues to success. These men are surrounded by women we’re led to believe are one-dimensional bimbos competing mostly for their attention.

Eventually, a shift takes hold. These men, none of them redeemable, flatten into a single interchangeable sleazebag. Meanwhile, the portrayals of Nomi, Cristal (Gina Gershon) and Molly (Gina Ravera) deepen. Remarkably, the film passes the Bechdel test in spades.

“Showgirls” is also not sexy in the slightest, a main criticism initially but perhaps the entire point. That it was marketed to young men (ads promising a sexy romp were placed near box scores in newspaper sports sections) feels intentional, part prank and part lesson.

Some critics, spotting its subversive streak, have defended the movie along the way. In 1998, Jacques Rivette called “Showgirls” a great American film about surviving in a world of fools. In 2006, the critic Michael Atkinson said Verhoeven “may be the bravest and most assured satirist in Hollywood.” And a 2020 headline in The Guardian called the movie “a misunderstood gem.”

What Makes It Bad

Nomi’s evolution, and the film’s overall vibe shift, is hastened by the shocking sexual assault of her best friend, Molly, in a highly debated scene that seems to come out of nowhere. It was also not lost on many that Molly is a woman of color.

Jeffrey McHale, the director of the 2019 documentary “You Don’t Nomi,” called the scene unnecessary and “completely offensive.”

On a podcast this year, Gershon recalled butting heads with Verhoeven about it: “When I saw that rape scene, I’m like, ‘Are you insane? You have to take this scene out.’”

With the benefit of hindsight, though, she said she understands why Verhoeven held firm: “It’s the grossest thing in there, and the powerful men, they’re all protected,” Gershon said, which makes Nomi’s vengeance all the more significant.

What Makes It Good-Bad

By early 1996, The New York Times had already declared “Showgirls” “high camp.”

It quickly became a midnight-movie darling, especially among gay audiences, and MGM leaned into the hype, hiring drag performers for the first midnight shows. “There can be nothing more hilarious than getting drunk and watching ‘Showgirls,’” a special-events director in Manhattan said at the time. “We think the script must have been written by a drag queen.”

The script was actually written by Joe Eszterhas, and it’s packed with odd, infectious phrases that were absorbed into the pop lexicon like “Versayce,” Nomi’s pronunciation of Versace.

Part of the movie’s charm, Quentin Tarantino has said, is the seemingly incongruous sensibilities of its director and writer: “I think Paul Verhoeven was in on the joke and Joe Eszterhas was not.”

While Berkley’s big-screen career never quite rebounded, she’s found success in theater, television and advocacy, and is proud of the film’s enduring relevance. “It has been embraced and celebrated by cinephiles, by the L. G. B. T. Q. community — academics investigate this film and write about it,” she said last year. “It’s incredible that it, through the years, has found its way.”

Maya Salam is an editor and reporter, focusing primarily on pop culture across genres.

What Russians Who Lost Sons in Ukraine Think About the War Now

The New York Times September 28, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

The Russian region of North Ossetia has suffered a heavy toll, yet many accept the Kremlin’s line that the fighting must continue until victory is secured.

Oksana Abaeva and her husband, Khetag Zaseyev, at the grave of her son, Albert Abaev, in Vladikavkaz, the capital of the Russian region of North Ossetia. Credit...

Supported by

By Valerie Hopkins

Visuals by Nanna Heitmann

Reporting from Vladikavkaz, Russia

Russia’s war with Ukraine shows itself in many ways in North Ossetia, a remote mountainous region with a centuries-long history of furnishing soldiers for Moscow’s battles.

It can be seen in the martial songs now sung in schools. In a government stocked with veterans. In a habit of making patriotic comments for public consumption and then whispering true feelings. In the scarcity of men. And in the scale of the loss.

So many soldiers have returned from Ukraine in body bags that they are now being buried in a dedicated plot in Vladikavkaz, the regional capital. The new tombstones are ornamented with color photographs of the fallen, retouched and then baked in a furnace at 1,800 degrees Fahrenheit.

In the growing graveyard lies the son of Oksana Abaeva, 47, who founded an organization for women who have lost loved ones in the war. She reflects a region pulled between a deep pride in fighting for the motherland and an aching lament for the erasure of its young men.

Ms. Abaeva’s son Albert Abaev was part of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. He would call home when he could, she said. He never complained about the cold and the hunger in the miserable frontline conditions. He promised her he would come home.

Less than a month after the first missiles fell on Kyiv, her husband, Khetag R. Zaseyev, joined the Russian military, too.

“He couldn’t take it,” she said of his discomfort in sitting on the sidelines while Albert, the stepson he had raised, was fighting. “He hoped to find Albert, or at least hug him, because we all understood what it was like where he was.”

On May 17, 2022, men in uniform knocked on her door, saying that Albert, 20, had been killed. Her husband was on the front lines. When they spoke, she could hear the roar of artillery shells for the first time.

Granted leave, Mr. Zaseyev journeyed alone through Ukraine — on foot, motorcycle and bicycle — until he reached the Russian military morgue in Rostov-on-Don. He collected Albert’s body and returned with it to Vladikavkaz.

“We have all endured such grief, of course. We are no longer the same as we were,” Ms. Abaeva said. “Over these four years, our life has been turned upside down into a ‘before’ and ‘after.’”

She wants the war to be over. But not yet.

President Vladimir V. Putin has told Russians for years that they are in a fight for survival against a fascist regime in Ukraine and against Kyiv’s European masters. The propaganda has set the foundation for a normalization of war as a permanent feature of Russian life. While fatigue is rising as Ukrainian strikes exact a growing economic toll, the Kremlin has used the attacks as a rallying cry for Russians to remain united behind Mr. Putin and the military.

Russia should stop fighting, Ms. Abaeva said, only once what she called the Nazis in Ukraine are vanquished.

“I do not wish for any mother to bury her child, neither in Ukraine nor here,” she said. “I want peace. I want there to be no Nazism.”

The photographer Nanna Heitmann and I spent a week in North Ossetia to understand how deeply the war had penetrated society there.

A majority-Orthodox Christian region of 680,000 people abutted by predominantly Muslim areas, Ossetia has a proud warrior culture dating to ancient times.

Everyone we spoke with had a family member or a close friend who had fought in Ukraine or died there. Most had more than one.

That is reflected in a death toll that is about a third higher than the national average, according to a report by a banned human rights watchdog, Memorial, using information collected from newspapers and social networks. Impoverished regions like North Ossetia have disproportionately supplied soldiers for the Russian military, keeping big cities insulated from the war.

The Ossetians we met encapsulated the conflict’s complexities. One of them was Anatoly Betruzov, a 65-year-old veteran of three wars. The first was in Afghanistan, the last in the Donbas region of Ukraine, where his leg was permanently injured in 2015, a year after Russia began to stir up conflict there.

Even as he parroted the Kremlin line about Nazis in Ukraine, he said there was “no justice” in the current war, with people dying “who have nothing to do with it.” He said he had forbidden his 33-year-old nephew to go to Ukraine. The nephew went anyway, called by a sense of duty, Mr. Betruzov said, and was now dead.

We met Zelimkhan Kozaev, director of the region’s traditional dance ensemble, which toured across Europe even during the Cold War but now finds itself ostracized overseas as the Ukraine invasion has made Russia a pariah on much of the continent.

Sitting in his office under a portrait of a young Mr. Putin, Mr. Kozaev did not overtly bemoan the isolation or criticize the war. But he said he was not encouraging the men in his troupe to fight. “Not everyone has to run around with machine guns,” Mr. Kozaev said.

We also spoke with Aza Biragova, who works in human resources for a home-and-garden chain. She told us how the war had remade the region’s economics and civilian life.

In 2019, she helped open a store in North Ossetia. It once employed about 80 men. In September 2022, when Moscow carried out a mobilization for the war, the company received large numbers of draft summonses. Other men decided on their own to go.

She and her colleagues decided to decrease the size of their team to 60, because they did not think they could find enough workers and because the scarcity of men had driven up salaries. Eventually, she said, “everyone started hiring women.”

One person who declined to meet with us was the head of the region, Sergey Menyaylo. He instead sent a member of his press team, Batraz Ilaev, a former journalist who collected humanitarian aid for troops before becoming a soldier himself.

Mr. Ilaev is one of many Ossetians who have entered government service after fighting in Ukraine, a trend that Mr. Putin has promoted nationwide and was reflected in parliamentary elections this month.

Over pots of fruit tea, Mr. Ilaev described new housing developments and employment efforts for veterans. He told of a plan to hire a veteran in every school to serve as an adviser on “patriotic education.”

It’s all part of a Kremlin campaign to militarize society now and for generations to come.

Many of those we met with spoke of the need to defend Russia in a hostile world. That worldview was shaped in part by a terrorist attack that took place two decades ago at School No. 1 in Beslan, 30 minutes from Vladikavkaz.

On Sept. 3, 2004, after a three-day standoff with armed militants linked to an insurgency in neighboring Chechnya, Russian special forces stormed the school. By the time the siege was over, 334 hostages were dead, 186 of them children. Mr. Putin, furious that Western governments were fighting in Iraq and Afghanistan while condemning his war against Chechen separatists, accused the West of trying to bring Russia down.

I heard echoes of that when I spoke to Timur S. Adyrkhaev, 53, who was among those who carried hostages out of the school and is now a member of North Ossetia’s Parliament. He said that the current war was a profound “tragedy” but that the conflict was a historically inevitable outcome of Western powers’ use of Ukraine to encroach on Russia.

School No. 1 is now a heart-wrenching museum. A new building with the same name was built across the street. When we visited, younger students were assembling for a patriotic concert. A song performed by fifth graders had three soloists, each one representing a generation of soldiers. It was a march, with the children shouting the minor-key harmonies over a synth-pop track.

The refrain went:

A fallen soldier protects his homeland, The Russian soldier protects you and me.

The school opens its doors to veterans who deliver lectures to students. Erik G. Bagaev, a volunteer with a group that helps the families of killed or disabled veterans, said that members emphasized “love for the homeland” when addressing children.

“If, for example, in American comics the heroes are Batman and Spider-Man, we want our kids to view the soldiers the same way,” Mr. Bagaev said.

Boxes of supplies in his organization’s storage room were heaped with letters from schoolchildren. I read a few, in loopy cursive. “I want to say ‘Thank you’ for giving your life for us,” said one. “I believe in you!”

We returned to the cemetery in Vladikavkaz on a Saturday, when Ms. Abaeva gathered with a dozen other women to recite a panihida, a Russian Orthodox prayer for the departed.

As we spoke with a priest, some of the women began arguing, agitated by the presence of foreign journalists, whom Russian media has taught citizens to mistrust.

“We do not have a war in this country, there is no war!” said Marina M. Danilova, who was wearing an old-fashioned tippet and veil with a red cross.

“We have a special military operation,” she continued, using the Kremlin’s euphemism for the war. The conflict in Iran, which President Trump had started that morning, using a euphemism similar to the Kremlin’s, was a “real war,” Ms. Danilova said.

Her comments were met with murmurs of disagreement.

“For some, it is not a war. For us, it is a war,” said another woman, whose son was a paratrooper based in Pskov, a region in western Russia.

“Everyone expresses their condolences, they pity us, but when we close the door, everyone lives with their own grief,” added the woman, whose name is being withheld to protect her from possible repercussions with the authorities. “Understood? Let them call it whatever they want.”

The women went their separate ways. As they departed, shots rang out from the far end of the cemetery, where the fresh graves lie, adorned not yet with tombstones, but with flags that whip in the wind.

It was a military honor guard. Another funeral.

Ms. Abaeva went to Albert’s grave. Her husband and her son David, 8, helped as she patted the plastic wreaths.

As I watched David, I remembered something she had told me: “He already says, ‘I will also go to war, and I will defend our people.’”

Milana Mazaeva, Oleg Matsnev and Alina Lobzina contributed reporting.

Valerie Hopkins covers the war in Ukraine and how the conflict is changing Russia, Ukraine, Europe and the United States. She is based in Moscow.

A torch bearer for the great 19th-century tradition of social realism, she’s become one of the most important novelists of her generation.

Credit... Ruvén Afanador for The New York Times

Supported by

By Marcela Valdes

“Smell that?” The novelist Min Jin Lee closed her eyes and drew in a breath. Garlic, ginger, turmeric, old floor polish, stale sweat, rat poison, glass cleaner, oregano. “It doesn’t smell like that on the Upper East Side,” she said with a laugh.

We were standing in the foyer of the apartment building on Van Kleeck Street, in Queens, where Lee lived with her parents and two sisters after they arrived from Korea in 1976. Everything looked the same: the dull metal mailboxes, the checkered linoleum in the hallway, the dusty glass wall facing the street. Only the names marking the buzzers had changed. In Lee’s childhood, they were mostly Irish, Greek and Eastern European. Now they were mostly Latino, Korean and Chinese.

The first thing that struck Lee about her new home was its ugliness. In Seoul, her mother kept their home impeccable. In Queens, their first rental was a one-bedroom furnished with grimy rugs, roaches and mice. Even at 7 years old, she understood that her family’s move to New York meant that they’d come down in the world.

In Seoul, they lived in a comfortable house in a middle-class neighborhood. Her father worked as a marketing executive. Her mother, who had studied music at Korea’s prestigious Yonsei University, taught children piano. But her father, who lost his home and most of his family as a teenager during the Korean War of the 1950s, feared that the violence of the Vietnam War might spread to South Korea and hurt his children. A relative in New York sponsored the family for visas, and they decamped for America, where her parents eventually found work in a wholesale jewelry shop in Midtown Manhattan. Every morning except Sunday they left the apartment at 6 to catch the subway, while the girls readied themselves for school alone.

For Lee, the move proved a social nightmare. In Korea, she’d been a peaceful introvert, the kind of child who often sat alone daydreaming. In America, she became a target. Tall, shy, not yet fluent in English, dressed in hand-me-downs, she was bullied ruthlessly for five years, starting in second grade.

“I was like a mark,” Lee recalled. “It was just like, You want to pick the big, goofy, quiet one.” Terrified, she turned nearly mute in public.

At home, though she was loved, she also felt there was something wrong with her. Her two sisters immediately tested into top academic classes, while she was tracked into the lowest classes for two years. Her father nicknamed her Turtle.

She had one superpower. At the age of 3, Lee taught herself to read. And in Queens, she discovered America’s great, humble treasure: the public library system. For an immigrant girl with no money, nowhere to go and no friends besides her sisters, the existence of a place that would lend her as many books as she wanted — for free! — was paradise. She read endlessly, rolling volumes home in a collapsible shopping cart. “A book only gives,” she explained to me. As a girl reading, she felt “infinite.” She became especially well versed in the classics of American and European literature, because those were the books the librarians recommended.

Now 57, Lee is considered one of the most important novelists of her generation — and a torch bearer for the great 19th-century tradition of social realism. Like George Eliot, she has a gift for combining intimate character portraits with sweeping macroeconomic narratives. Like Charles Dickens, she seems determined to expose the indignities of poverty and the resilience needed to survive them.

But even as she inherited her tools from these social realists, she uses them in modern ways to chronicle the lives of Koreans around the world. She set her first novel, “Free Food for Millionaires” (2007), among the Korean diaspora in New York City. The book’s central character, Casey Han, lives on Van Kleeck Street, until she escapes to Princeton and Manhattan. Lee’s second novel, “Pachinko” (2017), is a saga about four generations of Koreans. Set in colonial and post-colonial Japan, the novel is grounded in interviews that Lee conducted with elderly Koreans around Osaka and Tokyo. For her, “Pachinko” was a passion project; she never believed that it would find a big readership. After it was published, however, the novel became a global best seller and a critical sensation. In 2024, The New York Times Book Review ranked “Pachinko” No. 15 on its “100 Best Books of the 21st Century.”

“The fact that I can make that interesting to a general audience is really just a testament to what all those dead writers have taught me,” Lee told me. Her third novel, “American Hagwon,” debuted this month. Set in Korea, Australia and California during the years surrounding the Asian financial crisis of 1997, it contains more than a dozen characters from several interconnected families. The word “hagwon” means “private tutoring center” in Korean, and the novel examines how an unbridled obsession with gaining admission to name-brand universities may damage both parents and children. Among the book’s characters are parents who erase their savings paying for hagwons, teachers who coach SAT prep at hagwons and a young girl whose parents abandon her in California with the expectation that she will study hard, get accepted to U. C. L. A. and become a doctor — so that she can save her family in Korea from poverty.

For Lee, fiction has always been a way to wrestle with big social and historical dilemmas. Unlike many novelists, she begins her books with ideas and issues, not characters and scenes. Her chosen medium — the class-crossing realist narrative — has a long history as a weapon of social critique. Edith Wharton used it to savage the hypocrisies of old-money New York. Upton Sinclair used it to provoke reform in the slaughterhouses of Chicago. In “American Hagwon,” Lee herself is trying to shift the way we understand the purpose of higher education and to demonstrate how seemingly crazy behavior, like dropping off a 9-year-old in a foreign country, may be driven by a tremendous sense of fear and economic impotence.

When I asked Lee about the possibility of writing as a form of self-expression, she winced. “That’s not even interesting to me,” she said. “It sounds sort of corny, but if I didn’t think that these stories had value to my reader, I would never share it. Never.”

“History has failed us, but no matter.” The first line of “Pachinko” is a declaration of resilience and defiance, the pronouncement of someone who knows the score yet still forges ahead. The sentence is often interpreted as an indictment of the way historians tend to ignore the less-documented lives of the poor and the defeated. It may also be read as a wry summary of Lee’s own journey to “Pachinko.”

In college, she never planned on becoming a novelist. Her great intellectual romance, discovered at the Bronx High School of Science, was with history. For her, history was a way of trying to understand how the world worked, and how the circumstances of the present day were created by decisions made in the past. At Yale, she was mesmerized by the lectures given in the department’s survey courses, and she fantasized about getting a doctorate in the subject.

Inspired by classes that she took in African American studies and women’s studies, Lee spearheaded a campaign to persuade Yale to offer courses in Korean language and history. She had the ingenious idea of asking students to petition their parents for the changes rather than plead with the administration directly. One of these parents, she said, ultimately raised $100,000 for a pilot program. More than 20 years later, Yale still teaches Korean language as a result of these efforts.

Despite this triumph, Lee’s affair with history ended badly. During her junior year, the university finally offered the class on Korean history that she’d longed for. But when the professor returned her midterm exam, she felt socked. Lee’s blue book, she told me, contained no guiding corrections or annotations. On its last page, there was only one handwritten line — “Ah, me, what’s to say?” — next to the letter F.

Most of the students crying near her in class that day were Asian. So Lee asked the professor, a white man who specialized in Japanese history, for a demographic breakdown of the grades. When he presented it at the following class, it was clear that most of the students he’d failed were, in fact, Asian. The reason, he said, was that they were STEM majors. Outraged by his assumptions, Lee published an article in a campus newspaper detailing the incident. It raised a furor at Yale. A white student labeled her a politically correct “terrorist.” After that, she told me, students and professors in the history department regarded her as a troublemaker.

“I think my heartbreak was proportionate with how much I really wanted the class, which sounds so dorky,” Lee told me. She wasn’t worried about her grades. What she wanted was to be treated with respect. She passed the class, but after the scandal she couldn’t stomach approaching any professor in the department for a recommendation to a doctoral program.

Instead, Lee pivoted to a practical future: She went to law school at Georgetown. There she fell in love with a bank salesman, Christopher Duffy. For a year, she hid the relationship from her parents because Duffy is half-Japanese. “If you marry him, you are not my daughter,” her father said, when she told him that they were engaged. But Duffy was the kindest man that Lee had ever met, and ultimately he won over her father as well.

Lee married Duffy after her graduation and began working as a corporate lawyer in Manhattan, specializing in mergers and acquisitions. As a junior member of a firm, she read thousands of pre-existing contracts, combing them for liabilities that might hurt clients after they closed a deal. “I was really good at this,” she said, “because once you tell me to turn every page, I’m like, Yes, I’ll turn every page.” She wore suits, earned more than $80,000 a year and worked seven days a week. In theory, she was living the American dream. In practice, she was growing seriously ill.

In high school, after donating blood, Lee learned that she was an inactive chronic carrier for the liver disease hepatitis B. Though she never smoked or drank alcohol, the condition flared acutely during her sophomore year of college. A doctor at Yale New Haven Hospital told her that she would probably develop liver cancer by her early 30s. With luck, he said, she might get a transplant and be cured. After that consult, Lee feared that she might die young. Then, at 26, the long hours of corporate law were leaving her wrecked with exhaustion. She decided that she’d rather try writing fiction.

At Yale, Lee had won two literary prizes: one for short fiction, the other for an essay. When she initially submitted the same essay to a history professor, he gave it a C and suggested that she needed remedial English tutoring. But the literary contests were hosted by the university’s English department, which scrubbed students’ names from their entries before judging. Her wins surprised her and came with such ease that they misled her into believing that writing a great novel would be less challenging than practicing law. She thought it might take her a year to finish a book and start earning roughly the same as she had reading contracts. Instead, completing the manuscript for “Free Food for Millionaires” took 11 years.

During that time, Lee’s writing earned her approximately nothing. She and Duffy, meanwhile, accumulated the joyous responsibility of caring for their first child and the unexpected necessity of supporting his parents through catastrophic debt. Her acute hepatitis recurred, making her wrists so weak that she had trouble lifting coffee cups. In a prologue to the 10th-anniversary edition of “Free Food for Millionaires,” she remembers her apprenticeship as an extended humiliation. “It is never a financially prudent idea to be a fiction writer,” she explains. “After six years, I had not yet written a published novel, and I was broke from the choices I had made.”

Because she was young and liver transplants were hard to obtain, a gastroenterologist suggested that she try an experimental drug: Interferon alfa. The treatment made her hair fall out and provoked unpredictable vomiting and diarrhea. But less than a year after starting it, she was miraculously cured.

At the same time, she kept trying to compose the kind of juicy, realist book that enthralled her as a child. Lee often names “dead writers” as her teachers, including Leo Tolstoy, George Eliot, Edith Wharton, the Bröntes, Willa Cather, F. Scott Fitzgerald and James Baldwin. She read, reread and reverse-engineered their books. But in her prologue to “Free Food for Millionaires,” Lee recognizes that a host of contemporary authors taught her, as well. She took classes at the Asian American Writers’ Workshop and the 92nd Street Y in New York City, and participated in a private workshop with several aspiring writers, including the novelist Sharon Pomerantz, who remains a close friend. “You could look back on it with nostalgia,” Pomerantz said of this period in their lives, “but I think we were both filled with terror.”

From her legal experience, Lee carried over two unfashionable traits. The first was an attitude of advocacy. “This is the one part about being a lawyer I didn’t mind,” she told me. “I was arguing for somebody else.” All her novels are composed in defense of the overlooked, the tormented, the powerless. Though she published “Pachinko” a decade after “Free Food for Millionaires,” she worked on both books simultaneously. In one, Lee exposed the pressures and hypocrisies that Korean professionals faced in New York City. In the other, she laid bare an entire history of discrimination against Koreans in Japan. She felt as if she needed to write these stories for the sake of other Koreans, and this sense of responsibility kept her researching and revising even when the tasks she set for herself seemed absurdly hard.

“I would love to have that sort of freedom of saying, Oh, I don’t care what I stand for, but whether I like it or not, I do represent a group,” she said. “People still see you as the envelope that you’re in, whether you like it or not.”

The other practice Lee carried over from her legal work was due diligence. Her research for every novel involves reading dozens of books, interviewing scores of people and scouting opportunities for anthropological observation and immersion. To build the character Casey Han in “Free Food for Millionaires,” Lee took a class in hat making. To add nuance to the character who marries Casey’s closest friend, Lee interviewed Koreans who worked on Wall Street.

For “American Hagwon,” Lee brought this process to a new level. Not only did she read scholarly works, she also interviewed nearly 100 college students of Korean descent and attended parts of the Varsity Blues trial about bribery in college admissions and of the federal trial leading to the Supreme Court case about affirmative action at Harvard. She visited hagwons in Korea, Singapore, Hong Kong, Taiwan, Japan, Australia, New Jersey, California and Massachusetts, interviewing students, parents and teachers.

When Lee’s not traveling, she does most of her work on the sunny top floor of a Harlem brownstone that she and Duffy purchased in 2012. When I visited, her office was crowded with photographs, awards, maps, mementos and two computers: one for writing, one for emails. Along one wall, books were sorted into verticals. One set of floor-to-ceiling shelves was filled with volumes she’d read while researching “Pachinko.” Another held books related to “American Hagwon.”

“I wish I could be more efficient,” Lee said, lamenting that her third novel had taken nine years to complete. Behind her, I could see the signs she’d put in her office to encourage herself along the way. One read: “Time Is Your Friend.” It was something her old therapist once said that made her weep. Even after her liver had been saved, Lee couldn’t shake the feeling of imminent mortality.

I remember reading “Middlemarch” when I was in my 20s and wanting to hurl it against a wall. The novel was a masterpiece, I knew, but the premise of its central plot — that the happiness of a woman depended on serving the right husband — irritated my young, single heart. When people discuss Lee’s novels, they often kneel before the dead social realists. But by and large, those authors no longer speak to the values and realities of our age. What makes Lee’s work so satisfying is its anachronism. She honed a Victorian technique and applies it with the sensibilities of a woman who loves reading bell hooks.

Take, for example, Lee’s attitude toward the marriage plot, a favorite trope of the 19th century. Though Lee’s novels always contain romance, they never revolve around marriage. Instead her suspense hangs on questions of economic survival and individual self-actualization. The challenge for Lee’s characters is that, like real people, they often need many things at once: food, respect, shelter and love. Chapter by chapter, these dilemmas get dramatized through nuclear families. How will a son weigh his needs against his mother’s? Will a daughter sacrifice her dreams for the sake of her family? What more will parents endure to feed their children?

In “Pachinko” and “American Hagwon,” these family dramas get woven into examinations of the harms inflicted by bigger systems and calamities. First, colonialism and World War II. Now, neoliberalism and the currency crisis of 1997. In each case, it’s like watching the characters get hit by a natural disaster. The tsunami is upon them. It’s not their fault; yet they must swim or drown.

Lee operates so deftly that casual readers may not notice the architecture for these ideas being erected as they read. Consider a seven-page chapter that Lee delivers early in “American Hagwon” which establishes the novel’s theme while linking together a dozen characters.

The setting is an influential Presbyterian megachurch in Seoul’s fashionable Gangnam neighborhood. Its main pastor, an affable, 50-something man, is preaching on the sin of idolatry. His sermon opens with Leviticus: the Israelites who disobeyed God by sacrificing their children to a pagan deity. “What do you love more than your child?” the pastor asks his rich congregants. “What do you love more than God?”

His questions resonate throughout “American Hagwon,” but in this chapter, Lee treats them lightly, directing our attention mostly away from the pulpit and toward the pews.

A pair of sisters, Helen and Sonya, sit near each other with their two husbands, their five children and a father-in-law. Lee establishes their back story in two tight paragraphs. As girls, they “lived at subsistence level.” Their parents were gamblers, and they survived on charity from the Catholic Church. After they graduated from a prestigious women’s college, the gorgeous Sonya went to work for a real estate baron, who married her to his nephew. At the church, Sonya sports an elegant cashmere suit with “a thick rope of rare Tahitian pearls.” Helen wears a fancy wool suit that’s getting a little tight; Sonya bought it for her years earlier. Another woman, Nari, appears near the end of the chapter with her daughter. When Nari stands next to the sisters, she realizes that her expensive red dress with “dramatic black sequin flowers” looks tacky in church. She introduces Helen to the idea of sending her children to a budget-breaking hagwon.

These scenes don’t feel especially significant the first time you read them. But within a few hundred pages, two of these characters will be broke and working at a fried-fish joint in California. Another pair will be entangled in an eye-popping affair. Two acquaintances will have turned into best friends. And the six children will have attended five different universities on three different continents. One of them will drop out.

These are the techniques that Lee gleaned from the old social realists: intricately braided story lines, characters who cross social classes, an emphasis on plots that expose true morals. Many also deployed a nearly invisible third-person narrator. In “American Hagwon,” this device is so neutral as to be disconcerting. Flaubert eyed his characters — even those based on himself — with sly condescension. Dickens regarded his with sticky sentimentality. Lee’s vision is like bright, afternoon light; it casts no shadows. The rhythm of her sentences is conversational, and their diction is deliberately plain, barely adorned. It’s as if she wants to make reading her long, complicated novel as easy as possible, knowing that its most moving effects are felt not in the paragraphs but across the arc of chapters.

In college, Lee spent her most meaningful hours hanging out in the basement of Durfee Hall, where students of color held gatherings at the women’s center. The legacy of those sustaining female friendships appears in her work, where women are often rescued from hardship and despair by other women. In this sense, Lee’s books have more in common with Elena Ferrante’s Neapolitan novels than with anything by Eliot or Wharton.

“There’s a lot of different ways to circumvent patriarchy, because it’s such a heavy machinery,” Lee told me. “Whatever oppressive system you have, we get around it through other interpersonal relationships.”

Lee’s next novel is likely to push this theme even further. In our conversations, she referred to it as her “Marshall Plan book.” It would explore, she said, how the post-World War II rise of South Korea in the 1960s was underwritten by remittances sent home by Koreans living abroad, including culture-crossing wives. “When we think about all the glamour and beauty of South Korea today, we don’t think about all the bar girls who married G. I. s, who lived in Texas, and people called them hookers,” Lee said. “But if it weren’t for them, they wouldn’t have sponsored citizenship for their cousins and their brothers and sent money back for their education.”

It was hard for Lee to think about these women because it was so upsetting how they were mistreated. They sacrificed so much and, in return, they were slurred by other Koreans. It was too outrageous. She’d already begun filling a set of floor-to-ceiling shelves in her office with volumes of research.

One afternoon, Lee and I stood on Queens Boulevard staring at the Gothic face of the First Presbyterian Church of Newtown in Elmhurst. “This is the church I grew up in,” Lee said. “I remember thinking it was so much bigger.”

The bell tower seemed to waver in the July heat. In front, a wrought-iron gate was padlocked but a side door was cracked open. We slipped in.

“Nothing has changed,” Lee said, as she took a seat. Rib-like ceiling trusses graced a soaring ceiling; the stained-glass windows shimmered. The nave held no more than 20 pews. It smelled of wood polish and old velvet.

You could call this sanctuary Lee’s most important school. Together with her family, she attended services and youth groups, ate coffee cake and doughnut holes. Back then, the congregation was mostly Anglo American, but at Sunday school, unlike elementary school, people were nice to her.

Churches have always played a central function in Lee’s fiction. Her halls of worship allow characters to swap information, forge friendships, rustle up business, preserve their traditions and repair the damage done to their dignity by the turbulence of emigration. But sitting next her in the silence of First Presbyterian — seeing how her shoulders relaxed and her nervous energy dissipated as she stared at the pulpit and the lilac-colored organ chamber — I realized that underneath all her anthropological accuracy lay genuine faith.

“You believe it all, right?” I asked. “Heaven. Hell. Souls.”

“Yeah, I do,” she answered softly, adding a moment later: “It makes things harder and easier.”

Life is easier with faith, she explained in a whisper, because if you truly believe in the gospel, then you understand that you’re already saved. “It’s like: ‘It’s done. So you’re good.’” But then, she added, if you sincerely believe that you’re saved, then why aren’t you doing all the good that you can as a saved person in this world?

“It means this responsibility. That’s why it’s so hard, but at the same time it’s so easy,” she said. “It’s actually walking as if you are fully loved.”

“By God?”

“Yeah, by God.” She glanced at my face, raised her eyebrows and smiled. “I know. I can see why people don’t believe it.”

I had known for a long time that Lee reads the Bible every morning before she writes — a habit inspired by Willa Cather — but in other interviews she’d explained it as an interest in biblical sentence structure and tone.

“That’s how it began,” Lee clarified now, suggesting that over time the purpose changed.

In America, there’s a tendency to see nonwhite novelists as ethnographers, and to overlook the more philosophical ambitions of their work. Yet Lee, like many of the 19th-century novelists, is also a moralist, and to think of her only as a Korean chronicler of the Korean diaspora is to misread her deeper project. “American Hagwon” contains clear indictments of education and materialism in America and Korea. Those bold plot lines, however, also lure readers into a more subtle consideration of the place that power, status, love, sacrifice, God and family hold in modern society. I had been puzzled at Lee’s home in Harlem when she told me that what she wanted to communicate to readers in her new novel was “the love that you need to feel a sense of sacrifice.”

Sitting in the pew with her in Queens, it clicked into place. Sacrifice has been a concern in all of Lee’s fiction. Some of her characters rebel against the expectation of it. Others are destroyed by it. A few find their purpose through grueling acts of selflessness. Lee told me that she thought about sacrifice more while writing “American Hagwon” than she had with any other book. All its most appealing characters forsake some desire or ambition for those they love. Its end hardly makes sense without the concepts of sacrifice and grace.

“Sacrifice always gets a bad rap, and it isn’t always bad,” Lee said to me in Queens. Her first novel suggests that children may ditch their parents’ expectations and pursue their own dreams. But that book was set in a Wall Street boom. The heroes of “American Hagwon” must survive a global meltdown. To carry their families through calamity, they shed pride and personal ambition.

“A man with your education should not be in the kitchen frying shrimp and making fish sandwiches,” one character scolds another. “Do you know how terrible you can smell?” Yet the father insists on taking the job. The next day he puts on the apron, the hairnet, the knee-high rubber boots, and starts work without complaint. There’s no time for self-pity. He has children to feed and rent to pay.

Marcela Valdes is a staff writer who has been covering immigration issues for more than a decade.

Marcela Valdes is a staff writer for The New York Times Magazine, writing primarily about Latino and Latin American politics and culture.

Could Homeownership Reverse the Decline in Birthrates?

The New York Times September 28, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Researchers looked back at the baby-boom era and found that federal mortgage programs played a part in the country’s population upswing after World War II.

By Sabrina Tavernise

Puzzling over the reasons for today’s baby bust, a pair of economists went back to the last baby boom for answers.

What they found sheds new light on how personal finances affect the decision to have children: Homeownership increases the birth rate.

Experts have long been skeptical that the two-decade decline in the birthrate was related to people’s pocketbooks. They reason that as the birthrate has been falling, household income has been rising and poorer women have been more likely to have more children than richer women.

But Melissa S. Kearney, an economics professor at the University of Notre Dame, and Lisa J. Dettling, an economist at the Federal Reserve Board, found an economic connection that was less about price and more about ownership.

The finding, published in its final version by the National Bureau of Economic Research in September, offers new insights into what policies could actually raise the birthrate, which has hit historic lows around the world. Governments have tried multiple strategies, including tax credits, subsidized child care and paid maternity leave, to encourage people to have more children, but nothing has made much of a difference.

Dr. Kearney and Dr. Dettling found a policy that did: government-backed home mortgages, mostly issued under the postwar G. I. Bill.

“This mortgage program was not meant as a pronatalist policy, but it seems to have had that effect,” Dr. Kearney said.

The finding comes as the cost of living has taken center stage in midterm election campaigns. Housing in particular has felt increasingly out of reach for younger Americans: The median age of first-time home buyers rose to 40 in 2025, a historic high. Last week, mortgage rates jumped to 7 percent, the highest since January 2025, raising the hurdle to home buying even higher.

The baby boom began in 1946, after the Allied victory in World War II. By 1957, the total fertility rate had risen by about 30 percent, reaching 3.7 children per woman, a modern high.

Researchers over decades have tried to explain that burst of fertility. Hypotheses included the economic security that families felt in contrast to the war years and the sharp drop in health risks during pregnancy.

But Dr. Kearney and Dr. Dettling wanted to look for new clues. They decided to examine homeownership, which also expanded during that time. The G. I. Bill in particular gave millions of returning soldiers the ability to buy houses with low or no down payments.

That policy was transformational, helping to build the American middle class. Young families, in particular, benefited: Among Americans of childbearing age, homeownership rose to 50 percent in 1960, from 20 percent in 1940.

But how could economists figure out if rising homeownership had fueled the baby boom? They discovered that the Federal Reserve held a trove of data: thousands of pages of mortgage records.

Undergraduate research assistants digitized them over two years. The researchers then linked them with demographic data from each state to test if there were any effect.

“We kept cutting the data and looking at it,” Dr. Kearney said. “It kept lining up.”

The result was startling: For every 1,000 new mortgages issued through the government programs, there were about 300 additional births the following year.

The mortgages were not the only driver, nor were they predictive for everybody: Black women, whose families were unfairly shut out of the postwar mortgage program, also had increases in childbearing.

The findings also help explain a related shift in the demographics of the era, Dr. Kearney said. Women married younger, and started to have children earlier than previous generations. They also went on to have larger families.

She emphasized that the effect of the government programs on births was not related to housing costs, but to homeownership. Having your name on a deed represents a certain kind of emotional and financial security, one that can create confidence in the future. Women today often say they want that before having children.

Other researchers who looked at the study said it was sound, but that it was historical.

“The empirical work seems pretty strong and they find a pretty good-sized effect,” said Phillip Levine, an economics professor at Wellesley College who has written papers with Dr. Kearney but was not involved in this one.

But, he added, it is not clear how much the past can be applied to the present. “Does that mean that we would get the same result today? We don’t know.”

Dr. Kearney said the findings are relevant today, but the context is different. Making it easier for young families to get a mortgage could still spur earlier and more childbearing. But such a policy today could also push up home prices, given that today’s supply of housing is far more restricted, compared to the mid-20th century when the suburbs were forming. That, she said, is the challenge for policymakers.

Sabrina Tavernise is a writer-at-large for The Times, focused on political life in America and how Americans see the changes in Washington.
